        context of the assessment of the Transaction, Lufthansa  itself prepared  its own
         regression modelling showing that the number of competitors active on a route is an
        important factor for prices: having fewer competitors active on a route is associated
        with higher  prices.600 Also, during  the Commission's  investigation  the  Parties
        submitted a supplementary cross-sectional regression analysis to support the their
        claim that Ryanair exerts significant competitive pressure on Lufthansa on routes
       where Ryanair  is present,601 and that ITA does not exert the same competitive
         pressure on routes where ITA is present.602 While these various regression analyses
          differ in some of their technical and specification details, their results consistently
         point towards similar conclusions. Namely, all these regression models show that, on
         the relevant airline markets, competition matters, and having fewer competitors on a
        given route is associated with higher prices. In this general sense, the quantitative
        evidence on file supports the rest of the evidence gathered and assessed during the
         investigation.
(491)   Regression  analysis  is  a  statistical  tool commonly  used  in  economics  for
        understanding the relationship between two or more variables. In this case, the main
         variables are on the one hand Lufthansa’s prices, and on the other hand the number
         of competitors. To shed light on the relationship between these two variables, the
         analysis has to control for the role played by other variables, for example demand
       and supply factors that can also influence Lufthansa’s prices on a route.
(492)   The Commission  applied a methodology commonly known  as  ‘fixed  effects’
         regressions to a panel of data that allows to isolate the factors that influence
        Lufthansa’s prices. The fixed effects methodology takes account of important but
        unobserved (or unmeasured) effects on price that do not vary over time on any given
         route or that vary over time but are the same across all routes. In addition, further
         control variables take account of important observed effects that may vary over time
       on a given route. As a result, the estimated effects will capture changes in prices on a
         route when changes in competition occur on that route (as opposed to simply
       comparing prices across routes where competition may differ).
(493)   The data and analysis can then show whether Lufthansa offers lower prices on
        average on a route when there is more competition compared to when there are less
         operators. That  is, the regression models and the data give rise to the testable
        hypothesis that other operators’ presence is associated with a statistically603 and
        economically significant reduction in Lufthansa’s prices in the various routes where
        they overlap.
(494)   The results of the regression analysis for short-haul routes suggest that (i) increased
        competition on a route  is associated with lower average Lufthansa prices; and
            (ii) ITA’s presence on a route is associated with lower average Lufthansa prices.
       These results indicate that a reduction in the number of competitors active on a route
           is likely to increase prices.

9.     COMPETITIVE ASSESSMENT – HORIZONTAL OVERLAPS ON SHORT-HAUL ROUTES
9.1.   Common considerations on horizontal overlaps on short-haul routes
9.1.1.   Competitive landscape
9.1.1.1. Actual Competition
(510)   The direct competitors of the Parties on the short-haul routes where the Transaction
        gives rise to competition concerns, based on the Commission’s assessment, (see
         sections 9.2, 9.3 and 9.4) are the following low-cost carriers (“LCCs”) and ultra-low-
         cost carriers (“ULCCs”).624 The Commission highlights that there are no other
        network carriers active on these routes (other than Lufthansa and ITA) and therefore
         the only carriers exerting competitive pressure on Lufthansa and ITA are LCCs or
      ULCCs.
9.1.1.1.1.     Ryanair
(511)   Ryanair is a ULCC headquartered in Dublin, Ireland. The Ryanair group consists of
        Ryanair, Ryanair UK, Buzz, Lauda and Malta Air and connects 240 destinations over
       40 countries, offering low fare options.
(512)   Ryanair operates a point-to-point (“P2P”) business model on short-haul routes. The
       P2P model entails offering direct, non-stop routes without connecting passengers
        through a hub.
(513)    It  is Lufthansa and ITA’s only other competitor on the following routes where
        Lufthansa and ITA currently compete: Milan – Brussels (BGY-CRL), Milan –
        Düsseldorf (BGY-CGN), Milan – Frankfurt (BGY-HHN), Milan – Hamburg (BGY-
      HAM), Milan – Stuttgart (BGY-FKB), Rome – Brussels (CIA-CRL and FCO-BRU),
      Rome – Frankfurt (FCO-HHN) and Rome – Munich (FCO-FMM). Ryanair is also
         active on the routes Milan – Vienna (MXP-VIE) and Rome – Vienna (FCO-VIE)
       which ITA currently plans to enter.
(514)   Ryanair primarily flies to secondary / regional airports (such as HHN or CRL) and
         usually has only a limited presence on primary airports (such as VIE or BRU).




624     LCCs and ULCCs are similar in terms of business model, as both type of airlines provides P2P services,
       and their choices are primarily driven by costs. However, LCCs, such as easyJet, may choose to operate
       from primary airports and also attempt to be attractive to both leisure and business travellers. On the
         other hand, ULCCs usually aim to provide the most cost-effective solutions, with little to no regard to
         other considerations (various services, appeal to business or time-sensitive demand, etc.) and generally
         operate from secondary  / regional airports. See non-confidential minutes of a conference call with
         easyJet, dated 24 October 2023, paragraph 8, ID 1054, and non-confidential minutes of a conference
          call with Vueling (IAG Group), dated 18 October 2023, paragraph 5, ID 1026.

9.1.2.   Closeness of competition
(532)   This section contains a number of general remarks with respect to the closeness of
        competition between the Parties and their competitors, which to varying degrees are
         relevant  for  all  short-haul  routes  covered by  this  Decision. As  set  out  in
        Section 7.1.1, when  the combined market  shares  are  in  excess  of 50%,  the
       Commission’s competitive assessment does not generally require the parties to be
         close competitors for the Commission to find that a merger would significantly
       impede effective competition as market shares above 50% lead to a presumption of
       dominance and may in themselves be evidence of the existence of a dominant
         position. The assessment of closeness of competition  is however more relevant
       where the combined market shares remain below 50% or where the Parties’ products
        appear prima facia very different. However, as confirmed in the recent CK Telecoms
        judgement, even in oligopolistic markets, the Commission is only required to assess
        whether the merging parties are close competitors (rather than “particularly close” or
        “the closest” competitors).636
(533)   In  airline markets, the  air transport services provided by different  airlines are
         differentiated based on prices, schedules, frequency of service, on-board and off-
        board service, business model, the existence of a network or hub, and other factors.
       Based on the market investigation, the most important parameters to compete on the
         relevant  short-haul  routes  are  the  price,  the  direct  or  indirect  nature  of  the
        connections, the frequencies offered, the time of departure and arrival, and the
        distance/connection of the airport to/from the city centre. The overall passenger
         experience637 may also be an important factor. At the same time, the financial
         strength of the carrier, the on-board services, the airline brand, the loyalty program
         available and sustainability considerations seem less important based on the results
         of the market investigation.638

         the possibility of lounge access or luggage included in the fare price, etc.

(534)   For two airlines to be considered as offering services which are close substitutes to
        each other, it is not necessary that the two services are identical. Some services may
        be closer substitutes than others. What matters from a competition perspective is the
         relative degree of substitutability between the services of the various carriers on the
        overlapping routes considering the city and airport pairs.
(535)   Therefore, it is relevant to compare the Parties, but also the remaining competitors in
        each affected market. Accordingly, a route-specific assessment of the closeness of
        competition between the Parties and with the remaining competitors on the relevant
         routes is conducted below in sections 9.2, 9.3 and 9.4. However, some aspects of the
         analysis of the closeness of competition between the Parties and with remaining
        competitors apply generally on the affected markets and are therefore already
        presented in this section 9.1. Those aspects concern the Parties’ and competitors’
        market positions, their business models, their brands, and the existence of significant
        bases in Italy (Rome and Milan) on the one hand and Austria, Belgium, Germany,
       and Switzerland on the other hand.
(536)   In prior decisions,639 the Commission has found that carriers offering scheduled air
         transport services form a heterogeneous group, with significant differences among
         carriers relating mainly to operating model (“network” carriers as opposed to “point-
         to-point” carriers) and level of service offered (“full-service” as opposed to the
         limited services offered by LCCs). Airlines were considered close substitutes for one
        another if they operated closely related business models and had a similar level of
         service.
(537)   Against  the above-mentioned background,  in  its  Article  6(1)(c) Decision  the
       Commission preliminarily concluded that the Parties are closer competitors to one
        another than to their LCC and ULCC competitors.
(538)   In their response to the Commission’s Article 6(1)(c) Decision as well as in a
        supplementary submission,640 the Parties claim that the Commission’s closeness of
        competition assessment is flawed, for the following reasons:
          (a)   Because although the assessment takes into account the Commission’s past
               decisional practice in Ryanair / Aer Lingus III,641 it does not adequately justify
          why the distinction between full-service network carriers on the one hand and
          LCCs and ULCCs on the other is still relevant;642
         (b)   Because the assessment fails to take into account (i) similarities and differences
               in the prices, frequencies and/or time of departure and arrival offered by the
               Parties and their competitors on each O&D route of concern, and (ii) passenger
               behaviour;643


        experience” were inconclusive, as 50% of the respondents who responded to these questions considered
          their importance 4 or 5 on a scale from 1-5, while the others considered it lower.

(541)    First, the Commission considers that a distinction between full-service network

        evidence in the Commission’s file suggests that there is still differentiation between
         full-service network carriers and their LCC  / ULCC competitors that  is highly
         relevant for customer’s choice, and that there are several differences in their product
         offering. More specifically, evidence in the Commission’s file (and described below
         in section 9.1.2.1) suggests that the Parties compete more closely on prices and
        frequencies with one another than with  their competitors on each  route. The
        circumstances which render Lufthansa and ITA closer competitors compared to their
     LCC  / ULCC counterparts are primarily attributable to the fact that the business
       model of network carriers is still distinct compared to that of LCCs and ULCCs.

9.1.2.1. Closeness of competition on short-haul routes between full-service network carriers
       on the one hand and, LCCs and ULCCs on the other hand in terms of business
        model, business strategy, pricing and frequencies
(546)   In the light of the results of the market investigation and the evidence presented in
          this section, the Commission considers the Parties to be close, even each other’s
          closest, competitors on the short-haul routes of concern, because both Lufthansa and
      ITA are full-network carriers, whereas the remaining competitors are mostly LCCs
          (e.g., easyJet) and ULCCs657 (e.g., Ryanair and Wizz Air). More specifically, the
       Commission draws this conclusion by considering that the business model operated
       by the Parties, and that operated by their competitors to be a relevant factor for its
        closeness of competition assessment, for the following reasons.
(547)    First, full-service network carriers target larger market segments than LCCs and
      ULCCs do.
(548)   In the  first place, LCCs and ULCCs are primarily focused on maintaining low
        operating costs, and in offering the cheapest fares so as to attract price sensitive
         passengers.658 In practice, they primarily target P2P and leisure-oriented customers,
       and as a consequence compete with full-service network carriers on this segment.659
         Full-service network carriers, however, also target connecting passengers, as well as
        those passengers that have a higher willingness to pay  (e.g., business-oriented
        customers).
(549)   The Commission acknowledges that several ULCCs express the view that that the
         services offered by full-service network carriers on short-haul routes are becoming
         increasingly similar to those offered by LCCs and ULCCs.660 In this context, Ryanair
        submits that “[d]espite its focus on leisure traffic, Ryanair’s business model became
       more flexible, in order to attract also some business customers” and that “in Europe,
         there is a trend of convergence in this way in the sense that both leisure-focused and
        business-focused carriers take some traffic of the other kind, making the distinction
        between them increasingly blurred.”661
(550)   However, LCCs and ULCCs do not distinguish between classes and thus offer the
       same basic air travel services to all types of passengers, whereas on the contrary,
        both Lufthansa and ITA offer business class options for their short-haul flights,

(552)   In the Parties’ Response to the SO, the Parties continue to argue that customers (with
         special focus on business customers) have become increasingly price sensitive on
       European  short-haul  routes and  all  airlines compete  for  all  customers.662 The
       Commission notes that the considerations set out in the Parties’ Response to the SO
       have been taken into account by the Commission in  its assessment. While  all
        customers may consider all the options available to them, including flights operated
       by LCC carriers, business customers may also consider, or place more weight than
         other customers do, on other factors, such as the (i) time of departure/arrival, (ii)
        frequencies offered per day or (iii) the distance/connection of the airport to/from the
         city centre.663 As ULCC and LCC carriers often fly fewer times during the day,
         outside of peak hours and to/from secondary/regional airports, business customers
         are less likely to choose these carriers, even if they primary consideration might be
         the price of the flight. At the same time, ULCC and LCC carriers generally offer
        lower prices, which may be not only the primary, but the sole consideration of leisure
        customers, which may, in turn, be more prone to choose ULCC and LCC carriers for
          their purposes. This is substantiated by Lufthansa’s internal document in Figure 34.
        In addition, the Commission notes that LCC and ULCC carriers are focusing on
         point-to-point traffic and their schedules and business in general are not optimised
         for connecting traffic.664 This different business model constitutes one of the main
         differences between network carriers and LCC/ULCC carriers and its implications on
         the Commission’s assessment is explained further below.665
(553)   In the second place, both Lufthansa and ITA, in contrast to their LCC competitors,
         offer loyalty programs (i.e., Lufthansa’s Miles&More and ITA’s Volare) to attract
        frequent  fliers. In particular, according to Air France-KLM, Lufthansa’s loyalty
       program is the “largest one in Europe”666 and according to Ryanair, frequent flier
       programs “give flag carriers a large advantage (…). Business passengers earn
         loyalty points in their own name while travelling for work and this has proved very
          difficult  to compete  against”.667 Moreover, Ryanair adds  that  “[w]ith  loyalty
        programs, customers who regularly  fly for business purposes will earn loyalty

(573)   Contrary to the arguments in the Parties’ Response to the SO, the Commission
        considers that its assessment on pricing is relevant for the closeness of competition
        assessment, as  it indicates significant differences between the business model of
        Lufthansa and ITA and their competitors, in particular their approaches to their
        customers and how they differentiate (or do not differentiate) between customer
        groups. The Commission  considers  that  the  internal documents  of  Lufthansa
        underpin the above, even in light of the additional explanations provided in the
         Parties’ Response to the SO, which argued that the pricing approaches of airlines are
        not relevant from the customers’ perspective, and even  if  it was, the pricing
        approaches of ULCC/LCCs and network carriers do not differ. In particular the
         Parties explain that Lufthansa simply offers bundles to attract more customers.696
       The Commission notes that while the approach behind pricing might not be relevant
         for the customers, the price the customer has to pay as a result of a distinct pricing
        approach (e.g. when their trip is identified as “business motive” and thereby priced
         differently) is.
(574)   Fourth, whilst full-service network carriers like Lufthansa and ITA target customers
        with a high willingness  to pay, LCCs and ULCCs  are primarily focused on
        maintaining low operating costs, and in offering the cheapest fares so as to attract
         price sensitive passengers.697 Consequently, the prices offered by Lufthansa and ITA
       on each of the overlapping routes are closer and more comparable to each other than
         to the prices offered by their LCC and ULCC competitors, which are generally the
         lowest. This shows that the Parties are positioned similarly in terms of price/quality
          ratio and are positioned differently in terms of price/quality ratio than are their LCC
       and ULCC competitors. The Commission concludes that the Parties compete more
         closely on prices with each other compared to how closely they compete with the
         other direct competitors (LCCs and ULCCs) on each route.

(580)   In the fourth place, the closeness of competition between the Parties, in terms of the
         fare prices on the short-haul O&D routes of concern is also evident from the fact that
        Lufthansa’s prices on each of the routes are the prices that are primarily monitored

(581)   The Commission notes  that, contrary to what the  Partis’ Response to the SO
         implies,700  it does not contest the fact that the distinction between business and
         leisure passengers has become increasingly blurred recently. Nevertheless, this does
        not change the Commission’s assessment and conclusions, as the data submitted by
         the Parties clearly shows differences in pricing between the Parties and LCC/ULCC
       even in the passenger categories in which they compete. This evidence indicates that
      LCC/ULCC carriers remain the prime options for price-sensitive customers, while
         less price-sensitive customers and business customers may opt for the services of
        Lufthansa and ITA based on  various  factors  (such  as  airport  of  operations,
         frequencies, more convenient time of arrival/departure) even if they may consider
         price as an important parameter for their choice.
(582)    Fifth, in terms of network schedule and routes operated, network carriers operate
         different business models compared to LCCs and ULCCs. Network carriers generally
        operate to and from their hubs, which are main city airports (e.g., FRA and MUC for
        Lufthansa and FCO for ITA), in which they build a significant presence in terms of
          slot holding and routes operated, and bring-in  traffic  (i.e., feeder  traffic) from
         destinations to their hub airports, connecting passengers to other destinations. Due to
          their business model, network carriers require a strong presence at hub airports, and
         thus, enjoy certain benefits including a strong slot portfolio, frequency advantages,
        access to feed-traffic and economies of scale and scope.
(583)   In addition, network carriers have the ability to offset any losses associated with
        aggressive price retaliation on short-haul routes. As an example, such retaliation may
        take place against LCCs or ULCCs attempting to enter the routes operated by the
        network carrier with potentially a lower priced offering. The business model of LCCs
       and ULCCs does not allow these competitors to easily offset losses generated on
         certain short-haul routes. Therefore, Lufthansa and ITA compete more closely than
        they do  with LCCs  or ULCCs, which may  not have  the same  underlying
         characteristics and therefore cannot exert the same level of competitive constraint on
        network carriers as Lufthansa and ITA.
(584)   This is due to multiple factors associated with the operation of network carriers:
                (a)  Network carriers are often able to offer better frequencies due to the
                     larger slot holdings at their hub airports.
               (b)   Similarly, they benefit from economies of scale (large slot portfolio,
                  based aircraft, airport services, connecting  traffic, etc.) on short-haul
                    routes involving their hub airports.
                (c)  Most importantly, they can utilize potentially unprofitable short-haul
                    routes to feed traffic to other, more profitable routes, such as long-haul
                     routes. Long-haul flights are typically associated with network carriers.


699     Response of Lufthansa and MEF to a Commission’s request for information (RFI 30) dated 09 February
        2024, paragraph 43.
700       Parties’ Response to the SO, paragraphs (104) to (125).

[PÁGINA PDF 137]
               (d)   Lastly, network carriers are typically able to better capitalize on other
                     profitable services, such as providing business class and other such
                     services to their customers (for more information on ITA and Lufthansa’s
                   business models see sections 7.5 and 7.6 above).
(585)  By contrast, LCCs and ULCCs operate a P2P business model. LCCs and ULCCs are
         cost-oriented, and thus often avoid operating from main airports (see section 9.1.2.2
         below),701 and  opt  for  smaller   /  regional  airports  because  they  offer more
        “competitive prices and limited operational restrictions (i.e., to allow for a for a
        25-minute turnaround time)”.702 LCCs and ULCCs business model focuses on
        ensuring profitability on each route (and thus, unlike network carriers, they cannot
          fly on  unprofitable  short-haul  routes and  recuperate  their  losses  otherwise).
        Moreover, to ensure profitability LCCs and ULCCs prefer to operate slots during
       peak hours (early morning hours and late afternoon hours) and to rotate in and out of
         airports throughout the day, rather than optimising their network according to feeder-
          traffic considerations.703
(586)   These differences in the operation of full-service network carriers and LCCs/ULCCs
         are important on the short-haul O&D routes of concern (where part of the Parties
          traffic is also P2P). More specifically, as shown in Figure 2 above for Lufthansa to
        operate […]. Therefore, in order for the Parties to operate their long-haul network
         profitably, they need to ensure high frequencies from short-haul destinations that will
        then feed their long-haul network.
(587)   In this context, Lufthansa and ITA compete more closely by offering a higher
       number of frequencies on a weekly basis on the short-haul O&D routes to/from
         either of the Parties’ hubs, compared to how closely they compete with the LCC
        competitors that are active on those routes. Due to ITA’s increase of operations over
         the past IATA seasons, the frequencies offered in the winter 2023/24 and the summer
       2024 seasons are most representative of the frequencies to be expected going
        forward. Table 23 below demonstrates that the Parties are each other’s closest
        competitors in terms of weekly frequencies offered, with the exception of the routes
        Milan-Brussels and Rome-Brussels, where Ryanair flies at an equal or higher weekly
        frequency compared to ITA (and Lufthansa in the case of Rome-Brussels over the
       summer seasons). The Commission notes that, the frequencies offered by Ryanair on
         these routes to and from Brussels are exceptional among the O&D routes assessed in
          this decision, considering Ryanair’s large base in Charleroi Airport, and the fact that
             it operates each route from multiple airports, including from the regional airport
         Charleroi, while the Parties each operate from the main airport Brussels Zaventem
            (i.e., Ryanair operates Rome-Brussels from CLR-CIA and BRU-FCO and Milan-

(588)    Sixth, the Commission notes that on certain routes of concern (i.e., Milan-Düsseldorf,
         Milan-Stuttgart, Milan-Hamburg and Rome-Hamburg), Lufthansa operates through
           its LCC carrier, Eurowings. The only other competitor operating these routes apart
       from the Parties is Ryanair (largely through airports in proximity and not from the
       same airports as the Parties). In this context, the Commission’s market investigation
         identified differences between the operations of LCCs (e.g., Eurowings) and ULCCs
          (e.g., Ryanair).
(589)   More  specifically, an ULCC’s business model deviates further from  that of a
        standard LCC, with the former being more cost-oriented and having minimal

      Summer IATA 2023 Season: 0 frequencies, Winter IATA 2023/2024 Season: 3 frequencies, Summer
      IATA 2024 Season: 0 frequencies.

[PÁGINA PDF 139]
         inclusions in the fare and a greater number of add-on fees. According to easyJet
        (which is an LCC), “[u]nlike ultra-low-cost carriers like Ryanair and Wizz Air,
        easyJet does not always opt for cheaper regional airports. Instead,  it usually
        operates from primary airports, i.e., those located closest to the city centre. This is
        because easyJet wants to be attractive to different types of customers (e.g., business
       and leisure), including the time-sensitive ones, to ensure that they achieve certain
         levels of demand throughout the year. Nevertheless, easyJet operates from secondary
         airports as  well,  usually when  the primary  airport  that  is serving a  city  is
         congested”.705 Similarly, Vueling (another LCC) explains that  its main strategic
        focus is on primary airports, and that “[t]his is a difference between (…) (a “low-
        cost” airline) and “ultra low-cost” carriers such as Ryanair or Wizz Air whose
        business model may entail sacrificing some elements of the quality of their offering,
        including among others, by choosing to operate from secondary airports. In general,
        Vueling puts more emphasis on  its product/service compared to ultra low-cost
         airlines and aims  to  provide a  better  service, hence  the  focus on primary
         airports”.706 easyJet and Vueling’s business model presents similarities to that of
        Eurowings, as they both choose to operate also from main airports, instead of mostly
         regional airports/airports of proximity to the main airport.
(590)  By  contrast, Ryanair chooses  to  fly mainly from  regional  airports/airports  of
        proximity  to the main  airport  in the above-mentioned routes of concern. For
        example, on the route Milan-Stuttgart, Eurowings operates from MXP to STR, whilst
        Ryanair operates from BGY to FKB. The higher closeness between Eurowings and
       ITA’s activities compared to those of Ryanair have also been confirmed by Air
       France-KLM, regarding those carriers’ operations on the route Milan-Hamburg,
       where Air France-KLM submitted that “Eurowings, part of Lufthansa Group is the
         closest competitor [of ITA] on the route with 1.1 daily flight from MXP, as Ryanair
        with the same number of frequencies operates from farther BGY (see appendix
       03_EA7b), which is not ideal for premium passengers”.707 For more information on
        competition between airlines operating on a route from different airports, see section
         9.1.2.2 below.
(591)   In addition, Wizz Air explained that “Eurowings, despite being called a low-cost
         carrier,  is part of a group which feeds into  full-service carriers and transfer
        passengers into its wider network, it offers lower fares but typically does not have the
       same cost structure as a ULCC. It provides an offering of a wide range of services
       and amenities to their passengers, which often includes in-flight meals, multiple
        cabin  classes, and generous baggage allowances. […]  Therefore, while both
       Eurowings and Wizz  Air  operate  within  the  low-cost  carrier  segment,  they
         differentiate themselves through their service offerings, and operating strategy.
       Eurowings leverages its association with the Lufthansa Group to offer a more full-
         service-like experience”.708
(592)   The Commission therefore concludes  that, on the routes  that are operated by
        Eurowings, Lufthansa and ITA remain closer competitors compared to Ryanair.

      DLH. As explained more in detail in Annex I, these analyses are characterised by
         serious methodological flaws which make their results unreliable. In particular,
          (a)    First, studying  the  relationship between  price and competition  in  airline
             markets through descriptive722 or cross-sectional regression analyses alone
             fundamentally ignore business and market dynamics. As explained in more

722     The Parties submitted a series of charts where two variables measured at the city-pair level are
       compared against each other, for example a chart shows the average price on a city-pair route and the
       number of competitors active on that city-pair route across all city-pair routes.

[PÁGINA PDF 142]
                detail  in  Section  6,  in mergers  involving  airlines,  the Commission has
                traditionally followed the O&D approach, which the Parties did not contest.
           The analyses submitted by the Parties, however, completely ignore differences
              across city-pairs, and implicitly assume that all city-pairs are the same, whereas
               significant heterogeneity across  different  city-pair  routes  exist  in  reality,
              including variations in demand, airport infrastructure, regulatory environments,
            and competitive conditions.
         (b)   Second, drawing a link between prices across routes and competitors’ presence
            on that route while ignoring differences across city-pair routes is equivalent to
            assuming that carriers decide to enter a certain city-pair for reasons unrelated to
           demand and supply factors specific to the city pair itself. In essence, comparing
               prices across city-pair routes without accounting for the variations in demand
            and supply factors among the different city pairs is equivalent to suggesting
                that Ryanair, ITA, and other competitors make decisions to enter specific
              routes  entirely  at  random,  disregarding  any  economic  considerations
             underpinning their strategic choices.
          (c)   Third, such descriptive analyses are inconsistent with established best practices
               in economics and econometrics. Pricing and competition are fundamentally
                interrelated, and hence endogenous in econometrics jargon, meaning they are
             mutually determined by underlying factors. Without addressing endogeneity
              concerns,  scatterplots and  cross-sectional analyses cannot  disentangle  the
               direction of the relationship between price and competition. Scatterplots and
               cross-sectional analyses that treat all markets homogeneously oversimplify the
               pricing and competition dynamics. As described in Section 2 of Annex I, the
              standard econometric methods mitigate endogeneity concerns are the so-called
               fixed-effect methods. Fixed-effect econometric models, by controlling for city-
               pair  fixed  effects and  other  unobserved  factors,  explicitly  account  for
              heterogeneity across markets, and help isolate the impact of changes in the
            number of competitors on prices while holding constant other influences
               specific to each route.
         (d)   Fourth,  descriptive  or  cross-sectional  regression  analyses  that  examine
              snapshots of data at a single point in time may overlook temporal trends and
                  fail to capture the dynamic nature of competition and pricing behaviour. This is
               true even if a month like April 2023 or October 2022 is chosen:723 Prices and
              the number of competitors on city pairs fluctuate over time due to various
            exogenous shocks, seasonal  patterns, and market dynamics. Ignoring  this
              source of variation leads to biased and inconsistent results. On the other hand,
              as explained in the paragraph above, fixed-effect methods provide a reliable
            framework to account for temporal dynamics and trends.
          (e)   Fifth, in any event, and notwithstanding the severe limitations of the analysis,
              the results of the Parties’ cross-sectional regression analysis indicate that in
              addition  to  Ryanair  other  competitors  also  exercise  a  significant  price
               constraint on Lufthansa. The Parties’ analysis predicts that Lufthansa’s prices
              are […]% lower  if  it faces competition from Ryanair and […]% lower  if
             Lufthansa  faces competition from an  airline  carrier  other  than  Ryanair,
              including ITA. Even taken at face value, the Parties’ cross-sectional regression

9.1.2.2. Closeness of Competition between  airlines operating from  different airports in
        proximity on short-haul routes
(604)  One of the key considerations behind the Commission’s view regarding Lufthansa
       and ITA being close, even each other’s closest, competitors on the O&D routes
        assessed in this Decision, is that Lufthansa and ITA mostly operate from the same
        primary airports on both ends of the routes of concern. At the same time, the
        competitors of Lufthansa and ITA, including Ryanair which the Parties consider as
         the closest competitor of Lufthansa, primarily compete from distinct secondary  /
         regional airports, which are often time-consuming and costly to access for customers
       and there are usually fewer transportation options available to do so compared to
        primary airports. Secondary / regional airports also maintain a lower level of services
       compared to primary airports, as shown below.
9.1.2.2.1.     General remarks regarding the competitive dynamics between primary and
             secondary / regional airports
(605)   There are only a few instances out of the routes discussed in this Decision where
        Lufthansa and ITA are not utilising the same airports. These are:
          (a)   Milan-Brussels, where ITA operates from LIN and Lufthansa operates from
             both LIN and MXP. Both Parties operate from the same airport on the Brussels
            end of the route (BRU);
         (b)   Milan-Düsseldorf, where Lufthansa operates the routes BGY-DUS, MXP-
          CGN, MXP-DUS and ITA operates the route LIN-DUS; and,
          (c)   Milan-Frankfurt, where ITA operates from LIN and Lufthansa operates from
             both LIN and MXP. Both Parties operate from the same  airport on the
              Frankfurt end of the route (FRA).
(606)  By  contrast,  the  Parties’ competitors  (if any) operate mostly from  regional  /
        secondary airports that are located further away from the relevant city centre (in the
        majority of cases on both ends of the routes of concern, and to a smaller extent on
       one end). These are:
          (a)  BGY on the Milan end and
               (1)  CRL on the Brussels end on the route Milan-Brussels;
               (2)  CGN, NRN on the Düsseldorf end on the route Milan-Düsseldorf;
               (3)  HHN on the Frankfurt end on the route Milan-Frankfurt;
               (4)  FKB on the Stuttgart end on the route Milan-Stuttgart;
               (5)  BTS on the Vienna end on the route Milan-Vienna.
         (b)  On the Rome end of the routes of concern the Commission considers that FCO
            and CIA belong to the same market (see 6.5.3.9 above). However regional /
             secondary airports are utilised by competitors on the other end of the routes of
              concern, namely:
               (1)  CRL on the Brussels end on the route Rome-Brussels;


                                    142

[PÁGINA PDF 145]
               (2)  HHN on the Frankfurt end on the route Rome-Frankfurt;
               (3)  FMM on the Munich end on the route Rome-Munich;
               (4)  BSL on the Zurich end on the route Rome-Zurich.
(607)   The Commission’s investigation has clearly shown that, considering the operations
        of Lufthansa and ITA, which are network carriers that mainly fly to primary airports,
         the passenger air transport services provided by competing airlines flying mainly to
         regional / secondary airports (even if they are potentially within the same catchment
         area) are less close substitutes compared to those airlines, which are flying to the
       same primary airports as Lufthansa and ITA.
(608)    First, the customers that expressed a view in the Commission’s market investigation
        confirmed that the distance of the airport from the city centre  is a somewhat
        important factor that they take into account when they purchase tickets on the short-
        haul  overlapping  routes.727 More  importantly,  the  vast  majority  of  customer
        respondents  that  expressed  a  view, confirmed  that  the  closest  alternative  of
        Lufthansa’s offering on each affected short-haul route is ITA’s offering, and not one
        of their competitors’ offerings (e.g., Ryanair’s etc.).728
(609)   Second, the view that the airport of operation matters for customer choice was
       echoed by  specific explanations given by individual customers,  stressing  their
         perspective as business customers:
          (a)  [A customer] (a customer) explained that “[f]or business travellers the location
            and convenience of the airport largely drives the purchasing choice”. The
               airport of operation as a pivotal aspect of customer choice is further highlighted
            by the fact that, while [A customer] noted that where network and LLC airlines
             both fly to an “acceptable airport” both would be considered by customers, it
               also noted that HHN, FMM, BSL, CGN, DTM, NRN, LBC, BGY, and FKB
              are not acceptable substitutes for their primary airport counterparts.729
         (b)  [A customer] remarked that “[l]ow cost from secondary airports are not
               competition”.730
          (c)   Similarly, [a customer] explained that “For the majority of short haul routes in
              the  annex,   there   is  no   sufficient   competition   especially  between
             Germany/Belgium/Switzerland/Austria to Italy and vice-versa. The existing low
               cost carrier competition is not relevant to most corporate customers and takes
              place to a large extent on secondary airports with a different catchment area
            and often poor accessibility and connectivity.”731
(610)   Third, in the course of the Commission’s market investigation, the competitors of
        Lufthansa and ITA have confirmed that  (i) generally LCCs  / ULCCs, such as
        Ryanair and Wizz Air and network carriers, such as Lufthansa and ITA usually fly to

              route with 1.1 daily flight from MXP, as Ryanair with the same number of
              frequencies operates from farther BGY (see appendix 03_EA7b), which is not
               ideal for premium passengers”733, thereby also indicating that the airport of
              operation is an important element of closeness of competition. Air France-
        KLM added in a later submission that “LCCs do not have exactly the same
                  utility  for  customers,  even  on  short-haul”  (indicating  that  there   is
               differentiation between network carriers and LCCs) and referred to a variety of
               differences between ULCCs and LCCs belonging to large airline groups and
                full-service network carriers, including the airport choice of ULCCs, such as
             Ryanair and Wizz Air.734
          (c)  Wizz Air noted that “[w]hile secondary airports offer alternative market
              access to regions driving demand, primary airports generally provide more
                efficient ground accessibility and proximity to cities. This results in a higher
             customer preference for primary airports over their secondary counterparts”.
           From the supply side perspective Wizz Air adds that “[g]iven the robust
            ground connectivity of secondary airports and the broad catchment areas
              driving demand, these secondary alternatives should be taken into account for
              the transaction. The merged entity, by maintaining their dominant position at
           LIN airport for example, secure a superior competitive stance, owing to the
               strategic location of LIN airport. In this instance, while Milan Malpensa and
            Milan Bergamo provide a secondary airport for the Milan catchment area, the
              distance is too long to be a  full substitute. Instead, LIN, thanks to better
              transport connections, has a unique advantage.”735 These statements indicate
                 that, while airlines flying to secondary / regional airports may compete with
              those flying to primary airports, due to clear customer preference toward
             primary airports, the latter have a “unique advantage”, which in turn indicates
                that they compete closely with each other, and in any event more closely than
             with carriers flying to secondary / regional airports.
(611)   Fourth, The Commission notes  that, as described in section 6.5, many of the
        secondary / regional airports on the routes of concern are significantly more difficult,
        time-consuming and costly to access for customers compared to primary airports.

(612)   In the first place, secondary / regional airports736 relevant for the routes discussed in
          this Decision are between 45 (BGY) and 124 (HHN) km away from the centre of the
          cities they serve. For primary airports this distance is between 7 (LIN) and 39 (MUC)
      kms away. Importantly, none of the secondary airports are connected by direct train
         to the city centre, while all primary airports are. A bus connection between the city
         centres and the secondary airports is also not always available. For more information
        see section 6.5.
(613)   In the second place, the Commission notes that secondary / regional airports are – in
       most cases – significantly harder and more time-consuming to access for customers,
         especially  for customers without access  to  their own passenger  cars. A very
         significant portion of customers would only be able to rely on public transportation
       by bus, train or possibly taxi to reach an airport.
(614)   In fact, there are several arguments which indicate that travel by personal passenger
         car or taxi or taxi to secondary / regional airports are likely to be far less relevant
       modes of transport compared to other options for the following reasons:
          (a)   Cars are not available to all potential passengers. Based on the latest data
               available from Eurostat, on average there are 563 cars for every thousand
               inhabitants  within  the EU.  In  addition,  the  countries  affected by  the
              Transaction are not  all amongst the countries with the highest number of
             passenger cars for every thousand inhabitants within the EU.737
         (b)   Regarding taxis, the Commission notes that, while customers without cars
             could potentially utilise a taxi journey to reach the secondary / regional airport,
              considering the level of taxi fares in the EU, the cost savings (price advantage
              generally associated with LCCs) which customers may realise on the basis of
              the lower air fares from secondary / regional airports would likely be negated
               to a large extent by the cost of the journey to the airport. In fact, in several
              cases the price of the journey considering the taxi fares to and from secondary /
              regional airports may be significantly higher than the prices of network carriers
               flying to primary airports.
          (c)   At the same time, even those customers who have access to a passenger car
          may need to consider the costs of parking this car at the airport, which is again
             a factor potentially negating any cost savings the customer may realise with
           LCCs.
         (d)   Lastly, the Commission notes that even those customers who have access to
             passenger cars, would likely have such access only to either the origin or the
               destination airport and would need to rely on other transportation method on at
                least one end of their journey.738
(615)   Therefore, the Commission considers in its closeness of competition assessment that
         the car travel option to secondary  / regional airports may not be available to a
         significant portion of the customers within the EU Member States, while the taxi
         travel option may raise the price of the overall journey to an extent which renders the

         offering of LCCs uneconomical. This, in turn, requires the Commission to assign
       more weight in its closeness of competition assessment to the more affordable travel
        options available to the general public, i.e. train and bus options, which imply longer
         travel times (including getting to and from the  airport) for secondary/regional
         airports than from primary/ more central  airports. In essence, the cost savings
        achievable by flying to regional/secondary airports will only benefit those customers
      who are willing to significantly extend their travel time and use the different and less
        convenient transportation options available from secondary/regional airports.
(616)   In  the  third  place,  the  investigation  of  the Commission  indicates,  that  train
        connections play a significant role in considering a secondary / regional airport as
         substitutable and convenient  for customers. As an example, Air France KLM
        submitted regarding a potential future train connection between Milan and BGY that
        “This will add an alternative airport similar to MXP (within same reach), with
      (U)LCC competition”. Which indicates that Air France-KLM does not consider the
         existing travel options between Milan and BGY (directly connected to Milan only by
        bus) as sufficient to consider BGY as a true alternative for network and LCC carriers
          (their customers) alike.739
(617)    Fifth, the strong differentiation between consumer preferences regarding  flights
        operating to and from secondary / regional airports and flight operating to and from
        primary airports is also indicated by the fact that Ryanair’s load factor has decreased
        following  its switch from FRA  to HHN  (airports which  the  Parties consider
          substitutable).740 This example indicates that even when the changes in the service
        provided relate in essence solely to the airport of operation within a potential
        catchment area, it is already capable of shifting consumer choice.
(618)   The Commission notes that it has received particularly strong feedback with regard
         to certain secondary  / regional  airports, which are  illustrated in the following
         sections.
(619)   Contrary to the Parties Response to the SO, the Commission’s assessment does not
         contradict (i) its previous practice, or (ii) its own methodology. The Commission
         assesses the relevance of airport choice as a key factor, but not the only factor for the
        closeness of competition assessment considering the routes of concern identified.
        This is in line with the approach taken in previous cases, such as M.6663 – Ryanair /
       Aer Lingus. Contrary to what the Parties imply in the Parties’ Response to the SO,
         the Commission does not conclude that airlines operating from different airports
        cannot be close or closest competitors, but relies on a closeness of competition
        assessment, including detailed market investigation feedback, of which the airport of
        operation is a relevant criterion. Similarly, the Commission’s methodology allows
         for ITA and Lufthansa to be close or even the closest competitors on a route, even if
        they operate from different airports on that route.741 In addition, the Commission
        notes that larger industry trends (e.g. ULCC/LCC carriers choosing to operate from
        primary airports in some cases) do not change the Commission’s closeness of
        competition assessment in the present case, as these trends have no bearing on the
         current competitive dynamics on the routes of concern and the Commission’s market

(620)   The Commission notes that contrary to the Parties’ Response to the SO, there are
         clear-cut differences in airport choices made by consumers, as shown by the market
         investigation and considered in the Commission’s assessment.743
(621)   Importantly, the Parties’ Response to the SO is based on mistaken notions regarding
         the accessibility of secondary airports. While some consumers might indeed live
         closer to the secondary airports, due to differences in population density between
         large cities and the regions where secondary airports located, it cannot be argued that
         the average customer is just as likely to live closer to the secondary airport as it is to
         live closer to the primary airport. This is supported among others by the Parties
        submission which shows that far more passengers chose to fly from primary airports
       compared to secondary airports.744 In addition primary airports are more likely to be
        well  connected  through  public  transportation compared  to  secondary/regional
          airports. The claims of the Parties, suggesting without evidence that some customers
        might have a preference for secondary/regional airports is not supported by the
        market  investigation  and  does  not  impact  the  conclusions  drawn  by  the
        Commission.745
(622)   The Parties also argue that the Commission’s assessment regarding passenger cars or
         taxis  as  transportation  is flawed and  the Commission should  give  far more
        importance to these modes of transport. In particular, the Parties argue that (i) car
        ownership numbers in Germany and Italy are above average, (ii) a 2010 report from
         the European Commission noted that cars remain the most important access mode to
        nearly all European airports, and that half of the passengers in Germany arrive to the
         airports by car and 18% uses taxis, moreover (iii) a 2019 report regarding BGY
       shows that 20 % of business passengers and 29 % of leisure passengers utilise the
        bus or train and bus options. 746 In response, the Commission notes that none of the
       above impacts its assessment significantly, as the information provided for Germany
           is highly outdated and potentially obsolete, while the information provided for Italy
           is specific to BGY and is more likely to be indicative of the lack of connections to
          this specific airport than the general importance of passenger cars in Italy for
        reaching airports. The Parties arguments also do not address the issues arising around
         the potential costs associated with taking taxis to or parking cars at airports or the
        necessary lack of personal passenger cars on the destination end of the route (even if
       one were to be “dropped off” at the origin airport). The Commission also notes that
         the Parties provided no information on countries other than Germany from the
     DACHB region. Lastly, regarding the Parties arguments on car ownership, see
        paragraph (612) above.

(623)   Lastly, the Commission notes that the Parties arguments relating to the overall
        market  position  of Ryanair  in  Italy and on a pan-European  level,  its brand
         recognition and the fact that it considers itself the closest competitor of Lufthansa
       and ITA does not change the Commission’s assessment. Even considering these
          factors, the evidence of the market investigation and the competitive dynamics
        described in the Commission’s assessment (including airport choice, frequencies,
         prices, etc.) clearly show that Lufthansa and ITA closely compete with each other on
         the routes of concern. The Commission notes that, the Commission does not contest
         that Ryanair exerts competitive pressure on Lufthansa and ITA. However, the
        evidence, which is available in the Commission’s file and which has been set out in
          detail in this Decision, shows that in terms of closeness of competition, Ryanair
       competes less closely with Lufthansa compared to ITA. The fact that Ryanair is
         overall a strong player within the EEA and in Italy, which may even be a stronger
        player than ITA on some measures, has no bearing on the closeness of competition
         assessment.747 In addition, as confirmed in the recent CK Telecoms judgement, even
         in oligopolistic markets, the Commission is only required to assess whether the
       merging parties are close competitors (rather than “particularly close”).748 Even if
      ITA and Lufthansa were not the closest competitors, they are clearly, at the very
          least, close competitors.

9.1.2.2.2.1.   Frankfurt – main airport: FRA, secondary / regional airport: HHN
(624)   Regarding HHN, NEOS notes that “travelling time and cost between Hahn and
        Frankfurt city centre are considerably higher than between Frankfurt Main and
        Frankfurt city centre. In this context, the overall flight time in a short-haul flight
        to/from Frankfurt from the one hand and Italy on the other, might be less than the
         travel time from Frankfurt city-centre to Hahn”.749
(625)   Ryanair, which the Parties consider to be Lufthansa’s main competitor, and which
         recently exited FRA and started operations in HHN, explained to the Commission
         that this transfer of operations led to a significant drop in customer demand. More
         specifically, Ryanair explained that “[i]n IATA Summer 2019 we [Ryanair] carried
        81.0k passengers between Frankfurt Main and Milan. In IATA Summer 2023, after
      we halted operation to Frankfurt Main, we carried 22.8k passengers between
        Frankfurt Hahn and Milan.” In addition, Ryanair explained that  it operated daily
          flights between FRA and Milan, but it only operates biweekly flights between HHN
       and Milan. It noted that its load factor “dropped […] following the switch from Main
         to Hahn between IATA Summer 2019 and IATA Summer 2023”. It also explained that
       “Hahn  is not comparable to Frankfurt (transport links, proximity to population
         centres)”.750
(626)   Lastly,  in response  to the Commission’s eRFI  questionnaire, only 3% of the
        respondents considered that Ryanair’s offering to/from BGY on the one hand and
        to/from HHN on the other hand is the closest alternative to Lufthansa’s offering,

(638)   Lufthansa argues that on the routes Milan-Frankfurt, Milan-Stuttgart, Milan-Vienna,
       Rome-Munich and Rome-Zurich, the Parties face competitive pressure by attractive
         direct or indirect train options offered by Trenitalia, ÖBB, SBB and/or Deutsche
       Bahn (or a combination of those). In section 6.8 above, the Commission considers
          that, for the purpose of this decision, rail passenger services between city-pairs that
         are longer than 6 hours (such as the four services referred to by Parties in the
        previous sentence) should not be considered in the same market as air passenger
         services between the same city-pairs although they may be taken in consideration to
         the extent that they exert out of market constraints on air passenger services. By
         contrast,  rail services between city-pairs that are up to 3-4 hours long may be
        considered as  exerting  direct competitive  constraint on  air passenger  services
       between the same city-pairs.

        reasons listed below.762

9.1.4.   Barriers to entry and expansion
(646)   Based on the Commission’s market investigation, the most important criteria for an
          airline to decide whether to enter or expand operations on any of the overlapping
         short-haul routes are (i) whether Lufthansa (as one of the largest airlines in Europe,
       which has the possibility to exert significant competitive pressure) is active on a
         certain route (the criterion that was marked by the respondents to the Commission’s
        market investigation questionnaire as the most important barrier to entry and expand
         in all of the short-haul routes of concern);  (ii) the level of airport charges; and
            (iii) slot congestion at certain airports.773 Based on these results, which show how
          airlines consider the criteria to apply in their decision making regarding entry or
        expansion, the Commission’s market investigation identified several barriers to entry
       and expansion that reduce the likelihood of existing competitors and new entrants
        expanding their services or starting new services on the O&D routes assessed in this
        Decision: in particular, the availability of slots in LIN airport, the large slot portfolio
        of the Parties in certain airports and the Parties’ aggressive practices made possible
       by those slot portfolios, the airport charges at certain of Lufthansa’s hubs and the
        network effects of network carriers. These barriers are described in sections 9.1.4.1,
         9.1.4.2, 9.1.4.4 and (702) below. To the extent that barriers to entry and expansion
         are route specific, they will be further assessed on a route-by-route basis in sections
         9.2, 9.3, and 9.4 and their sub-sections.
9.1.4.1. Slot congestion at Milan Linate Airport
(647)  LIN is not only usually the preferred airport of airlines, due to its proximity to the
         city centre of Milan resulting in shorter travel times to and -rom Milan’s city center,
         for short-haul flights to and from Milan774 but also one of the centres of ITA’s
          activities as shown in the route-by-route assessment in sections 9.2, 9.3, and 9.4
        below. ITA is currently the largest operator at LIN in terms of slots holding with
        market shares of 53.5% in the 2023 summer and 55% in the 2023/24 winter season.
        In particular, during the last three IATA seasons, ITA held at least half of the slots
        during operating hours and around 60% of slots during peak hours. Lufthansa is the
        second largest player in terms of slot holding in LIN with around 7% of slots 775 (see
         section 11.4.1.1 for more information).

(648)   In their response to the Commission’s Article 6(1)(c) Decision as well as in a
        subsequent submission,776 the Parties argue the following:
          (a)   In line with the Commission’s conclusion on the market definition when
              considering barriers to entry in Milan, the slot availability of other airports
              within the Milan catchment area should be taken into consideration;777
         (b)  The Commission’s approach to consider LIN in isolation does not depict an
               issue that is specific to the Transaction, as the concerns raised in the market
               investigation are related to the current situation at LIN, namely that very
               limited slots are available778 and to ITA’s slot holding therein (being the only
                airline with a base in LIN) as a result of having been transferred 175 daily slots
              previously held by Alitalia through a State Aid decision of the Commission;779
            and that,
          (c)   Lufthansa does not bring a significant increment to ITA’s position at LIN, as it
              primarily operates from MXP in 2023.780
(649)   The Commission notes the following.
(650)    First, based on the results of its market investigation despite the existence of at least
     MXP within the Milan catchment area, competitors consider that slots at LIN give a
        strong competitive advantage to those who operate them, due to its strategic location
       and proximity to the city centre compared to MXP (see section 6.5.3.6 above, section
       11 below, and paragraph (655) et seq.). Therefore, the inability of competitors to
        obtain slots at LIN is considered a significant barrier to entry, despite the availability
        of slots at MXP.
(651)   Second, the Commission’s assessment on barriers to entry and expansion are not
         limited to those that are created because of the Transaction. Factors that make entry
        or expansion difficult, costly or impossible make it unlikely that competitors would
       expand or start new operations in the future, independently of whether those factors
         existed before the Transaction or whether they have been caused or exacerbated by
         the Transaction. Accordingly, the Commission takes all barriers to entry into account
       which give incumbent firms advantages over potential competitors, independently of
         the origin of those barriers.781
(652)   Third, in any event, the Parties are, already pre-Transaction the two largest entities
        operating from LIN in terms of  slot holding, with ITA being the largest one
        (53.5-55%), followed by Lufthansa which will bring an increment of around 7% of
         slot-holding, a non-negligible increment, post-Transaction.

(653)   The Commission concludes that the slot congestion LIN constitutes a significant
         barrier to entry and expansion as is apparent from the results of the Commission’s
        market investigation. In this context the Commission considers the following.782
(654)    First, LIN  is a  level 3 coordinated  airport under  the IATA Worldwide  Slot
        Guidelines,  which  indicates  that demand  significantly  exceeds  the  airport’s
         capacity.783  For  a  detailed  overview  of  the  congestion  levels  at  LIN,  see
         section 11.4.1.3 below.
(655)    In this context, the Commission notes the importance of operating during peak hours
         for the Parties’ competitors, based on their P2P business model (see paragraph (583)
        above).
(656)   In  this  context, the Commission’s market  investigation confirmed  that market
         participants consider LIN as a highly congested airport where it is extremely difficult
         to obtain appropriate slots. Notably, Luxair S.A. explained that despite “continuous
          efforts […] it has not managed to obtain any slots in LIN” and that the Transaction
       “would eventually hinder the entry of new competitors at LIN airport”.784 easyJet
         similarly explained that “LIN is an airport where slots are especially hard to access.
       LIN is a congested and slot constrained airport, and there has been little churn,
         unlike at other airports’ and that its “ability to effectively compete with the combined
          entity will depend on whether it will manage to obtain slots, and if so, on the number
         of those slots that it will manage to obtain” in LIN.785 Wizz Air confirmed that LIN
           is congested and noted that the Transaction “could be problematic in Linate Airport,
         especially considering the difficulty other market players face in obtaining slots”.786
        In addition, Air France-KLM not only confirmed that LIN is highly congested, but
       added that “growth is not possible given slots scarcity”.787 Lastly, both Ryanair and
        Vueling confirmed that LIN is congested and IAG added that “it is very difficult to
        obtain slots’ in LIN.788
(657)   Second, the results of the Commission’s market investigation confirmed that LIN and
     MXP are substitutable from the point of view of customers (when deciding from/to
       where to book their flights; under the O&D approach) while the results were mixed
       and the Commission  left the market definition open with respect to BGY (see
         section 6.5.3.6). By contrast, the Commission’s market investigation showed that
       LIN, MXP and BGY are not substitutable from the point of view of airlines when
        deciding from/to where to offer their flights (under the airport-by-airport approach,
        see section 6.10.1.3). See also paragraph (648) above.

       between the airports, further indicating the advantages stemming from being active

(664)   In response, the Commission notes that it does not contest the fact that there exist

       Commission considers that carriers operating at these secondary / regional airports
       do not compete as closely with Lufthansa and ITA as competitors operating at the
       same primary airport, such as FRA, MUC and ZRH (for more details please see 9.1.2
        above) and are therefore less competitive when competing with services of the
       merged entity from primary airports. Therefore, the Commission considers that its
         barriers to entry assessment remains valid as there are barriers to entry and expansion
         in terms of slot availability in terms of offering services that would compete closely
        with the merged entity and could constitute a strong constraint. The Commission
        notes that slot availability on secondary/regional airports means that technically entry
       on any of the routes could be technically feasible on the routes of concern, but only
       between secondary/regional airports. Nevertheless, the competitive constraint such
         services would generate would be limited. To reflect on the Parties’ claim that they
        “never heard  of [such] […]  concept”,809  the Commission  clarifies  that  for a
         (hypothetical) entrant to exert a sufficiently strong competitive pressure on Lufthansa
       and ITA on the direct-direct overlap routes, this entrant would likely need to have –
      among other characteristics – at least a partial presence at the primary airports on the
         particular   route,  not  only   at  secondary/regional   airports.  Therefore,  the
       Commission’s assessment above does not change as a result of the Parties arguments
         in the Response to the SO.810
9.1.4.3. Strong combined market position of the Parties post-Transaction  (i.e., combined
        market  presence on each  affected  route and combined  slot  portfolio  at hub
         airports/airports of focus)
(665)   In M.6663 - Ryanair/Aer Lingus III, the Commission concluded that the presence of
        a strong competitor on a route can act as a very significant barrier to entry and
         expansion.811 This dynamic – confirmed by the market investigation and the Parties’
         internal documents as explained below – is caused by a number of market conditions,
       some of which are particular to the air passenger services market.
(666)    First, a carrier with a strong presence (hub or base) at a particular airport has the
          ability to quickly re-allocate flights and frequencies in order to offer the most
          attractive schedules in response to new entry, for example by re-arranging departure
        times close to those of the entrant.812

(667)   Second, customers in the passenger air services market are relatively price sensitive,
       and the market is characterised by low switching costs and a relatively high degree of
         price transparency.
(668)   While  these market  features  can, dependent on  circumstances, promote  price
        competition, they may also allow for a strong incumbent to efficiently price new
        competitors out of the market. This is particularly true, if the incumbent benefits
       from a frequency advantage and/or economies of scale associated with having a large
        base at the relevant airport.813 The incumbent may also be able to (partially) offset
         the losses associated with aggressive price retaliation by feeding the traffic to other,
       more profitable routes and/or through servicing the more profitable passenger groups
          (e.g., business class, time-sensitive passengers), which typically require a frequent,
         regular schedule that only the incumbent can provide. As such, the presence of a
        strong competitor on a route, and the risk of aggressive retaliation, may in itself deter
      new entry and thereby act as a significant barrier to entry.814
(669)   In a submission made by the Parties, it is argued that the latter do not benefit from
         particular advantages at hub airports that would raise barriers to entry or expansion
         for competitors.815 This is because ITA only has a limited position at Lufthansa’s hub
         airports and/or airports of focus and only brings a minimal increment in terms of
          slots or shares of passengers, flights and seats and that similarly, Lufthansa does not
        bring a strong increment at ITA’s hub in Rome FCO where the combined position of
         the Parties remains moderate, with sufficient slots remaining for competitors to enter
        or expand.816
(670)   In this context, the Commission reiterates its view that its assessment on barriers to
         entry and expansion should not be and is not limited to those that are created or
        exacerbated because of the Transaction.
(671)   Furthermore, the Commission concludes that the Parties’ strong combined market
         position post-Transaction on the short-haul routes of concern, and  their strong
       combined slot portfolio at hub airports and/or other airports of focus would act as a
         barrier to entry and/or expansion on the short-haul routes of concern for the reasons
          listed below.
(672)   In the first place, post-Transaction, the Parties’ combined market shares in almost all
         the affected routes will be very high (for more information see sections 9.2, 9.3 and
        9.4 below), and in most cases indicative of a dominant position and at least of market
        power. These market shares would allow Lufthansa and ITA to take advantage of
          their slot-holding and economies of scale, and to potentially render their competitors’
          activities unprofitable. On this basis, the majority of competitor respondents to the
       Commission’s market investigation that expressed a view consider that Lufthansa
       and ITA’s combined presence on the affected routes will act as a strong barrier to
         entry and/or expansion.817 For example, on the city pairs Milan-Brussels and Rome-
         Brussels, Air France – KLM, which expressed an interest in entering through its LCC
        Transavia, specified that it has not yet decided whether to enter, and it will assess,

9.1.4.4. Airport charges at Lufthansa’s hub airports
(694)   The Commission concludes that the high airport charges at Lufthansa’s hub and
        focus airports constitute high barriers to entry and expansion on the short-haul routes
        of concern for the following reasons.
(695)    First, the Commission’s conclusion has been confirmed by the results of its market
         investigation, where the majority of competitor respondents that expressed a view
        consider the high airport charges at Lufthansa’s hub airports, to be barriers to entry
       and expansion on the short-haul routes of concern.
(696)   Second, according to the Parties’ submissions, the total cost per passenger in FRA
       amounts  to EUR 42.82,  in MUC EUR 29.49,  in ZRH EUR 35.81,  in BRU
     EUR 30.30 and in VIE EUR 29.90.848
(697)   In view of the relevant high fees per passenger, the Commission considers that they
         constitute a barrier to entry for the reasons set out in paragraph (690) below The
       Commission also notes that Ryanair suggested that in the case of Frankfurt and
       Munich Airports, Lufthansa might have the power to influence airport charges:
        “Lufthansa is a very significant player in Germany, and in particular MUC and FRA,
       and it is not in its best interest (both as a dominant airline in those airports but also
        as a minority shareholder of Fraport) to vote in favour of the reduction of airport
         costs in FRA and MUC. Notably, Ryanair considers that the presence of Lufthansa in
      FRA and MUC influences airport charges in that Lufthansa allows airport charges
         to remain high  to  disincentivise entry  in these  airports by low-cost  carriers.
        Therefore, Lufthansa is protecting its market by making sure barriers to entry such
        as high airport charges are not removed. Ryanair explains that Under the Airport
       Charges Directive, airports must consult with airlines on changes to charges. How
         the consultation is done depends on the airport, and may not always be by majority
         vote, but a proposal to increase costs can only realistically be resisted if the most
        important users object. If Lufthansa accepts increases in charges at airports where it
        has a significant share, then it is inevitable they will go through. In airports where
        Lufthansa holds the majority of  slots  (e.g., FRA and MUC), there will be no
         resistance  to charges  increases  at  that  airport from  users, because  it  is  in
        Lufthansa’s interest to keep costs high in order to keep other potential other –

(700)   Third, contrary to the Parties’ view that airport charges do not prevent LCC/ULCC
         carriers from being present on primary airports,853 the Commission understands that,
       due to their cost-oriented business model, high airport charges have a more negative
        impact on LCCs compared to full-service hub carriers, as the former’s business
       model is designed to capture the most price sensitive passenger demand. LCCs and
      ULCCs have lower margins to absorb potential fluctuations in their costs. Moreover,
          their business model is geared towards profiting on each and every customer as they
        cannot absorb losses of short-haul traffic on the higher margin long-haul operations
        as opposed to network  carriers. Furthermore, Ryanair explains  that “[l]ow-cost
         carriers have significantly lower profits per passenger than flag-carriers. Therefore, the
        margin for error for low-cost carriers is much smaller. Flag-carriers attract higher
         yielding customers who are willing to pay significantly higher fares to fly with their
        chosen carrier. Low-cost carriers rely on low costs to maintain the lowest fares to
          attract customers. When airport charges increase, flag-carriers business model allows
