(1122) On the Rome-Hamburg city pair the following plausible alternative geographic
        market definitions exist in line with the market definition findings on the catchment
         areas:
          (a)  On the Rome end of the route FCO and CIA belong to one catchment area (See
               section 6.5.3.9 above).
         (b)  On the Hamburg end of the route HAM and LBC may belong to one catchment
               area. Alternatively, LBC and HAM may be considered as a separate market
             (See section 6.5.3.12 above).
(1123)  The  Commission’s  assessment  below  considers  the  widest  plausible  market
         definition, which includes FCO and CIA on the Rome end of the route, and HAM
       and LBC on the Hamburg end of the route.
(1124)  However, the assessment below would remain applicable even in case the market
       would be defined more narrowly, encompassing fewer airports (i.e., only HAM on
         the Hamburg end of the route).
(1125)  The Commission notes that in case LBC on the Hamburg end of the route was
        considered as a separate geographic market, there would be no need to assess the
      Rome-LBC route, as there would be no overlap arising because of the activities of
         the Parties. Therefore, and due to the lack of overlapping activities at LBC, the
        (narrowest  possible)  alternative market  definition concerns  the catchment area
        including FCO and CIA on the Rome end of the route and HAM on the Hamburg
       end of the route.
(1126)  The Commission notes that due to the fact that both Lufthansa and its competitors
         currently operate between the same airports (FCO-HAM), and that ITA  is also
         currently planning to enter the same airport pair (i.e., FCO-HAM),1181 there is no
       need to assess this alternative market definitions. In addition, the market shares
       would remain unchanged, regardless of the market definition.

9.3.1.3. The Commission’s assessment
(1130)  For a merger with a potential competitor to have significant anti-competitive effects,
       two basic conditions must be fulfilled.
          (a)    First, the potential competitor must already exert a significant constraining
              influence or there must be a significant likelihood that it would grow into an
               effective competitive force. Evidence that a potential competitor has plans to
               enter a market in a significant way could help the Commission to reach such a
              conclusion. Contrary  to  the  Parties arguments,  if  the Commission  finds
               significant like likelihood that the potential competitor would grow into an
               effective competitive force, this condition is met.1189

(1142)  Third, contrary to the Parties’ view that there is sufficient competitive pressure on
         the route,1204 the Commission considers that the market  is highly concentrated.
        Together with Wizz Air, which entered on the route with 4 weekly frequencies year-
         round,1205 Lufthansa is the only other airline active on the Rome – Hamburg route
        with direct services, whereas, Air France-KLM has a very low market presence, and
        provides only indirect services. Accordingly, the Transaction would prevent the
        market structure increasing from two direct competitors (one network carrier and a
      ULCC) to three (two network carriers and a ULCC) (considering only those airlines
       which are providing direct services).
(1143)  Additionally, Marabu Airlines, indicated by the Parties as a competitor on the route
         for just one season (IATA Summer 2023 Season), is not active on the route anymore.
       Marabu Airlines is a recently founded Estonian Airline which is focused on leisure
          travel.  In response  to  the  questionnaire  of  the Commission, Marabu  Airlines
        submitted that its ticket sales are entirely handled by the German airline Condor
        (which is focused on leisure travel) and that it operates flights between Hamburg and
       Munich in Germany on the one hand, and Portugal, Spain, Sardinia, Croatia, Greece
       and Egypt on the other hand. It is therefore not active on the route Rome-Hamburg.
        Accordingly, Hamburg is not indicated as a destination on Marabu Airlines’ website
       and Marabu Airlines has not listed this route amongst routes it intends to enter.1206
         Lastly, the Parties confirm, and the data submitted by the Parties indicate, that
       Marabu Airlines did not submit capacity data for Rome-Hamburg for the Winter
        2023/24 and the Summer 2024 seasons.1207
(1144)  Neos, the only airline with a non-negligible market share on this route with a 5%

       Hamburg and Rome are inclusive tour charter flights which are operated on behalf of
         cruise operators. This means that customers cannot purchase dry seats solely for
         transportation, and without purchasing the entire service of the cruise operator. As
         indicated above in Section 6.7, the Commission considers that these services are not
         in the same product market as scheduled air passengers services.1208 The Parties
        confirm that to the best of their knowledge, Neos did not submit capacity data for
       Rome-Hamburg for the Winter 2023/24 season.1209

         in predatory pricing. They have network strength, pricing power, market power and
          slot flexibility throughout the day to keep competition out of the market. They can
        optimize their offer on specific route. They will also be the biggest customer at the

       would not have the competitive clout, nor the slot portfolio or pricing power to
       compete for profit where such unfair competition is present.”1212

         position  after the Transaction. As described  in Section  9.1.4.5, Lufthansa has
       managed to achieve and maintain consistently high market shares on such routes;
       where entry events are scarce and in the vast majority of the cases short-lived.
(1150)  The above shows, that contrary to the Parties arguments, even considering Wizz
         Air’s past successes in terms of entry into routes from Rome, the Commission cannot
        consider Wizz Air as a particularly stable and likely long-standing competitor based
       on the information available. The Commission notes, that even if it would consider
       Wizz Air as such, this would not change the overall conclusions drawn from the
       Commission’s competitive assessment because the existence of one competitor on
         the  route does  not  necessarily  indicate  that  the  Transaction would  not  raise
        competition concerns, especially considering the fact that Wizz Air  is a ULCC
         carrier with limited frequencies and a different business model compared to that of
        Lufthansa and ITA (see Section 9.1.2 above).1214

         particular paragraphs (586)-(587)). The majority of competitors that expressed a
       view in the Commission’s market investigation considered that Lufthansa and ITA
         are closer competitors of each other on many of the routes of interest compared to
       Wizz Air or other ULCCs (See section 9.1.2.1 above for more information). The
       Commission notes that the above does not mean that Wizz Air exerts no competitive
        pressure on Lufthansa on this route. However, it shows that the competitive pressure
        exerted by Wizz Air is limited, while ITA would be at least a close competitor to
        Lufthansa, if not the closest upon entry.1219
(1157)  Seventh, as further explained in section 9.1.4, there are several barriers to entry and
        expansion on the route.
(1158)  In the first place, the relevant airports are to an extent congested. In particular, HAM
           is a level 3 coordinated airport. Moreover, the average congestion level per hour
       band for the scheduled weekly flights of Lufthansa on the ROM-HAM pair are as
         follows: from ROM (FCO) during Summer IATA Season 2023 ranging between
       37-58% and from HAM ranging between 0-46%. During the Winter IATA Season
        2022/23 the same congestion levels were ranging between 44-63% (FCO) and
       21-46% (HAM).1220 In addition, from Hamburg more than half of the departing
         direct flights are operated by Lufthansa.1221 (See also 6.5.3.5 above).]
(1159)  In the second place, the Parties’ market share on the route and combined slot holding
         in HAM will be significantly high, indicative of market power and will act as a
         barrier to entry and expansion. Furthermore, the merged entity would hold a high
       number of slots at FCO. The Parties’ market shares and slot holdings are a strategy
        advantage that they can and do use to prevent entry or expansion by competitors
        and/or to make competitors reduce or terminate operations on a route; and this
         strategy has shown success  in  the  past (See  section  9.1.4.2 above  for more
         information). Specifically, the merged entity would account for around 51% of the
          flights at HAM airport as well as 25-27% of the flights at FCO airport.1222
(1160)  Despite the fact that the HAM catchment area is potentially served by two airports,
         the results of the Commission’s market investigation and internal documents of the
         Parties support that (i) “there is a general preference of the majority of passengers to
           fly from their local airport”1223 and thus entering a secondary airport would not allow
        competitors to compete closely with the Parties (see section 9.1.2.2 above for more
         information); and that  (ii) Lufthansa uses  its strong market position in primary
         airports to eliminate competition on both primary and secondary airports of the same
        catchment area. (See section 9.1.4.3 above for more information and in particular
        Figure 54).
(1161)  Eighth, there is specific evidence showing that the Transaction is likely to result in
        negative effects.
(1162)  In the first place, while some indicated that they did not know, the vast majority of
        competitors active on short-haul routes and expressing an opinion considered the
        impact of the Transaction on potential competition or future competition on routes
       between Italy on the one hand and Germany, Austria, Belgium and/or Switzerland on

9.3.1.3.2.     There are no sufficient number of other potential competitors which could
             maintain sufficient competitive pressure post-Transaction
(1165)  The Commission’s market investigation has not been able to confirm the likely,
        timely and sufficient entry by any other carrier than the entry by Wizz Air discussed
       above in section 9.3.1.3.1.1226 In addition, the Commission’s investigation has not
        revealed any further information which would substantiate the Parties claim that the
         route is attractive for new entrants.
9.3.1.4. Conclusion
(1166)  In light of the common considerations on short-haul routes explained in section 9.1,
       and in view of the above findings related in particular to the fact that Lufthansa holds
        a dominant market  position on  the Rome-Hamburg  route,  that  the market  is
        concentrated with only one other competitor active (Wizz Air), that ITA would likely
       become the main and a close, if not the closest, competitor of Lufthansa absent the
         Transaction, that there are barriers to entry and expansion, that there is a lack of
        prospect of likely, timely and sufficient entry on the route and that there is specific
        evidence on the likely negative effects of the Transaction, the Commission concludes
         that the Transaction would significantly impede effective competition as a result of
         the creation or strengthening of a dominant position under any plausible market
         definition on the route Rome – Hamburg by removing the potential competition
        exerted by ITA on the market.

(1169) On the Milan-Vienna city pair the following plausible alternative geographic market
         definitions exist in line with the market definition findings on the catchment areas:
          (a)  On the Milan end of the route LIN and MXP may belong to one catchment area
              together with BGY or, alternatively, LIN and MXP may be separate from BGY
             (See 6.5.3.6 above).
         (b)  On the Vienna end of the route VIE and BTS may belong to one catchment
              area or VIE may be considered as a separate market from BTS (See 6.5.3.11
              above).
(1170)  The  Commission’s  assessment  below  considers  the  widest  plausible  market
         definition, in which LIN, MXP and BGY on the one hand, and VIE with BTS on the
         other hand belong to the same catchment areas. Therefore, the market shares and
        concerns outlined below reflect this plausible definition.
(1171)  However, the assessment below would remain applicable even in case the market
       would  be  defined more  narrowly,  encompassing  fewer  airports  (where  the
        Transaction would still give rise to potential horizontal overlaps).
(1172)  The Commission notes that if on the Milan end of the route:
          (a)   only LIN and MXP were to be considered, the concerns outlined below would
              not only continue  to be  relevant under any  plausible  alternative market
               definitions on the Vienna end of the route but would be amplified due the
             removal of a significant portion of Ryanair’s activities from the competitive
             landscape as Ryanair mostly operates from BGY. In this context, the narrowest
              possible market definition would be the one where, the activities of the Parties
            would overlap on LIN and MXP on the Milan end of the route and VIE on the
            Vienna end of the route.
         (b)    if only BGY were to be considered on the Milan end of the route, there would
             be no need to assess any of the overlaps under any plausible market definition
            on the Vienna end of the route because there would be no overlap arising due
               to the activities of the Parties (as neither operates from BGY). .
(1173)  The Commission also notes that if on the Vienna end of the route:
          (a)   Only VIE were to be considered, the concerns outlined below would not only
              continue to be relevant but would be amplified due to the reduction of
              Ryanair’s activities, under all plausible market definitions on the Milan end of
              the route.
         (b)  Only BTS were to be considered, there would be no need to assess any of the
              overlaps under any plausible market definition on the Milan end of the route
             because there would be no overlap arising due to the activities of the Parties (as
               neither operates from BTS).
(1174)  The Parties' market share would increase under all the plausible narrower market
         definitions where the Transaction gives rise to horizontal overlaps (i.e., with fewer
         airports considered) since this would lead to a reduction of Ryanair’s activities.

9.3.2.2. Lufthansa and MEF’s view
(1176)  Lufthansa and MEF submit that Lufthansa (Austrian Airlines) and Ryanair are the
       main airlines serving the route Milan-Vienna. The Parties explained that if ITA was
         to operate this route, the merged entity would face a sufficient pressure from (i)
        Ryanair which held a very strong market share of 75% in Summer 2023 IATA
       Season and increased its frequencies both Winter IATA 2023/2024 and Summer
      IATA 2024, and  (ii) potential additional entry or expansion by airlines such as
         easyJet and Wizz Air which already operated the route and would not face any slot
          restriction that could prevent them from entering the route. Moreover, the Parties
        submit that ÖBB offers a daily direct overnight train connection between Milan and
       Vienna that constitutes a viable alternative for some passengers.1229 In response to
         the Commission’s Article 6(1)(c) decision Lufthansa and MEF have added that the
       Commission (i) should perform a route-specific closeness of competition assessment,
            (ii) should consider the airport of operation of Lufthansa, its competitors and ITA,
       and   (iii)  did  not  make  an  accurate  interpretation  of  Lufthansa’s  internal
        documents.1230 In their Response to the SO, the Parties argue that [details on ITA’s
         future plans]. Moreover, the Parties note that, as ITA is currently not active in
        Vienna,  its entry in VIE would result in sunk costs and significant additional
        investments which need  to be taken  into account,  especially considering also
        Ryanair’s active presence. The Parties also consider that evidence that ITA would
       become Lufthansa’s closest competitor upon entry is “very thin” while Ryanair has
       been growing on  this  route. The  Parties  also argue  that  there  is  confidential
        information on potential new entry in the Commission’s case file and contest that the
     LCC presence in VIE would be shrinking based on certain metrics.1231

9.3.2.3. The Commission’s assessment
(1178)  For a merger with a potential competitor to have significant anti-competitive effects,
       two basic conditions must be  fulfilled, as explained in paragraph (400) above.
        Evidence that a potential competitor has plans to enter a market in a significant way
        could help the Commission to reach such a conclusion.1235
(1179)  For the reasons set out below, the Commission concludes, that the Transaction would
         significantly impede effective competition as a result of the creation or strengthening
        of a dominant position on the route Milan – Vienna by removing the potential
        competition exerted by ITA on the market. In any event, the Commission also
        concludes that the Transaction would also significantly impede effective competition
        as a  result of the elimination of important competitive constraints  that ITA’s
         potential market entry had exerted on Lufthansa on the route Milan-Vienna.

       Season and will hold a market share of 57% in the Summer IATA Season 2024. The
       Commission notes that large majority (around 75%) of the operations of Ryanair on
         the Milan-Vienna route is from BGY which suggests less close competition between
        Ryanair and Lufthansa and (potentially) ITA as explained above in paragraph (1201).
(1192)  Second, Lufthansa does not currently compete with a network carrier on Milan –
        Vienna. Instead,  it competes solely with an ULCC. Accordingly, the Transaction
       would prevent the market structure from increasing from two competitors (one
        network carrier and a ULCC) to three (two network carriers and a ULCC).
(1193)  Fourth, Ryanair is unlikely to exert a sufficiently strong competitive constraint on
         the merged entity’s operations in the future. A large majority (around 75%) of the
        operations of Ryanair on the Milan-Vienna route is already from BGY as explained
         in paragraph (1201) of this Decision. While Ryanair has expressed  its general
         intention to continue operating at VIE, the Commission considers that there is the
         clear risk that Ryanair as a dynamic and cost-driven airline would discontinue
        operating or operating at lower scale the route Milan-Vienna and/or more generally
          at VIE in the medium- and long-term for the following reasons: In the first place, the
     ULCC competitors Ryanair and Wizz Air (which is currently not active on this route
       and plans to maintain this situation dependent on the outcome of the Transaction)1255
       have both explained to the Commission that (i) they have a general preference for
        low-cost secondary / regional airports as cost driven carriers and (ii) it is pivotal for
       them to ensure that each and every short haul passenger generates profit in order for
          their low-cost business model to function. In particular:
          (a)   Ryanair has submitted that “[t]here is a general bias toward flag carriers
             [such as Austrian] that immediately puts Ryanair at a disadvantage”  (i.e.
             customers have a preference for flag/network carriers as opposed to ULCCs).
             Moreover, Ryanair explained that “Low-cost carriers have significantly lower
                profits per passenger than flag-carriers. Therefore, the margin for error for
              low-cost  carriers  is much  smaller.  Flag-carriers  attract  higher  yielding
             customers who are willing to pay significantly higher fares to fly with their
             chosen carrier. Low-cost carriers rely on low costs to maintain the lowest fares
               to attract customers”. Ryanair added that “When airport charges increase,
               flag-carriers business model allows them to pass on cost increases to the
             customer without impacting demand to the same extent that passing cost
              increases on to customers would for a low-cost carrier. As explained above,
              Lufthansa’s business model allows them to absorb cost increases by passing
            them onto the customer. As low-cost carriers cannot do this without impacting
            demand, cost increases hurt Lufthansa’s competition and often reduce in
              capacity cuts that result in Lufthansa gaining higher market share on routes
            and in airports without having to increase capacity themselves. As a result,
            consumers end up paying  higher  fares”. These  statements  indicate  that
              Ryanair’s position at primary airports in general (such as VIE) is far more
              precarious than that of Lufthansa and ITA, which are capable of extracting
              higher prices from passengers and offset any of their potential losses on short-
              haul by relying on their long-haul operations. Ryanair also explained that it had
               to cease its operation in FRA and close its base in BRU due to airport charge

         (604). While BTS may be in the catchment area encompassing VIE, these ULCCs
       would then lose the level-playing field maintained by having operations in a primary
          airport, and customers would lose convenient access to the air transport services of
         these ULCCs. This would result in less close competition between Lufthansa and the

       Commission, Ryanair has explained that, while it may open new route or expand on

         airports as seen above [in VIE, BRU, ZRH, FRA, MUC and DUS],  it becomes
        extremely difficult for Ryanair to compete. Loyalty programs, bias towards national
         carrier and feeder  traffic for long-haul  flights give Lufthansa and Lufthansa’s

       from being profitable on Lufthansa dominated routes and airports and as a result we
       have had to leave.”1263 In view of the above, while Ryanair may currently have a
         relatively strong presence and some growth perspective  at VIE, based on  its
         substantiated submissions, it appears that Ryanair is deprioritizing / exiting routes
       where it competes with Lufthansa. In particular, Ryanair has submitted that it has
        cancelled the routes Oslo Torp-Vienna, Dortmund-Vienna, Kosice-Vienna, Menorca-
        Vienna, and Sibiu-Vienna. On all of these routes Lufthansa currently has a strong
        market position (market shares above 50 %) according to Ryanair as indicated
         above.1264 Considering also the slot portfolio which would become available to
        Lufthansa on the Milan-end of the route post-Transaction (in particular a dominant
         position at LIN) and the fact that Milan-Vienna would become a route for the merged
         entity between two airports where it holds a very strong, if not dominant position
          after the Transaction,  it cannot be excluded that the combined entity would be
         successful in achieving a Ryanair exit or capacity reduction on the route. This could
          result in achieving a dominant or even monopoly position for the merged entity as
       opposed  to a  scenario absent  the  Transaction, where dynamic competition  is
        considerably more likely to prevail.
(1198)  In the fourth place, evidence shows that competition is limited on routes between
         airports where Lufthansa holds a strong market position within the DACHB area.
       The route Milan-Vienna would become a route between airports where Lufthansa
        holds a strong,  if not dominant, position after the Transaction. As described in
         section 9.1.4.5, Lufthansa has managed to achieve and maintain consistently high
        market shares on such routes; entry events are scarce and in the vast majority of the
        cases short-lived.

        This also indicates that – even if they would operate from different airports on the
       Milan end of the route, the Parties would compete closely with each other, as two

         the past years on  this route,  this does not change the  facts  that the route  is
        concentrated with two players present and Lufthansa and ITA would compete closely
       upon ITA’s entry.1271
(1206)  Lastly, the Commission notes that the overall travel times submitted by the Parties
        (considering the travel time from city centre to city centre on both ends of the route)
         also show that airlines operating a city pair from secondary airports of proximity do
        not compete as closely with airlines operating a route from the same primary
          airports. Notably, the overall travel time considering MXP and VIE (Ryanair and
        Lufthansa present)  is around 2 hours 19-24 minutes. The overall travel time  is
        approximately 2 hours 9 minutes when considering BGY and VIE (Ryanair present).
        In contrast the overall travel time  is approximately 2 hours 55 minutes when
        considering BGY and BTS (Ryanair present). This shows that Lufthansa and ITA
       would (upon ITA’s entry) compete closely with each other considering the entirety
        of their activities and the shorter travel times than they do with at least a significant
         portion of Ryanair’s activities (those focused on BTS rather than VIE).1272

        scheduled weekly flights of Lufthansa on the Milan-Vienna city pair are as follows:

(1212)  In the third place, the Parties’ combined slot holding in VIE and LIN will be
         significantly high, indicative of market power and will act as a barrier to entry and
        expansion. The Parties’ market shares and slot holdings are a strategy advantage that
        they can and do use to prevent entry by competitors; and this strategy has shown

          at all direct flights departing from VIE, Lufthansa is historically strong at this airport,
       and continues to have a share above 40% considering direct flights departing from
         VIE.1278

9.3.2.4. Conclusion
(1220)  In light of the common considerations on short-haul routes explained in section 9.1,
       and in view of the above findings related in particular to the fact that Lufthansa holds
        a sizeable market position on the Milan-Vienna route, that the market is concentrated
        with only one other competitor active, that the medium- and long-term position of
         the current ULCC competitors in the primary airport VIE is uncertain in the light of
        Lufthansa’s aggressive strategies, that ITA would likely become the main and a
         close, if not the closest, competitor of Lufthansa absent the Transaction, that there
         are barriers to entry and expansion, that there is a lack of prospect of likely, timely
       and  sufficient entry on the route,  that  train services do not exert a  sufficient
        competitive constraint and that there is specific evidence on the likely negative
         effects of the Transaction, the Commission concludes, that the Transaction would
         significantly impede effective competition as a result of the creation or strengthening
        of a dominant position under any plausible market definition on the route Milan-
       Vienna by removing the potential competition exerted by ITA on the market. In any
         event, for the same reasons, the Commission concludes that the Transaction would
         significantly impede effective competition as a result of the elimination of important
        competitive constraints that ITA’s potential market entry had exerted on Lufthansa
       on the route Milan-Vienna.
9.3.3.   Conclusion
(1221)  In light of the common considerations on short-haul routes explained in section 9.1,
       and the considerations above regarding the routes of concerned, the Commission
        concludes that (i) in the Rome-Hamburg route the Transaction would significantly
       impede effective competition as a  result of the creation or strengthening of a
       dominant position under any plausible market definition and  (ii) in the Milan –
       Vienna route the Transaction would significantly impede effective competition as a
          result of the creation or strengthening of a dominant position or, in any event, as a
          result of the elimination of important competitive constraints that ITA’s potential
        market entry had exerted on Lufthansa) under any plausible market definition.
9.4.    Competitive assessment of direct-indirect overlaps (current)
9.4.1.   Introduction
(1222)  The Transaction gives rise to 287 direct/indirect overlaps on O&D routes between
          Italy on the one hand, and Austria, Belgium, Germany and Switzerland on the other.
      As explained in section 6.6 above, indirect short-haul flights do not generally provide
        a competitive constraint to direct short-haul flights absent exceptional circumstances,
         for example, the direct connection does not allow for a one-day return trip or the
        share of indirect flights in the overall market is significant.
(1223)  Given that, as eventually confirmed at this stage by the market investigation in the
         present case and evidence in the file, it cannot be excluded that indirect flights exert
        a competitive constraint on direct flights, the Commission will consider that direct
       and indirect flights between the same O&D are part of the same market when

         data room process.

[PÁGINA PDF 281]
         indirect flights represent at least 10% of passengers on the route (see section 6.6
        above).
(1224)  In this context, the Commission clarifies that it does not take into account indirect
          flights in its assessment of the direct/direct overlaps in sections 9.2 and 9.3 above,
        unless the share of passengers choosing to fly indirectly on each of these routes is
       above 10%. The only routes where the share of passengers flying indirectly is above
      10% are the Milan-Hamburg (actual overlap) and Rome-Hamburg (potential overlap)
         routes,  and  thus,  the Commission  considers  indirect  flights  and  takes  into
         consideration the competitive constraints exerted by indirect flights on direct flights
         (for more information, see Sections 9.2.4 and 9.3.1 above).
9.4.2.   Criteria for the assessment of likely problematic direct/indirect overlapping routes
(1225)  The Commission, consistent with its previous practice,1285 has applied the following
           filters for direct/indirect overlap routes to exclude likely unproblematic routes from
         the scope of its investigation (the criterion must have been met in all the four last
        completed IATA Seasons (i.e., Winter IATA 2021/2022 to Summer IATA 2023):
          (a)  The Parties’ combined market share was below 25%; or
         (b)  One of the Parties had a market share below 2%; or
          (c)   Short-haul routes where the total share of indirect operations in the relevant
             market was below 10%; or
         (d)  At least one end of the city pair is outside the EU and the total annual traffic
           was below 30 000 passengers; or
          (e)  The route was below the HHI thresholds of paragraph 20 of the Horizontal
            Merger Guidelines.
(1226) By applying these filters, the Commission excluded 234 routes from the scope of its
         investigation.
(1227)  Furthermore, following the exclusion of 234 routes, in order to assess whether a
         significant impediment to effective competition would arise on any of the remaining
       53 routes with direct/indirect overlaps, the Commission conducted an individual,
         route-by-route assessment, and although  its assessment was not  limited  to,  it
        focussed in particular on, those where:
          (a)  The Parties’ combined market share was equal to or above 40% in at least one
              of the four IATA Seasons between IATA Winter 2021/2022 and IATA
          Summer 2023; and,
         (b)  The increment brought by the Transaction was equal to or above 5% in at least
            one of the four IATA Seasons between IATA Winter 2021/2022 and IATA
          Summer 2023.
(1228)  The Commission’s approach is in line with (i) paragraph 17 of its Horizontal Merger
         Guidelines, which indicates that very large market shares (50% or above) may in
        themselves be evidence of the existence of a dominant position but that also mergers
        with firms holding market shares between 40% and 50% could lead to the creation or
        strengthening of a dominant position; and (ii) Union Courts’ past decisional practice,


1285     Cases M.9287 – Connect Airways / Flybe, paragraph 379; M.7541 – IAG/Aer Lingus, paragraphs 151
          et seq.; and, M.7333 – Alitalia/Etihad, paragraphs 171 et seq. See also Case M.5830 – Aegean/Olympic,
         footnote 365.


                                    279

[PÁGINA PDF 282]
       where they consistently held that there is a presumption of dominance when an
        undertaking enjoys a market share of 50% or above. Moreover, this view is also in
         line with the Commission’s past decisional practice, as it focusses the Commission’s
        assessment on  those overlapping  routes where  the increment brought by  the
        Transaction is 5% or above to identify those markets where the competition removed
           is likely to matter for customers.1286
(1229)  That said, the Commission has also taken into account in its assessment the pre-
         existing market position of the merging parties, mainly whether one of the merging
         parties already holds an entrenched dominant or near-monopoly position on the
         route, and whether the Transaction would therefore remove in essence the only
        outstanding competitive constraint in the market, even if the increment in market
        share is relatively low.
(1230)  Based on  its  route-by-route  assessment,  the Commission  considers  that  the
        Transaction would significantly impede effective competition in either both or one of
         the two IATA seasons on 8 routes.
(1231) On 7 of these routes, (i) the Transaction would result in a high combined market
        share held by the Parties post-Transaction (>50%), (ii) the increment brought by the
        Transaction would be sizeable (>5%), (iii) the passengers choosing indirect flights
         represent a significant amount in relation to the overall market size (>10%); and, (iv)
         there are no other competitors apart from one of the two Parties (Lufthansa)
        operating direct flights (either from the same airports or from secondary airports of
         proximity). These routes are the following: from Brindisi to Düsseldorf (‘BDS –
       DUS’), from Bari to Frankfurt (‘BRI – FRA’), from Bari to Munich (‘BRI – MUC’),
       from Bari to Hamburg (‘BRI – HAM’), from Naples to Frankfurt (‘NAP – FRA’),
       from Naples to Düsseldorf (‘NAP – DUS’), and from Cagliari to Munich (‘CAG –
       MUC’).
(1232) On 1 of these routes, (i) the Transaction would result in a high combined market
        share held by the Parties post-Transaction (>50%), (ii) the increment brought by the
        Transaction would be smaller than 5%, but there are specific circumstances related to
        expected growth by ITA or an expected monopoly position after the Transaction
        (meaning  that  the  Transaction would remove  in  essence  the  only remaining
         constraint),  (iii) the passengers choosing indirect  flights represent a significant
       amount in relation to the overall market size (>10%); and, (iv) there are no other
        competitors apart from one of the two Parties (Lufthansa) operating direct flights
         (either from the same airports or from secondary airports of proximity). This route is
        Naples – Hamburg (‘NAP – HAM’).

(1241)  For the direct/indirect short-haul routes where the Commission was concerned about
        a potential significant impediment to effective competition, ITA’s indirect offer
        cannot be considered a significant competitive constraint over Lufthansa’s direct
          offer. Given that the latter does not offer direct services daily, the driver for indirect
          traffic is the fact that the direct offering is not available to passengers on a daily basis
        (and hence the indirect option becomes attractive only on the days of the week when
        a direct flight is not available). According to the Parties, this means that ITA’s
         indirect offer is complementary to and not in competition with Lufthansa’s direct
          offering.1314 That the city pairs where the Commission was concerned about a
         significant impediment  to  effective  competition   are  characterised by  strong
         seasonality (i.e., the city pairs mostly popular over the summer season and serve as
        holiday / leisure routes) which justifies why the share of passengers flying indirectly
           is lower over the summer seasons and why the share of direct flights is low over the
        winter seasons. Thus, indirect flights do not provide a material competitive constraint
         to direct flights over summer.1315

         services. That is to say, the overlap arising on some of these routes over Winter
      IATA Season is, in reality, an indirect/indirect one. Consequently, the Parties argue

         Transaction, the Parties’ services only overlap indirectly for a significant share of the
         relevant seasons, these indirect/indirect overlaps should be assessed accordingly, and
         separately from the direct/indirect overlaps.1316

(1251)  Fourth, the Commission notes that the use of bi-directional data to count the overall
        market sizes is in line with its past decisional practice. For example, in M.3280 – Air
       France  / KLM,1322 the Commission explains that  it uses MIDT1323  (i.e., Market

1322     Case M.3280 – Air France / KLM.
1323     Case M.3280 – Air France / KLM, paragraphs 86 et seq.


                                    286

[PÁGINA PDF 289]
        Information Data  Tapes, which  is  information  sourced from  airline booking
        systems). The number of passengers reported using MIDT corresponds to the sum of
         the number of bookings for each of the two legs or one-way flights (and not for each
         return flight); and thus provide bi-directional data, in the sense that they count each
        passenger twice if they purchased a round-trip and once if they purchased a one way
           trip.
(1252)  Moreover, in M.5335 – Lufthansa/SN Airholding,1324 and M.5747 – Iberia/British
         Airways,1325 the parties refer to MIDT traffic data. Finally, even though in M.5747 –
         Iberia/British Airways, the Commission acknowledges certain limitations of MIDT
         in terms of coverage  (i.e.,  it does not cover direct bookings with airlines, thus
        excluding LCCs) it did not change approach in terms of the use of bi-directional data,
         for the application of exclusion filters (i.e., those mentioned in paragraph (1222)
        above). The Commission has followed this practice of using bi-directional data ever
         since. Deviating from this practice now, in line with what the Parties suggest, would
          result in doubling the filter the Commission has used in the past to exclude certain
         routes from its review.
(1253)  Fifth, the Commission’s exclusion filters (i.e., those mentioned in paragraph (1222)
        above) are consistent with its past decisional practice.
(1254)  In the first place, the Parties assert that the application of a 30 000 annual passenger
         threshold is necessary for the assessment of short-haul direct/indirect overlaps.1326
        Nonetheless, this view is inaccurate because, as established in the Commission’s past
         decisional practice (see paragraph (1222) above), this filter does not constitute a
        general filter applied by the Commission, unless one end of the city pair is outside
         the EU.
(1255)  Even though the Commission took into consideration the number of passengers on
        intra-EU short-haul direct/indirect overlaps in the past,1327 this was one element
       among others in the Commission’s assessment and was not used as filter to exclude
         routes entirely from the Commission’s assessment. Furthermore, the Commission is
        not bound to follow its past practice if that means that it would leave unaddressed
        markets where the Transaction would significantly impede effective competition.
       The Commission, however, reviews the past decisions that the Parties refer to below:
– M.9287 – Connect Airways/Flybe

(1256)  In Connect Airways/Flybe, the transaction gave rise to 22 direct/indirect short-haul
         affected markets after the application of the filters in paragraph (1222) above,1328 Out
         of these 22 overlaps, all of which were ultimately cleared, the Commission did not
         find a significant impediment to effective competition on the basis of very low
        passenger numbers on 8 routes. On 5 of these 8 routes, the annual passenger number
       was <5 000, whereas for the remaining 3, the annual passenger number was between
       15 000 and 30 000.

(1257) By way of comparison, the present case gave rise to 53 direct/indirect short-haul
         affected markets  after the application of the  filters in paragraph (1222) above
            (i.e., more than double the overlaps of Connect Airways / Flybe, indicating that the
        network issue arising in this present case is, more significant than that in Connect
        Airways / Flybe. This is because Lufthansa and ITA are network carriers which cover
       more routes, by offering connectivity to many destinations from their hubs, and thus
         resulting in several overlaps). Furthermore,  if the Commission were to disregard
       from  its assessment, routes where the annual passenger number did not exceed
       30 000 in its assessment of the short-haul direct/indirect overlaps arising as a result
         of this Transaction,  it would have dismissed, without conducting a route-specific
        assessment 22 routes (i.e., almost three times the routes cleared in Connect Airways /
        Flybe based on annual traffic) and disregarding (i) the fact that on many of those
         routes, the Transaction would result in the elimination of the only competitive
         constraint  imposed  on  Lufthansa’s  direct  operations,  namely  ITA’s  indirect
         operations; and (ii) the effects on connectivity in on these routes resulting from the
        fewer available options, in terms of alternative carriers operating on the routes, post-
         Transaction.
(1258)  In the present case the Commission did not raise concerns on any routes with annual
        passenger number <20 0001329, whereas  it only finds a significant impediment to
         effective competition on 4 routes where the annual passenger number was >20 000
       and <30 000 (and  in 3  of  these  routes,  significant impediment  to  effective
        competition was found only on a seasonal basis). In the present case, the application
         of a 30 000 passenger  filter or fragmentation by season) to identify potentially
        problematic routes(would (i) disaggregate a competition problem caused by network
        competition; and (ii) would prevent the Commission from effectively looking into
         the clearly more significant network issue arising in this case (i.e., significantly more
         direct/indirect overlaps arising as a result of this Transaction) as a result of the
        Transaction resulting of the merger of the significant route coverage and networks
       which two network carriers, Lufthansa and ITA bring to the table and (iii) into routes
        with a larger amount of passengers in the aggregate compared to Connect Airways /
        Flybe. Consequently, it would be unjustifiable to leave unaddressed markets where it
        cannot  be  excluded  based on  objective  criteria  that  the  Transaction would
         significantly impede effective competition (and more specifically, that would result
         in a monopoly post-Transaction) based on a higher passenger traffic filter that was
         not, in any event, defined by the Commission as a filter for intra-EEA routes (for the
           filters, see 9.4.2 above).
– M.7333 – Alitalia/Etihad

(1259)   In Alitalia/Etihad, the Commission concluded no significant impediment to effective
        competition on one short-haul route (i.e., Copenhagen-Catania for the IATA winter
        season)  because  passenger  numbers  were  very  low  during   this  season
            (i.e., <3 000).1330 As  indicated  in  paragraph  (1255)  above,  in  this  case  the
       Commission  did  not  raise  concerns  on  any  routes  with  annual  passenger
       number <20 000.1331

–  M.6607 – US Airways/American Airlines

(1260)  The  Parties  compare  the  assessment  of  27  direct/indirect  overlaps  in US
        Airways/American Airlines with the direct/indirect short-haul overlaps arising in this
          case.1332 However, this comparison is inaccurate, as the direct/indirect overlaps in the
        former relate to routes where at least one end of the city pair is outside the EU and
         thus, the filter for the exclusion of routes of less than 30 000 passengers becomes
         applicable, as already explained in 9.4.2 above. By contrast, in this present case the
       Commission looked intosignificant impediment to effective competition in relation to
         direct/indirect overlaps in routes where both ends of the city pairs are located inside
         the EU. Considering that the Commission set different filters for routes with (at least)
       one leg outside of the EU and for routes with both legs within the EU as already
         indicated in paragraph (1222) above, US Airways/American Airlines is not a relevant
        precedent that binds the Commission’s assessment in this present case.
– M.3280 – Air France/KLM

(1261)  The Parties compare the assessment of 2 direct/indirect overlaps in Air France/KLM
        with the direct/indirect short-haul overlaps arising in this case.1333 However, this
        comparison is inaccurate.
(1262)  The Commission’s analysis of the Eindhoven – Paris city pair in Air France / KLM
        concerned potential overlaps,1334 and therefore, the question considered was whether
         the route would give incentives for market entry by one of the two parties. In the
         present case, the Commission only looked into the effects of the Transaction on
         actual overlaps in  its short-haul direct/indirect assessment, and thus, looked into
         significant impediment to effective competition on city pairs where both Parties are
        already  active (one with a  direct and the other with an  indirect connection).
        Moreover, similarly to Air France  / KLM, in the present case the Commission
        assessed and decided to not raise concerns on 7 direct/indirect short-haul potential
        overlaps where it considered that it would be too speculative to assume that one of
         the Parties would have the incentive to enter.
(1263)  Additionally,  as  regards  the  Clermont/Ferrand-Amsterdam  city  pair  in  Air
       France/KLM, the Commission concluded that no competition concerns were deemed
         to arise for a combination of reasons, including a low annual passenger number of
       <8 000 and the fact that less than 10% of transfer passengers took connecting flights
         in Amsterdam.1335 In this context, the Commission repeats its view that, as indicated
         in paragraph (1255) above, in the present case the Commission did not raise concerns
       on any routes with annual passenger number <20 0001336 with the exception of one
         route with 19 784 passengers (i.e., more than double the annual passenger number
        concerned on the Clermont/Ferrand-Amsterdam city pair in Air France/KLM).
(1264)   In the second place, the Parties argue for an application of the  filter excluding
        competition concerns from short-haul routes where the  total share of  indirect

(1265)  Further this filter is merely a first step in the analysis, identifying the routes where
         connectivity depends also on indirect services and where accordingly customers
        place value on indirect connections, across years and seasons. Even,  after the
         application of  this  filter,  routes where  indirect  flights do not  exert  sufficient

         the other merging party.
(1266)  The application in the present case of the criterion (i) over every relevant season

          Parties, would neither be justified nor appropriate, as it  not only would imply an
         unjustified departure from prior Commission practice but, more importantly, it would
        prevent the Commission from effectively looking into routes where the overall share
         of indirect flights remains substantial, and, in some cases, where the Transaction
       would result in the last constraint to the (only existing) direct flight removed or in

(1267)  In the third place, the Parties assert that the application of a “around 5% increment”

       on routes where the increment brought by the Transaction was 5% or above over at
          least one IATA Season between Winter IATA 2021/2022 and Summer 2023 already
       shows a more lenient approach than the Commission’s filters.
(1268)  Furthermore, the Commission notes the following regarding  its past decisional
         practice cited by the Parties.1338
– M.9287 – Connect Airways/Flybe

– M.8964 – Delta/Air France-KLM/Virgin Group/Virgin Atlantic

(1270)  The Commission concluded  that an increment  of up  to 5% on an  affected
         direct/indirect overlap was very low (also taking into account that other airlines
       would exert competitive pressure on the parties post-transaction).1340 The more
         lenient approach that the Commission followed in the above-mentioned case is in
         line with the Commission’s approach in the present case, where the Commission
        focuses its route-by-route assessment mostly on routes where the increment brought
       by the Transaction was equal to or above 5% in at least one of the four IATA
        Seasons between IATA Winter 2021/2022 and IATA Summer 2023 (see paragraph
        (1224) above).
(1271)  Furthermore,  the  Commission  notes   that,  in  Delta/Air  France-KLM/Virgin
        Group/Virgin Atlantic, the Commission did not focus  its assessment on certain
         direct/indirect overlaps, due to a combination of elements,  e.g., the increment
        brought by the transaction being up to 5%, together with the fact that other direct
        competitors were  active and  exercising  competitive  pressure on  the  parties.
         Similarly, in  the present case, the Commission considered but eventually excluded
       from its scope of concerns, routes where other direct competitors are active, and only
        focuses its assessment on routes where (i) there are no other competitors active and
         offering direct flights, and (ii) the competitors offering indirect flights collectively
        only capture an insignificant market share (a competitive fringe) compared to the
       combined market share of the  Parties, which resembles a monopoly or quasi-
       monopoly situation.
–  M.7541 – IAG/Aer Lingus

(1272)  The approach taken in the case M.7541 – IAG/Aer Lingus  is in line with the
       Commission’s approach in this present case as well, as the Commission focuses its
         route-by-route assessment mostly on routes where the increment brought by the
        Transaction was equal to or above 5% in at least one of the four IATA Seasons
       between IATA Winter 2021/2022 and IATA Summer 2023 (see paragraph (1224)
        above).
(1273)  Exceptionally, for the route NAP – HAM, where the increment brought by the
        Transaction would be  smaller  than 5%,  see  paragraph  (1229) above  for an
        explanation of the specific circumstances that led to the Commission finding a
         significant impediment to effective competition.
(1274)  Additionally, it shall be noted that that the low increment brought by the Transaction
       was accepted to justify that the Transaction does not result in significant impediment
         to effective competition in several short-haul direct/indirect overlaps where the
       Commission considered  it as a sufficient  justification  (e.g., city pair Naples –
        Düsseldorf over the Summer IATA season, Bologna – Zurich and Genoa - Munich).
(1275)  Furthermore, the application of the criterion (i) over every relevant season and/or
            (ii) separately by Summer and Winter IATA seasons as suggested by the Parties,1341
       would neither be justified nor appropriate, as it would part from prior Commission
         practice without any justification and prevent the Commission from effectively
        looking into routes where there may be competition concerns, in particular where the

(1276)  Sixth, with respect to the Parties’ argument on alternative holiday destinations and
         “destination insensitive passengers”, the Commission notes the following.
(1277)  In the first place, the results of its investigation indicate that the O&D approach
        remains appropriate to investigate the effects on competition of the Transaction. In
         the first place, this was confirmed by market participants who explained that this
        approach adequately reflects the perspective of customers, as set out in section 6.1.3
        above. None of the market participants with whom the Commission interacted during
           its investigation brought up the issue of “destination insensitive passengers”. In the
        second place, the Commission has not been able to identify internal documents of the
         Parties that would reflect the relevance of “destination insensitive passengers” for the
        competitive interactions between airlines on the relevant routes.
(1278)  In the second place, even if the prices of flights to other holidays destinations may
         constrain to a certain extent the merged entity on these routes post-Transaction, the
       main constraint is the competitive pressure exerted by flights on the same routes and
       which the Transaction is likely to significantly reduce.
(1279)  In the third place, the Parties did not provide any evidence that would allow the
       Commission to assess the competitive constraint other holidays destination may
         exerts on the routes of concern. For example, the Parties did not explain which
        holiday destinations are substitutable,1342 which airline operates flights to these
         destinations1343 and what are the conditions offered for flights to these destinations,
        such as the airports used, the frequencies offered or the prices charged.
(1280)  In the fourth place, the choice of holidays destinations by “destination insensitive
        passengers” are influenced by the overall cost of the holiday, that includes several
         cost elements in addition to the cost of the flight (costs such as, accommodation, car
          rental, activities at the destination). It is therefore not clear, and the Parties did not
         explain, to what extent the price of the flight is important in the choice of holiday
         destination and to what extent the Parties take in fact into consideration flight prices
         to other holiday destinations.
(1281)  In the fifth place, the Parties provide no evidence allowing the Commission to
         estimate the share of “destination insensitive passengers” on the routes of concern in
        order to assess whether it is indeed significant enough to constrain the prices of the
       merged entity post-Transaction.
(1282)  In the sixth place, while the Parties argue that the tourist flows on these routes are
         relatively high in particular in summer, the concerns of the Commission are not
         limited only to the summer seasons but apply with respect to most routes also to the
        winter season.
(1283)  Consequently, since the Parties ultimately do not contest the general O&D approach
         to market definition, since the Commission’s investigation does not support that
         “destination insensitive customers” or the difference on the thickness of the O&Ds

(1284)  Seventh, the Parties unjustifiably consider Lufthansa’s direct offering and ITA’s
         indirect offering on each city pair as complementary because of customers’ choice
        being limited to indirect flights on certain days of the week (i.e., those when a direct
          flight is not operated by Lufthansa).1344 The Commission points out the following.
(1285)  In the first place, on the days where Lufthansa offers direct flights ITA’s indirect
          flights remain virtually the only alternative (as evidenced in the Parties’ combined
        market shares; see sections 9.4.5 and 9.4.6 below). In addition, often Lufthansa
        provides daily indirect flights either throughout the year or on a seasonal basis which
         are also in competition with ITA’s indirect services, calling into question the
        argument that the services are purely complementary because of the lack of daily
         direct flights.1345
(1286)  In the second place, neither the Commission’s market investigation in this case, nor
           its past decisional practice provide indications that customers would consider that
         there is no substitutability between flights to a city pair offered on different days of
         the week or even at different times of the day. Besides, the Parties’ argument is not
        supported by the conclusions on market definition either, namely that the O&D
        approach remains appropriate for the analysis of the Transaction (i.e., an analysis that
        does not distinguish flights based on the day of the week), and which in any event
        has not been contested by the Parties at any point of the process (see section 6.1
         above).1346
(1287)  In the third place, the Parties raise this argument only for direct/indirect short-haul
        overlaps while disregarding it for the competition on direct/direct overlaps where on
         several routes, the competitors offer limited weekly frequencies and do not operate
         direct flights on a daily basis (e.g., based on the Parties’ argumentation, on city pairs
        such as Milan – Frankfurt, Rome – Frankfurt and Rome – Munich where their
        competitors offer 2-3 weekly frequencies, the Transaction should then result to a
       monopoly for the remaining days of the week. See Table 23 above for more
         information).
(1288)  In the fourth place, the Parties’ argument is not supported by any evidence. Further,
             it was brought forward at very a very late stage of the proceedings (day 65) not
        allowing the Commission to investigate it further.

(1289)  Eighth, the Commission does not contest the seasonality of the city pairs identified

        passenger numbers)  over Winter IATA compared  to Summer IATA  season.
       However,  it considers that this seasonality element  is irrelevant as such for  its
        assessment, as it does not (and should not) have a bearing on whether the Transaction
         will result in a significant impediment to effective competition on a specific city pair
         for specific IATA seasons, which as results from the discussion at section 6, and
       more specifically, sections 6.1 and 6.2 of this Decision, where the context in which
         the impact of the Transaction needs to be assessed is defined.
(1290)  Ninth, the Commission disagrees that the certain overlaps should be assessed as
         indirect/indirect ones simply because both the Parties offer indirect connections only
        over one of the two IATA Seasons. More specifically, on routes where depending on
         the IATA Season, the overlap  is  either  direct/indirect or  indirect/indirect, the
       Commission’s assessment should be seasonal and should depend on the type of
        overlap that arises. By way of example, on routes Brindisi – Düsseldorf and Cagliari
           - Munich, where over the Winter IATA season the Parties confirm that neither
        Lufthansa or ITA operate continuous direct connections, the Commission considered
         the overlaps over the Summer IATA Seasons as direct/indirect and over the Winter
      IATA Seasons as indirect/indirect. ).1347 The Commission considers that it would not
       make sense to conduct an indirect/indirect assessment when the Parties’ overlap is a
         direct/indirect one, as the Parties seem to suggest.
(1291)  Tenth, in relation to the Parties’ argument on the routes involving Naples, namely
         that there are out-of-market constraints from the airports in Rome, as FCO  is

       Commission notes the following.
(1292)  In the first place, the Parties did not put forward an airport substitutability claim
       between the airports in Rome and Naples and therefore, the Commission did not
        formally investigate whether FCO and NAP are substitutable. However, according to
        Figure 74 below, which constitutes publicly available information from Italia Rail’s
         website,1349 the travel distance from Naples to FCO is 241 km, and the travel time
         (via train) lasts (up to) 3h 33 minutes. Therefore, even though there are 78 daily
          trains  available, based on  its  past  decisional  practice, where  the Commission
       compares actual distances and travelling times to the indicative benchmark of
       100 km or 1 hour/60 minutes driving time (for more information see section 6.5.1
        above), NAP and FCO are not substitutable.

(1294)  The indirect travel option from NAP however, is seamless, whereas the option to
         self-connect to FCO is more burdensome. This is because, none of the train options
       from Naples to FCO are direct and, in fact, require the passengers to change at Roma
        Termini, often with limited transfer time (e.g., 10 minutes). On the contrary, the
         indirect flight options that ITA offers from NAP require passengers from Naples to

(1295)  In the third place, self-connecting to FCO puts a certain level of risk on passengers.
        In particular, passengers chose to self-connect from Naples to FCO also carry the
         risk of losing their flight (e.g., in case of a train delay), and having to pay an
         additional ticket to be rebooked on another flight. On the contrary,  if they flew
         indirectly from NAP and missed their connecting flight due to a delay on the first leg
         of the route, the airline would be responsible to rebook them on another flight
        without additional cost, compensate them for the delay, and if applicable, for any
         additional expenses/losses caused as a result of the missed connection.

9.4.5.1. Bari – Munich
9.4.5.1.1.    Market Structure
(1298)  Considering  the  Bari  - Munich  city  pair,  the  following  plausible  alternative
        geographic market definitions exist based on the catchment areas (See section 6.5.3.7
        above): BRI – Munich (widest plausible market definition consisting of both MUC
       and FMM), BRI – MUC  (narrowest  plausible  market  definition where  the
        Transaction gives rise to horizontal overlaps) and BRI – FMM (the Transaction does
        not give rise to a horizontal overlap).1350
(1299)  The  Commission’s  assessment  below  considers  the  widest  plausible  market
         definition, where MUC together with FMM belong to the same catchment area,
         therefore the market shares and concerns outlined above  reflect  this plausible
         definition.
(1300)  However, the assessment below would remain applicable even if the market was to
        be defined more narrowly, encompassing only BRI - MUC, where the Transaction
       would  still give  rise  to  horizontal  overlaps. This  is because,  the competitive
        landscape would remain unaltered in this situation (as no other competitor operates
       on the route BRI – FMM).
(1301)  Moreover, there would be no need to assess the effects of the Transaction on the city
         pair based on the alternative plausible market definition that only encompasses BRI -
     FMM, because would be no overlap arising due to the activities of the Parties (as
         neither operates from FMM).
9.4.5.1.2.     Lufthansa and MEF’s view
(1302)  Lufthansa and MEF argue that on this city pair, indirect flights do not provide a
         material competitive constraint to direct flights over the Summer IATA seasons, due
         to the strong seasonality characterising the route, and the indication that most
        customers are leisure customers that chose to fly directly. In this context, Lufthansa

1350    On the substitutability of BRI see footnote 316 above.


                                    298

[PÁGINA PDF 301]
       and MEF consider that indirect flights must not be considered as forming part of the
       same market as direct flights over summer, and that, as a result there should be no
        overlap between Lufthansa and ITA’s activities over Summer IATA seasons.1351 The
         Parties also point to the low increment brought by the Transaction over Summer
      IATA seasons 2022 and 2023, namely 4.4% and 5.9% respectively.1352 The Parties
        argue that the Commission’s concerns should be limited to Winter IATA Seasons,
       and that they would not be justified, due to the low passenger demand during winter,
         the moderate increment brought by the Transaction over Winter IATA 2022/2023
       and 2023/2024, namely 10% and 11% respectively, as well as the fact that Wizz Air
         carried 300 passengers indirectly on the route (capturing 4% market share over
        Winter IATA 2023/2024, without submitting any direct capacity on this route, either
       on Winter IATA 2023/2024 or on Summer IATA 2024).1353
9.4.5.1.3.    The Commission’s assessment
(1303)  For the reasons set out below, the Commission concludes, that the Transaction would
         significantly impede effective competition as a result of the creation or strengthening
         of a dominant position under any plausible market definition on the route Bari -
       Munich.
(1304)  First, the Transaction would lead to the Parties holding a very high combined market
        share on the route. As set out in Table 61 above, the Parties’ combined share (by
     PAX number) between Winter IATA Season 2021/22 and Winter IATA Season
       2023/2024 was between 95-100%. These market shares indicate that the Parties
       would hold a monopoly  or a quasi-monopoly  position  after  the  Transaction,
        depending on the season.
(1305)  Second, the increment brought about by the Transaction from ITA would be large at
     4% to 11% in the last four IATA seasons. This corresponds to a high increase in the
      HHI of between 831 and 1 951.
(1306)  Third, the market is highly concentrated. Following the Transaction, the HHI would
        be higher than 9 000 in each of the last four IATA seasons (with a minimum HHI
         level of 9 741 over the last four IATA seasons). Thus, the high combined market
        share of the Parties, the large increment in the Parties’ joint market position, as well
         as the HHI and change in HHI post-Transaction, indicate that the Transaction would
         create or strengthen a dominant position.
(1307)  Fourth, even when looking  into the widest possible market  definition,  if one
        excludes the Parties, no other airline operates the Bari - Munich city pair with direct
        connections and therefore the Transaction would lead to a monopoly or quasi
       monopoly on the route, depending on the season. Although certain competitors offer
         indirect connections  (e.g., Vueling via Barcelona and Rome combined, Turkish
         Airlines via Istanbul or Air France - KLM via Amsterdam/Paris) they only manage to
        capture a negligible or no market share at  all, depending on the season. In this
         context, the Transaction would lead to the elimination of the only competitive
         constraint over Lufthansa, in the form of ITA, an airline that managed to capture

1351      Parties’ Supplemental submission on direct/indirect and potential future short-haul overlaps, dated
       2 May 2024, paragraph 29; and, Response of Lufthansa and MEF to the SO, paragraphs 392-395.
1352      Parties’ Supplemental submission on direct/indirect and potential future short-haul overlaps, dated
       2 May 2024, paragraph 29; and, Response of Lufthansa and MEF to the SO, paragraphs 392-395.

[PÁGINA PDF 302]
      11% of the market by offering indirect routes, in less than 3 years of operation. The
         fact that ITA was the only actual constraint on Lufthansa indicates that it was also its
         close competitor.
(1308)  Fifth, as results also from the considerations in section 9.1.4, there are several
         barriers to entry and expansion on the route. In particular, the Parties’ high combined
        market share on the route Bari - Munich city pair, as well as their market position in
        terms of combined  slot holding in MUC (which exceeds 66% as indicated in
        Table 24 above) are clearly indicative of dominance and therefore could act as a
         barriers to entry and expansion in the Bari-Munich city pair. (See section 9.1.4.3
       above for more information). Moreover, airport charges in MUC are high and could
         act as a  barrier to entry and expansion. (See section 9.1.4.4 above  for more
         information).  Munich airport is also congested at certain hours of the day (see
         section 9.1.4.2 for more information).
(1309)  Sixth, the Commission’s investigation does not support a finding of market entry that
       would be  likely,  timely and  sufficient  to  deter  or  defeat any  potential  anti-
        competitive effects of the Proposed Transaction.1354
(1310)  More specifically, the Commission contests the Parties’ view regarding Wizz Air’s
          entry,1355 over Winter 2023/2024 from Memmingen on the Munich end of the route
            (i.e., on BRI-FMM), capturing 4% market share. Even if Wizz Air operated some
         direct  flights, the Commission understands that Wizz Air  is not active on the
          route.1356 This has been confirmed by the Parties, by clarifying that Wizz Air did not
        submit a direct capacity on this route, either on Winter IATA 2023/2024 or on
      Summer IATA 2024, and that the passengers that Wizz Air carried on Winter IATA
       2023/2024 amounted to 300 indirect passengers that flew through Tirana.1357
(1311)  Taking into consideration the elements identified above, the Commission considers
         that the Transaction will result in the Parties not competing with one another,
       compared to before the Transaction where ITA was the main competitive constraint
        over Lufthansa, and, in the increase of the Parties’ market power. Consequently, the
       Commission considers that the Transaction will likely result in higher prices for
       consumers and potentially negative effects on connectivity in indirect routes between
          Italy and the DACHB countries, possibly with fewer frequencies operated by the
         Parties and/or even less incentives for competitors to enter the route with direct
        connections and compete with the Parties, as their strong combined position will act
         as barriers to entry. (See section 9.1.4.3 for more information on how the Parties
        strong market position can result in barriers to entry).
9.4.5.1.4.     Conclusion
(1312)  In light of the common considerations on direct/indirect short-haul routes explained
         in sections 9.1 and 9.4.4 above, and in view of the above findings related in
         particular to the Parties’ very high combined market shares, the limited constraint

9.4.5.2. Naples – Frankfurt
9.4.5.2.1.    Market Structure
(1313)  Considering the Naples  - Frankfurt city pair the following plausible alternative
        geographic market definitions exist based on the catchment areas (See sections
         6.5.3.4 and 6.5.3.13above): Naples - Frankfurt (widest plausible, consisting of both
     NAP and QSR on the Naples end of the route, and FRA and HHN on the Frankfurt
       end of the route), NAP - FRA (narrowest plausible where the Transaction gives rise
         to horizontal overlaps) Naples – FRA (consisting of both NAP and QSR on the
        Naples end of the route), Naples – HHN (consisting of both NAP and QSR on the
        Naples end of the route), NAP – HHN, and, NAP – Frankfurt (consisting of both
     FRA and HHN on the Frankfurt end of the route).
(1314)  The  Commission’s  assessment  below  considers  the  widest  plausible  market
         definition, where NAP and QSR belong in the same catchment area on the Naples
       end of the route, and FRA together with HHN belong to the same catchment area on
         the Frankfurt end of the route. Therefore, the market shares and concerns outlined
       above reflect this plausible definition.
(1315)  However, the assessment above would not only remain applicable, but would also be
        amplified if the relevant market was to be defined more narrowly (and where the
        Transaction would still give rise to horizontal overlaps) irrespective of the alternative
         plausible market  definition. This  is due  to  the removal of Ryanair from  the
        competitive landscape (which it only operates from HHN).
(1316)  Moreover, there would be no need to assess the effects of the Transaction on the city
         pair based on all the alternative plausible market definitions that only encompass
     QSR on the Naples end of the route and/or HHN on the Frankfurt end of the route,
        because there would be no overlap arising as a result of the activities of the Parties
         (as neither operates from either QSR or HHN).
9.4.5.2.2.     Lufthansa and MEF’s view
(1317)  Lufthansa and MEF argue that on this city pair, indirect flights do not provide a
         material competitive constraint to direct flights over the Summer IATA seasons, due
         to the strong seasonality characterising the route, and the indication that most
        customers are leisure customers that chose to fly directly. In this context, Lufthansa
       and MEF consider that indirect flights must not be considered as forming part of the
       same market as direct flights over summer, and that, as a result there should be no
        overlap between Lufthansa and ITA’s activities over Summer IATA seasons.1358 The
         Parties also point out to the low increment brought by the Transaction over Summer
      IATA seasons 2022 and 2023, namely 2.6% and 4.9% respectively.1359 The Parties
        argue that the Commission’s concerns should be limited to Winter IATA Seasons,

1358      Parties’ Supplemental submission on direct/indirect and potential future short-haul overlaps, dated
       2 May 2024, paragraph 32; and, Response of Lufthansa and MEF to the SO, paragraphs 396-400.
