       and that they would not be justified, due to the low passenger demand during winter,
         the moderate increment brought by the Transaction over Winter IATA 2022/2023
       and 2023/2024, namely 19% and 21% respectively, the fact that Ryanair is a possible
        candidate for re-entry and Wizz Air is a candidate for entry on the route.1360
9.4.5.2.3.    The Commission’s assessment
(1318)  For the reasons set out below, the Commission concludes, that the Transaction would
         significantly impede effective competition as a result of the creation or strengthening
         of a dominant position under any plausible market definition on the route Naples -
         Frankfurt.1361
(1319)  First, the Transaction would lead to the Parties holding a very high combined market
        share on the route. As set out in Table 61 above, the Parties’ combined share (by
     PAX number) between Winter IATA Season 2021/2022 and Winter IATA Season
       2023/2024 was between 49-100% and 95-100% in the last four IATA seasons. The
        lower market share in the 2021 winter season (at 49%) is not representative of the
         current competitive environment because Ryanair was active on the route at that time
        but is not operating the route anymore. These market shares indicate that the Parties
       would hold a monopoly or quasi monopoly position after the Transaction depending
       on the season, especially following Ryanair’s exit from the route on Winter IATA
        Season 2021/2022.
(1320)  Second, the increment brought about by the Transaction from ITA would entrench
        even more Lufthansa’s market position by up to 10% in the last four IATA seasons
        with an increment between 5-10% in the last two IATA seasons. This corresponds to
        a high increase in the HHI up to 1 653, with an increment between 922 and 1 653 in
         the last two IATA seasons.
(1321)  Third, the market is highly concentrated. Following the Transaction, the HHI would
        be higher than 9 000 in each of the last three IATA seasons (with a minimum HHI
         level of 9 098 over the last three IATA seasons). The lower HHI level in the 2021
        winter season (at 4 947) is not representative of the situation to be expected because
        Ryanair was  still active on the route at that time but is not operating the route
        anymore. Thus, the Parties’ high combined market share, the large increment in the
         Parties’  joint market  position, as well as the HHI and change  in HHI  post-
         Transaction, indicate that the Transaction would create or strengthen a dominant
         position.
(1322)  Fourth, even when looking into the widest possible market definition,1362  if one
        excludes the Parties, no other airline operates direct flights on the Naples - Frankfurt
         city pair and therefore the Transaction would lead to a monopoly or quasi monopoly

         context, the Transaction would lead to the elimination of the only competitive

         close competitor.
(1323)  Fifth, as results also from the considerations in section 9.1.4, there are several
         barriers to entry and expansion on the route. In particular, the Parties’ high combined
        market share on the route Naples - Frankfurt city pair, as well as their market
         position in terms of combined slot holding in FRA (exceeding 64% as indicated in
        Table 24) are clearly indicative of dominance and therefore could act as barriers to
         entry and expansion in the Naples - Frankfurt city pair. (See section 9.1.4.3 above for
       more information). Moreover, airport charges in FRA are high and could act as a
         barrier to entry and expansion. For instance, public sources indicate that Ryanair’s
         exit from FRA was linked to the airport management’s decision to increase its airport
         charges, which suggests that these charges act as barriers to entry and expand on the
          route.1363 (See section 9.1.4.4 above for more information). Frankfurt airport is also
        congested at certain hours of the day (see section 9.1.4.2 for more information).
         Finally, the market investigation revealed that the high congestion levels at NAP are
         also strong barriers to entry, as the airport “has an annual capacity limit - which has
        been met”.1364
(1324)  Sixth, the Commission’s investigation does not support a finding of market entry that
       would be  likely,  timely and  sufficient  to  deter  or  defeat any  potential  anti-
        competitive effects of the Proposed Transaction.1365
(1325)  More specifically, the Parties’ submission that Ryanair and Wizz Air are possible
         entrants on the route is merely an assumption that is based on Ryanair’s past activity
       on NAP-HHN and Wizz Air’s presence in NAP and HHN, it is not supported by any
        evidence and has not been confirmed by the Commission’s market investigation. In
          particular, the Commission notes that, Wizz Air indicated that it is undecided as to
        whether to enter  this  route,1366 and thus does not  fulfil the  likely, timely and
         sufficient entry criterion. The responses to the Commission’s market investigation
        only show vague considerations (if any at all) of potential actions on the routes of
        concern. In particular, the Commission did not find that potential entrants had
        developed specific plans or adopted preparatory steps to enter these routes, and the

9.4.5.2.4.     Conclusion
(1327)  In light of the common considerations on direct/indirect short-haul routes explained
         in section 9.19.4.4 above, and in view of the above findings related in particular to
         the Parties’ very high combined market shares, the limited constraint imposed by
         competitors, the fact that the Parties compete closely, the existence of barriers to
         entry and expansion, and the lack of prospect of likely, timely and sufficient entry on
         the route the Commission concludes, that the Transaction would significantly impede
         effective competition on the route Naples - Frankfurt by creating or strengthening a
        dominant position, in both the Winter and Summer IATA Seasons, under any
         plausible market definition.
9.4.5.3. Conclusion
(1328)  In light of the above, the Commission concludes that the Transaction would lead to a
         significant impediment to effective competition due to the creation or strengthening
         of a dominant position on the routes Bari – Munich and Naples – Frankfurt, in both
         the winter and summer IATA seasons under any plausible market definition.

9.4.6.1. Brindisi – Düsseldorf
9.4.6.1.1.    Market Structure
(1330)  Considering the Brindisi - Düsseldorf city pair the following plausible alternative
        geographic market definitions exist based on the catchment areas (See section 6.5.3.3
        above): BDS – Düsseldorf (the widest plausible market, consisting of DUS, CGN,
     DTM and NRN), BDS- Düsseldorf (the narrowest plausible market where the
        Transaction gives rise to affected markets, consisting of DUS and CGN), BDS –
        Düsseldorf (consisting of DUS, CGN and NRN), BDS – Düsseldorf (consisting of
      DUS, CGN and DTM).1368
(1331)  The  Commission’s  assessment  below  considers  the  widest  plausible  market
         definition, where DUS, CGN, DTM and NRN belong to the same catchment area,
         therefore the market shares and concerns outlined above  reflect  this plausible
         definition.
(1332)  However, the assessment below would remain applicable even if the market was to
        be defined more narrowly (including either DUS and CGN together or DUS only in
         the same market). This is because, the competitive landscape would remain unaltered
        under all plausible alternative market definitions (as no other competitor operates on
         the Brindisi – Düsseldorf city pair from the above-mentioned alternative airports).
(1333)  Moreover, there would be no need to assess the effects of the Transaction on the city
         pair based on the alternative plausible market definitions that only encompass either
     NRN or DTM at the Düsseldorf end of the route because would be no overlap arising
       due to the activities of the Parties (as neither operates from these airports).
9.4.6.1.2.     Lufthansa and MEF’s view
(1334)  Lufthansa and MEF argue that (i) the route is of no competitive relevance due to the
         limited annual passenger volume; (ii) the increment brought by the Transaction over
      Summer IATA seasons 2022 and 2023 is low; and,  (iii) ITA’s indirect offer is
       complementary to Lufthansa’s direct offer, in the sense that ITA’s increment is the
          result of passengers wishing to fly over days of the week that no direct flight is
          available.1369
9.4.6.1.3.    The Commission’s assessment
(1335)  For the reasons set out below, the Commission concludes, that the Transaction would
         significantly impede effective competition as a result of the creation or strengthening
         of a dominant position under any plausible market definition on the route Brindisi –
        Düsseldorf over the Summer IATA Season.1370

(1336)  First, the Transaction would lead to the Parties holding a very high combined market
        share on the route. As set out in Table 62 above, the Parties’ combined share (by
     PAX number) between Winter IATA Season 2021/22 and Summer IATA Season
       2023 was 100%. These market share indicates  that the  Parties would hold a
       monopoly position after the Transaction.
(1337)  Second, taking into account Lufthansa’s significantly high market share in the last
       two completed Summer IATA Seasons (2022 and 2023), namely ranging between
       95%-97%, the increment brought about by the Transaction from ITA would be
       between 3% to 5% in the last two completed Summer IATA Seasons (2022 and
        2023). This corresponds to an increase in the HHI of between 516 and 867, which in
        essence means that the Parties would have captured the entire market, leaving almost
       no increment to be gained. 1371
(1338)  Third, the market is highly concentrated. Following the Transaction, the HHI would
        be higher than 9 990 in each of the last two completed Summer IATA Seasons (2022
       and 2023) (with a minimum HHI level of 9 994 over Summer IATA Season 2022).
        Thus, the monopoly position of the Parties post-Transaction, the relevant increment
       on the Parties’ joint market position, as well as the HHI and change in HHI post-
         Transaction, indicate that the Transaction would create or strengthen a dominant
         position.
(1339)  Fourth, even when looking into the widest possible market definition, if one were to
        exclude the Parties, no other airline operates direct flights between the Brindisi -
        Düsseldorf city pair and therefore the Transaction would lead to a monopoly on the
         route.  Although   certain  competitors   offer  multi-stop   indirect  connections
          (e.g., Turkish Airlines via Istanbul and Rome combined, or Air France - KLM via
        Amsterdam/Paris and Rome combined) they did not manage to capture any market
        share over the last two completed Summer IATA Seasons (2022 and 2023). In this
         context, the Transaction would lead to the elimination of the only competitive
         constraint over Lufthansa, in the form of ITA, an airline that managed to capture 5%
         of the market over summer, by offering indirect routes, within less than 3 years of
         operation. The fact that ITA was the only actual constraint on Lufthansa indicates
         that it was also its close competitor.
(1340)  Fifth, as results also from the considerations in section 9.1.4, there are several
         barriers to entry and expansion on the route. In particular, the Parties’ high combined
        market share on the route Brindisi - Düsseldorf city pair, as well as their market
         position in terms of combined slot holding in DUS (which amounts to ~58% over the
       summer season, as indicated in Table 24 above) are clearly indicative of dominance
       and therefore could act as barriers to entry and expansion in the Brindisi - Düsseldorf
         city pair. (See section 9.1.4.3 above for more information).
(1341)  Sixth, the Parties do not make any arguments on potential market entry on the route.
         Similarly, the Commission’s investigation does not support a finding of market entry

          data). This is because, the overall seasonal traffic is well below 7 500 passengers (i.e., amounted to
       330 passengers over Winter IATA 2021/2022 and 812 passengers over Winter IATA 2022/2023).

(1342)  Taking into consideration the elements identified above, the Commission considers
         that over the Summer IATA Seasons the Transaction will result in the Parties not
        competing with one another, compared to before the Transaction where ITA was the
       main competitive constraint over Lufthansa, and, in the increase of the Parties’
        market power. Consequently, the Commission considers that the Transaction will
         likely result in higher prices for consumers and potentially negative effects on
         connectivity, in indirect routes between Italy and the DACHB countries, possibly
        with fewer frequencies operated by the Parties and/or even less incentives for
        competitors to enter the route with direct connections and compete with the Parties,
         as their strong combined position will act as barriers to entry. (See section 9.1.4.3 for
       more information on how the Parties strong market position can result in barriers to
         entry).
9.4.6.1.4.     Conclusion
(1343)  In light of the common considerations on direct/indirect short-haul routes explained
         in section 9.19.4.4 above, and in view of the above findings related in particular to
         the Parties’ very high combined market shares, the limited constraint imposed by
         competitors, the fact that the Parties compete closely, the existence of barriers to
         entry and expansion, and the lack of prospect of likely, timely and sufficient entry on
         the route the Commission concludes, that the Transaction would significantly impede
         effective competition on the route Brindisi - Düsseldorf by creating or strengthening
        a dominant position, in the Summer IATA Season, under any plausible market
         definition.

        Winter IATA Season on BRI-HHN. In this context, Ryanair confirmed its market

9.4.6.2.3.    The Commission’s assessment
(1349)  For the reasons set out below, the Commission concludes, that the Transaction would
         significantly impede effective competition as a result of the creation or strengthening
         of a dominant position under any plausible market definition on the route Bari –
        Frankfurt over Winter IATA Seasons.
(1350)  First, the Transaction would lead to the Parties holding a very high combined market
        share on the route. As set out in Table 62 above, the Parties’ combined share (by
     PAX number) between Winter IATA Season 2021/22 and Winter IATA Season
       2023/2024 was between 30-100% and (i.e., following Ryanair’s exit from the route
        over winter) the Parties held a monopoly over Winter 2023/2024).
(1351)  Second, the increment brought about by the Transaction from ITA would be large at
     8% to 33% in the last three completed Winter IATA Seasons (2021/2022, 2022/2023
       and 2023/2024). This corresponds to a high increase in the HHI of between 351
       and 4 262.
(1352)  Third, the market is highly concentrated. Following the Transaction, the HHI would
        be higher than 7 500 over the last two completed Winter IATA seasons (with a
      minimum HHI level of 7 583 over Winter IATA 2022/2023). Following Ryanair’s
         exit from the route over winter, the HHI over Winter IATA 2023/2024 was even
         higher, at 9 938. Thus, the high combined market share of the Parties, the large
        increment on their joint market position, as well as the HHI and change in HHI post-
         Transaction, indicate that the Transaction would create or strengthen a dominant
         position.
(1353)  Fourth, when looking into the widest possible market definition, in addition to the
          Parties, Ryanair used to operate the Bari – Frankfurt city pair on BRI-HHN and held
        a market share between 14-70% over Winter IATA Season 2021/22 to Winter IATA
        Season 2023/2024. However, following Ryanair’s exit, the Parties hold a monopoly
       on the Bari - Frankfurt city pair based on Winter IATA 2023/2024 data, in terms of

9.4.6.3.1.    Market Structure

       and BRI - LBC.1378
(1359)  The  Commission’s  assessment  below  considers  the  widest  plausible  market
         definition, where HAM together with LBC belong to the same catchment area,
         therefore the market shares and concerns outlined above  reflect  this plausible
         definition.
(1360)  However, the assessment below would remain applicable even if the market was to
        be defined more narrowly, encompassing only BRI - HAM, where the Transaction
       would  still give  rise  to  horizontal  overlaps. This  is because,  the competitive
        landscape would remain unaltered in this situation (as no other competitor operates
       on the route BRI – LBC).
(1361)  Moreover, there would be no need to assess the effects of the Transaction on the city
         pair based on the alternative plausible market definition that only encompasses BRI-
      LBC, because there would be no overlap arising as a result of the activities of the
         Parties (as neither operates from LBC).
9.4.6.3.2.     Lufthansa and MEF’s view
(1362)  Lufthansa and MEF argue that (i) the route is of no competitive relevance due to the
         limited annual passenger volume; (ii) the increment brought by the Transaction over
      Summer IATA seasons 2022 and 2023 is low; (iii) the route is highly seasonal; and,
          (iv) ITA’s indirect offer is complementary to Lufthansa’s direct offer, in the sense
         that ITA’s increment is the result of passengers wishing to fly over days of the week
         that no direct flight is available.1379 Moreover, according to Lufthansa and MEF,
        Ryanair is a candidate for entry in the route, in light of its strong presence in Bari,
       and Leav submitted limited capacity on the route with chartered flights and not
        scheduled direct flights  (i.e., Capacity of 1 frequency in Summer IATA 2023,
        corresponding to 180 seats throughout the entire season), which is, according to the
          Parties, an indication that an airline may offer seats on this route.1380
9.4.6.3.3.    The Commission’s assessment
(1363)  For the reasons set out below, the Commission concludes, that the Transaction would
         significantly impede effective competition as a result of the creation or strengthening
         of a dominant position under any plausible market definition on the route Bari –
       Hamburg over the Summer IATA season.

(1364)  First, the Transaction would lead to the Parties holding a very high combined market

         Parties’ combined share (by PAX number) over Summer IATA season 2022 and

         significant at 6% to 14% in the last two summer IATA seasons. This corresponds to
        a high increase in the HHI of between 1 019 and 2 261. Furthermore, as set out in
         section 9.3.1.3.1, ITA has plans to expand by offering services on the route Rome-
       Hamburg (in addition to service on the route Milan-Hamburg). This is likely to

      HHI level of 8 998). Furthermore, as set out in section 9.3.1.3.1, ITA has plans to
       expand by offering direct services on the route Rome-Hamburg (in addition to its
         direct services on the route Milan-Hamburg). Considering that ITA already offers 4
         daily connections on the Bari - Rome route (i.e., 28 weekly frequencies based on
      Summer IATA 2024, Winter IATA 2024/2025 and Summer IATA 2025 data),1381 the
        chances are that it will be in a position to offer additional convenient connections
        with  limited  layover  time  on  the  Bari  – Hamburg  route,  through Rome.
        Consequently, ITA’s expansion on Rome-Hamburg  is  likely to increase ITA’s
        market share on the route Bari-Hamburg. Thus, the Parties’ high combined market
         share, ITA’s potential expansion on Rome-Hamburg, as well as the HHI post-
         Transaction, indicate that the Transaction would create or strengthen a dominant
         position.
(1367)  Fourth, even when looking  into the widest possible market  definition,  if one
        excludes the Parties, no other airline operates direct flights on the Bari - Hamburg
         city pair and the Transaction would lead to a quasi-monopoly on the route over the
      IATA summer season. Although certain competitors offer indirect connections (e.g.,
        Air France - KLM via Amsterdam/Paris and Turkish Airlines via Istanbul) they only
       manage to capture a negligible market share over the IATA summer season. In this
         context, the Transaction would lead to the elimination of the only competitive
         constraint over Lufthansa, in the form of ITA, an airline that managed to capture
      14% of the market by offering indirect routes, with less than 3 years of operation.
       The fact that ITA was the only actual competitive constraint on Lufthansa indicates
         that it was also its close competitor.
(1368)  Fifth, as results also from the considerations in section 9.1.4, there are several
         barriers to entry and expansion on the route. In particular, the Parties’ high combined
        market share on the route Bari - Hamburg city pair, as well as their market position
         in terms of combined slot holding in HAM (which amounts to 51% as indicated in
        Table 24 above) are indicative of dominance and therefore could act as barriers to
         entry and expansion in the Bari – Hamburg city pair. (See section 9.1.4.3 above for
       more information).
(1369)  Sixth, the Commission’s investigation does not support a finding of market entry that
       would be  likely,  timely and  sufficient  to  deter  or  defeat any  potential  anti-

(1371)  In light of the common considerations on direct/indirect short-haul routes explained

       same catchment area, and, on the Düsseldorf end of the route DUS, CGN, DTM and
     NRN belong to the same catchment area. Therefore, the market shares and concerns
         outlined above reflect this plausible definition.
(1374)  However, the assessment below would remain applicable even if the market was to
        be defined more narrowly (under all other plausible market definitions where the
        Transaction would  still give  rise  to horizontal overlaps). This  is because, the
        competitive landscape would remain unaltered under all plausible alternative market
         definitions (as no other competitor operates on the Naples – Düsseldorf city pair
       from the above-mentioned alternative airports).
(1375)  Moreover, there would be no need to assess the effects of the Transaction on the city
         pair based on the alternative plausible market definitions that encompass either (i)
     QSR on the Naples end of the route; or (ii) NRN and/or DTM on the Düsseldorf end
         of the route, because there would be no overlap arising due to the activities of the
         Parties (as neither operates from these airports).
9.4.6.4.2.     Lufthansa and MEF’s view
(1376)  Lufthansa and MEF argue that (i) the route is of no competitive relevance due to the
         limited annual passenger volume; (ii) the increment brought by about the Transaction
        over Winter IATA Seasons 2022/2023 and 2023/2024 is moderate; and, (iii) ITA’s
         indirect offer is complementary to Lufthansa’s direct offer, in the sense that ITA’s
        increment is the result of passengers wishing to fly over days of the week that no
         direct flight is available.1384 Finally, according to Lufthansa and MEF, Wizz Air is a
         possible candidate for entry on the route.1385
9.4.6.4.3.    The Commission’s assessment
(1377)  For the reasons set out below, the Commission concludes, that the Transaction would
         significantly impede effective competition as a result of the creation or strengthening
         of a dominant position under any plausible market definition on the route Naples –
        Düsseldorf over the Winter IATA season.
(1378)  First, the Transaction would lead to the Parties holding a very high combined market
        share on the route over the winter IATA seasons. As set out in Table 62 above, the
         Parties’ combined share (by PAX number) between over the last three completed
        winter IATA seasons (2021/2022, 2022/2023 and 2023/2024) was between 96-98%.
(1379)  Second, the increment brought about by the Transaction from ITA over the winter
      IATA season would be significant at 5%-12% over the last three completed winter
      IATA seasons. This corresponds to a significant increase in the HHI of between 927
       and 2 014.
(1380)  Third, the market is highly concentrated. Following the Transaction, the HHI would
        be higher than 9 000 in each of the last three completed winter IATA seasons (with a
      minimum HHI level of 9 224). Thus, the Parties’ high combined market share, the
         significant increment in the Parties’ joint market position, as well as the HHI and

9.4.6.4.4.     Conclusion
(1385)  In light of the common considerations on direct/indirect short-haul routes explained
         in section 9.19.4.4 above, and in view of the above findings related in particular to
         the Parties’ very high combined market shares, the limited constraint imposed by
         competitors, the fact that the Parties compete closely, the existence of barriers to
         entry and expansion, and the lack of prospect of likely, timely and sufficient entry on
         the route the Commission concludes, that the Transaction would significantly impede
         effective competition on the route Naples – Düsseldorf by creating or strengthening a
        dominant  position,  in  the Winter IATA  Season, under any  plausible market
         definition.

9.4.6.5.3.    The Commission’s assessment
(1390)  For the reasons set out below, the Commission concludes, that the Transaction would
         significantly impede effective competition as a result of the creation or strengthening
         of a dominant position under any plausible market definition on the route Naples –
       Hamburg over the Summer IATA season.
(1391)  First, the Transaction would lead to the Parties holding a very high combined market
        share on the route over the summer IATA seasons. As set out in Table 62 above, the
         Parties’ combined share (by PAX number) between the last two summer IATA
         seasons, over Summer IATA Season 2022 and Summer IATA Season 2023 was
       between 96-98%.
(1392)  Second, even though the increment brought by the Transaction would be small (2-3%
         in the  last two summer IATA seasons) and the increase in the HHI moderate
        (between 307 and 572), post-Transaction Lufthansa’s dominant market position will
        be strengthened. This is because the market is highly concentrated. Following the
         Transaction, the HHI would be higher than 9 000 in each of the last two summer
      IATA seasons (with a minimum HHI level of 9 524 over the last two summer IATA
         seasons). Furthermore, as set out in section 9.3.1.3.1, ITA has plans to expand by
         offering direct services on the route Rome-Hamburg (in addition to its direct service
       on the route Milan  - Hamburg). Considering  that ITA already  offers 4 daily
        connections on the –Naples - Rome route  (i.e., 28 weekly frequencies based on
      Summer IATA 2024, Winter IATA 2024/2025 and Summer IATA 2025 data),1392 the
        chances are that it will be in a position to offer additional convenient connections
        with  limited  layover  time on  the Naples – Hamburg  route,  through Rome.
        Consequently, ITA’s expansion on Rome-Hamburg  is  likely to increase ITA’s
        market share on the route Naples  - Hamburg.Thus, the Parties’ high combined
        market share, ITA’s potential expansion on Rome-Hamburg, as well as the HHI post-
         Transaction, indicate that the Transaction would create or strengthen a dominant
         position.
(1393)  Third, even when looking into the widest possible market definition, if one were to
        exclude the Parties, no other airline operates direct flights on the Naples - Hamburg
         city pair and therefore the Transaction would lead to a monopoly on the route over
         the winter IATA season. Although certain competitors offer indirect connections
          (e.g., Air France - KLM via Amsterdam/Paris and Turkish Airlines via Istanbul) they

9.4.6.6.2.     Lufthansa and MEF’s view
(1402)  Lufthansa and MEF argue that on this city pair, indirect flights do not provide a
         material competitive constraint to direct flights over the Summer IATA seasons, due
         to the strong seasonality characterising the route, and the indication that most
        customers are leisure customers that chose to fly directly. In this context, Lufthansa
       and MEF consider that indirect flights must not be considered as forming part of the
       same market as direct flights over summer, and that, as a result there should be no
        overlap between Lufthansa and ITA’s activities over Summer IATA seasons.1396 The
         Parties also point out to the low increment brought by the Transaction and the low
         indirect passenger traffic over Summer IATA seasons 2022 and 2023, namely 2%
       and 6% respectively.1397 In addition, the Parties’ submit that ITA’s indirect offer is
       complementary to Lufthansa’s direct offer over summer, in the sense that ITA’s
        increment is the result of passengers wishing to fly over days of the week that no
         direct flight is available.1398

9.4.6.7. Conclusion
(1412)  In light of the above the Commission concludes that the Transaction would lead to a
         significant impediment of effective competition due to the creation or strengthening
         of a dominant position, on routes Brindisi – Düsseldorf, Bari – Hamburg, Naples –
       Hamburg and Cagliari – Munich over the Summer IATA season and on routes Bari –
        Frankfurt and Naples – Düsseldorf over the Winter IATA season, under all plausible
        market definitions.

        United Airlines or Air Canada currently operate a direct (i.e., non-stop) connection.
       These six routes are Rome-New York, Rome-Washington, Milan-New York, Rome-
       San Francisco, Rome-Chicago and Rome-Toronto. For the latter two routes, ITA’s
        market shares are not yet available, as it entered these routes in Summer 2024.
(1415)  Overlaps of direct and indirect flights (current): The Transaction results in 65
         horizontally overlapping long-haul routes where either Lufthansa (or one of its JV
         partners) or ITA currently operates a direct connection, whereas the other merging
         party (or one of its JV partners) operates an indirect, one-stop connection on that
         route.
(1416)  Overlaps of direct and indirect flights (future): The Transaction results in […]
         horizontally overlapping long-haul routes where either Lufthansa (or one of its JV
         partners) or ITA has concrete plans to operate a direct connection within the next
         three years, whereas the other Party (or one of its JV partners) operates an indirect,
        one-stop connection on that route only.
(1417)  Overlaps  of  indirect  flights:  The  Transaction  results  in  2 805  horizontally
        overlapping long-haul routes where both Lufthansa and/or its JV partners, as well as
      ITA currently operate an indirect, one-stop connection only.
(1418)  Of these long-haul overlaps identified above, the Commission concludes that the
        Transaction would  significantly impede  effective competition on the following
       3 routes where both ITA and one of Lufthansa’s JV partners has a direct connection:
       Rome-Washington, Rome-San Francisco, and Rome-Toronto (summer only).
10.1.  Common considerations on horizontal overlaps on long-haul routes
(1419)  This section sets out general considerations concerning the competitive analysis of
         the Transaction regarding passenger air transport services on long-haul routes. These
        general remarks are relevant, to different degrees, for all the overlapping long-haul
         routes discussed in sections 10.2 and 10.3. They lay out the reasons why the
          activities of Lufthansa’s metal-neutral A++ JV should be aggregated with the
          activities of ITA when assessing the Transaction (section 10.1.1) and the reasons
      why the presence of independent parties will still likely constrain Lufthansa when
         defining ITA’s strategic decisions, such as the planning of its long-haul operations
         (section 10.1.1, paragraphs (1431) to (1433)), explain that access to feeder traffic
        plays an important role in sustaining viable long-haul operations (section 10.1.2),
         describe the general competitive landscape on the long-haul routes discussed in this
        Decision (section 10.1.3), explain how whether an airline offers a direct or an
         indirect long-haul flight influences how closely it competes with other airlines active
       on the same long-haul route (section 10.1.4), and outline the main barriers to entry
       and expansion on the long-haul routes discussed in this Decision, namely access to
         feeder traffic, availability of traffic rights, availability of slots and the existing large
          slot  portfolios of the merged  entity, the  profitability of the  route, the strong
        competitive position of the Parties as well as the availability of aircrafts and crews
         (section 10.1.5).

10.1.1.  Treatment of Lufthansa’s metal-neutral JV partners
10.1.1.1. Introduction
(1420)  In previous decisions, the Commission considered the  activities of  certain JV
         partners of the parties to the transaction in relation to routes covered by joint venture
        agreements as part of the parties’  activities.1401 This decisional practice  is also
         relevant for the Transaction as, on the transatlantic routes between the EEA and
        North America, Lufthansa is a member of the A++ JV together with United Airlines
       and Air Canada.1402
(1421)  All partners of the above joint venture cooperate extensively in relation to key
        parameters of  airline competition, […]. In the Parties’ words,  this means  that
         […].1403 Moreover, parties to the A++ JV agreement cooperate […].1404
(1422)  The intensity and breadth of such cooperation has as a consequence that the partners
         of the joint venture are indifferent which airline effectively operates the “metal” (i.e.,
         the aircraft) and therefore, for all the reasons explained above, their joint venture
       becomes “metal neutral”.1405
(1423)  Against the above background, in  its Statement of Objections, the Commission
         preliminarily concluded that the activities of the A++ JV and ITA should be assessed
         as those of a single entity for the purposes of the competitive assessment involving
         routes between the EEA and North America.
10.1.1.2. Lufthansa and MEF’s view
(1424)  The Parties do not contest the relevance of the Commission’s decisional practice for
        Lufthansa’s A++ JV and indicate that, pursuant to such decisional practice, “DLH
        does not compete with the A++JV Partners on transatlantic routes (such that
        United’s and Air Canada’s market shares are to be attributed to DLH)”.1406

1401     See, e.g., Case M.8964 – Delta/Air France-KLM/Virgin Group/Virgin Atlantic, paragraphs 176-178. In
          this case, the Commission found that the joint venture agreement entered between Delta, Air France-
     KLM and Alitalia as well as the joint venture agreement entered into between Delta and Virgin Atlantic
        involved “extensive cooperation such as revenue-sharing and joint management of schedules, pricing
       and capacity”. The Commission therefore treated them as a single entity for the purposes of assessing
        market shares and aggregated their market positions with that of the other involved parties. Likewise, in
       Case M.7541 – IAG/Aer Lingus, paragraphs 146-147. In this case the Commission found that the joint
        venture agreement entered into between British Airways, American Airlines, Iberia and Finnair
        involved “extensive cooperation such as revenue-sharing and joint management of schedules, pricing
       and capacity on all routes between North America and Europe”. The Commission therefore treated
       them as single entity for the purposes of assessing market shares and aggregated the market positions of
      IAG and  its JV partners with those of Aer Lingus. Similarly, in Case M.6828 – Delta/Virgin,
        paragraphs 84-87, the Commission assessed the Transaction considering the market position of Delta as
        well as its JV partners Air France/KLM/Alitalia as a single one on all relevant routes and aggregated the
        market positions of Delta and its JV partners with those of Virgin. The Commission recently followed
         the same approach in Cases M.9637 – IAG/Air Europa and M.9489 – Air Canada/Air Transat, where, in

         routes.

10.1.1.3. Commission’s assessment
(1427)  The Commission contests the arguments made by the Parties to the extent set out
       below and, based on the results of the investigation, concludes that its prior practice
       on the treatment of the metal-neutral revenue-sharing joint ventures should also
        apply to this case for the following reasons.
(1428)  First, it is not disputed that, following Lufthansa’s acquisition of ITA, Lufthansa will
         exercise, under the meaning of the Merger Regulation, control over ITA and,
         therefore, that ITA will become one single entity with significant structural links
        with Lufthansa which, in turn, is coordinating its activities on the relevant long-haul
         routes with its JV partners and shares revenues with them. Even though each of the
         interested parties to the Transaction (namely Lufthansa, its JV partners and MEF)
        cannot independently  steer the key decision making of ITA, which as further
        explained below, will need to be taken into account both for the JV cooperation
       framework and the concurrent interest of MEF in expanding ITA’s operation on
         long-haul, the Commission considers that the structural link that the Transaction
         creates between Lufthansa and ITA means  that the incentives to compete are
       dampened as of closing of the Transaction for the following reasons.
(1429)  In the first place, ITA, controlled by Lufthansa and tied to its strategic management,
       would have fewer incentives to compete with its parent company Lufthansa and
         therefore, by extension, with the JV partners:
         (1)  Any strategy or action by ITA that would result in revenue loss for the JV
               partners on the overlapping routes (among which could be strategies such as
             lowering prices; opening new routes in competition with the JV; or cooperating
             with a JV’s competitor) would result in harm to Lufthansa’s revenues, as the
           JV will distribute less revenues to  its partners. ITA and MEF could only
             engage in such strategies with the consent of Lufthansa (which has veto rights
             over the Reserved Matters such as […], as set out in section 2.3).


1415      Parties’ submission on the treatment of the JV, dated 15 March 2024, paragraphs 14 et seq.
1416     Response to the SO, paragraph 494. Parties’ submission on the treatment of the JV, dated 15 March
        2024, paragraphs 24 et seq.
1417     Response to the SO, paragraph 495.


                                    326

[PÁGINA PDF 329]
         (2)   Conversely, any strategy or action by ITA that would result in revenue gains
               for the JV partners on the overlapping routes (among which could be strategies
             such as increasing prices; decreasing capacity; deferring or cancelling the
             opening of new routes; or ceasing to cooperate with a competitor) would result
               in gains in Lufthansa’s revenues, as the JV will distribute more revenues to its
               partners.  Therefore,  Lufthansa  would  have  incentives  to  support  such
              competitive strategy or action as part of its control rights over ITA, but would
            need to reach the consensus of MEF, which has veto rights over the Reserved
              Matters.
(1430)  In the second place, Lufthansa would have no incentives to compete with ITA as ITA
       would become Lufthansa’s controlled subsidiary after the Transaction and Lufthansa
       would partake in ITA’s revenues:
         (1)  Any strategy or action by the JV that would result in revenue loss for ITA on
              the  overlapping  routes would  result  in harm  to  Lufthansa’s  revenues.
             Accordingly, Lufthansa would have no incentives to approve such strategy or
              action as part of its rights in the JV.
         (2)   Conversely, any strategy or action by the JV partners that would be in line with
              the interest of the JV and result in revenue gains for ITA on the overlapping
              routes would result in gains in Lufthansa’s revenues. Therefore, Lufthansa
            would have incentives to support such strategy or action as part of its rights in
              the JV.
(1431)  In the third place, contrary to the Parties’ supplementary arguments, the dampening
        of effective competition between ITA and the JV partners will not be completely
        prevented by MEF’s  interest  in strengthening ITA’s long-haul operations and
          profitability. MEF may  still pursue the declared objective of increasing ITA’s
        network between Italy and North America, exercising, where appropriate, its control
       mechanism and veto rights over ITA’s strategic decisions, but, as a result of ITA’s
         structural links with Lufthansa, this could only happen in line with the concurrent
          interest of Lufthansa, which itself coordinates on these routes with its JV partners.
(1432)  Furthermore, MEF’s  interest  in  strengthening ITA’s  long-haul  operations and
          profitability can be consistent with a strategy of the Parties to dampen effective
        competition between ITA and the A++ JV. This is because a dampening of effective
        competition on long-haul routes would lead to increased profitability of ITA’s long-
        haul operations via increased prices charged to passengers (in addition to other
         potential synergies). Such profitable price increases could be carried out without
         either ITA or the A++ JV partners leaving the respective routes, considering that
         price increases, if kept below the level that would imply a drop in passenger numbers
         sufficient to necessitate frequency reductions, would not necessarily result in reduced
         operations.
(1433)  That said, while the structural change brought about by the Transaction will affect
         the competitive dynamics on all routes covered by the JV agreements, including the
         routes listed in this Decision, the Commission acknowledges that the Transaction
       would not completely remove ITA’s incentives to compete against Lufthansa’s JV
         partners considering that both the JV partners and MEF would still influence, even
        though to a different extent, the key decision making of the JVs and of ITA
         respectively. To this end, Lufthansa would still need to take into account both the JV
        cooperation frameworks and the concurrent interest of MEF in ITA.

(1434)  In the  first place, as further illustrated in section 2.3, Lufthansa cannot decide
        independently on ITA’s strategic decisions, which include decisions relating to the
        annual budget, business plan, fleet plan, route portfolio and changes to strategic
        cooperation agreements; likewise, Lufthansa cannot take decisions relating to the JVs
        without reaching consensus with its partners.
(1435)  In the second place, MEF, which will not profit from the operations of the JVs on the
        long-haul routes prior to ITA’s integration in the JVs (which, furthermore, remains
         subject to antitrust approvals at least for the A++ JV), will protect its interest in ITA,
        notably pursuing the objective of ITA’s industrial development and future growth,
        with particular focus on the strengthening of national hubs and its entry into strategic
        markets and increase of long-haul routes. To achieve these ends, MEF will continue
         to have extensive governance powers, including the veto rights on the Reserved
        Matter. Moreover, as further described in section 2.3, […].
(1436)  Consequently, the presence of independent  parties with  interests  potentially in
         conflict with one-another, namely United Airlines and Air Canada on the A++ JV
         side and ANA on the J+ JV side, and MEF on ITA’s side, will likely constrain
        Lufthansa to a certain extent when defining ITA’s strategic decisions, such as the
        planning of  its long-haul  operations. Therefore, despite the dampening of the
         incentives to compete as of closing of the Transaction particularly on long-haul
         routes, these incentives will not be completely removed as far as ITA’s strategic
         decisions can only be taken in compliance both with the interest of Lufthansa, which
           itself coordinates with its JV partners and in compliance with the concurrent interest
         of MEF in expanding ITA’s long-haul operations.
(1437)  Second, contrary to what the Parties claim, the above structural change in the
        competitive situation on the routes operated by the JVs and ITA constitutes the direct
         long-lasting effect of Lufthansa’s acquisition of control over ITA, which is precisely
       what the Commission has to assess under the Merger Regulation, irrespective of any
         current or prospective entry of ITA into the JV agreement and without prejudice to
       any  antitrust  proceedings,  including any  potential assessment  of a  future JV
        agreement under EU antitrust rules.
(1438)  This is in line with the core rationale of the Merger Regulation, which provides that a
        concentration that may impede effective competition in the internal market should be
         subject to ex-ante merger control, rather than to an ex-post behavioural control via
          antitrust rules.
(1439)  Third, the Parties’ arguments according to which strong competition will remain
       between ITA, Lufthansa and its A++ JV partners “pre-ATI”,1418 […],1419 […], as it
        does  not  consider  that,  under  the Merger  Regulation,  the Commission  should
         investigate, on a forward-looking basis, both the current and expected structure of all
         the markets concerned, taking into account any long lasting related effects of the
         Transaction, including the Parties’ declared objective of making ITA (and its related
     FCO hub) part of Lufthansa’s JVs as soon as possible.
(1440)  In addition to the outlined structural effect stemming immediately from the closing
         of the Transaction, the Commission considers that it should also take into account the
        planned integration of ITA in the joint ventures under the present merger control
        procedure, without prejudice to any antitrust proceedings, including any potential

10.1.2.  Relevance of feeder traffic for long-haul operations
(1457)  Access to feed traffic plays an important role in long-haul operations.
(1458)  In order to reach a profitable load-factor, long-haul routes generally connect larger
         metropolitan areas, since more regional destinations do not have sufficiently high
       demand for profitable operations. For the long-haul routes covered by this Decision,
         the hub-and-spoke model is by far the most common business model, because it is
         able to sustain regular and significant operations by feeding passengers into the long-
        haul network of the carrier. In the hub-and-spoke business model, network carriers,
        such as Lufthansa and ITA, rely on a dense network of domestic and short-haul
          flights which “feed” passengers into their airport hubs in order for these passengers
         to connect to a long-haul flight with the Parties from their airport hubs. For long-haul
          flights, passengers that connect with a short-haul or domestic flight at either or both
        ends of the long-haul route is commonly referred to as “feeder traffic”.
(1459) A more detailed discussion of ITA and Lufthansa’s specific hub-and-spoke business
        models and the importance of feeder traffic to the Parties’ business model is provided
         in sections 7.5 and 7.6, respectively.
(1460)  The importance of having access to a wide feeder network on one or both ends of the
         route to operate a route profitably is illustrated by Lufthansa’s internal documents.
        For example, in the internal document cited below, Lufthansa finds that […].
Figure 81: Lufthansa internal document
[…]
Source: […].
(1461)  During the market investigation, competitors were asked to explain the role of feeder
          traffic at each end of the route in their company’s ability to enter or expand their air
        passenger services on each route; and to what extent access to feeder traffic at any
        end of the route influences the competitive dynamics on the route. Contrary to the
        claim brought by the Parties in their Response to the SO,1433 the view of almost all
        competitors was that feeder traffic is generally indispensable and essential for the
          viability and economic sustainability of a route by filling seats and improving load
          factors.1434 This conclusion is not contradicted by the (selected) quotes from two
        competitors reported by the Parties in their Response to the SO.1435 Namely, while
      IAG indicates that there should not be a separate market definition for feeder traffic
         (as it is not the only way to create “economies of traffic density”), it still recognizes
          that “carrying connecting passengers can support long-haul operations due to
        economies of traffic density”, considering that “[b]y carrying more total paying
        passengers overall on a trunk long-haul route, airlines can raise load factors and
        lower average unit costs for all passengers”.1436 This further confirms that having

(1462)  Further, as indicated in sections 10.2 and 10.3, connecting passengers constitute a
         significant part of the overall passengers travelling on the trunk routes related to the
        long-haul overlaps of concern. On average, connecting passengers account for 34%
         of the total passengers travelling on the trunk routes Rome-Washington, Rome-
       San Francisco and Rome-Toronto.1437
(1463) A pure point-to-point business model (which does not rely on feeder traffic for the
         sustainable operation of long-haul flights) is rarely used for long-haul operations. In
          fact, for the long-haul routes of concern covered in this Decision, only Air Transat on
         the Rome-Toronto route operates under a pure point-to-point business model (during
         the summer seasons only).
10.1.3.  Competitive landscape
(1464)  For the transatlantic long-haul routes between Italy and North America for which the
       Commission concludes that the Transaction would significantly impede effective
        competition, this section discusses the main competitors that the Parties face and
       more generally the competitive environment in which the Parties operate on these
         routes.
(1465) On these routes, the A++ JV (including Lufthansa, United Airlines and Air Canada)
         as well as ITA primarily compete against two other transatlantic metal-neutral joint
         ventures: the Blue Skies joint venture between Delta Air Lines, Air France-KLM and
        Virgin Atlantic (“Blue Skies JV”), as well as the joint venture involving certain
       members of the Oneworld alliance, including American Airlines, airlines belonging
         to the IAG group (British Airways, Iberia, Aer Lingus) and Finnair (“AA-IAG JV”).
(1466)  The Blue Skies JV is a metal-neutral profit-sharing joint venture whose partners
         closely cooperate on pricing, schedules and connecting services. The geographic
        scope of the joint venture encompasses non-stop routes between the EU and the UK,
       on the one hand, and the United States, Canada, Mexico, and related beyond routes,
       on the other hand.1438 The Blue Skies joint venture has airport hubs in Paris (CDG
       and ORY), Amsterdam (AMS), and London (LHR) in Europe, and airport hubs in
      New York (JFK), Atlanta (ATL), Boston (BOS), Los Angeles (LAX), Minneapolis
       (MSP),   Salt  Lake  City  (STL),   Seattle  (SEA)  and  Detroit  (DTW)   in
        North America.1439
(1467)  Likewise, the AA-IAG JV is a metal-neutral revenue-sharing joint venture including
          joint management of schedules, pricing and capacity. The joint venture covers all
         routes operated by members of the JV between Europe, including Italy, on one end
         of the route, and Canada, Mexico and the United States, on the other end of the
          route.1440 The AA-IAG JV has airport hubs in London (LHR and LGW), Madrid

10.1.4.  Relevance of indirect connections for the assessment of closeness of competition on
        long-haul routes
(1476)  This section contains observations on closeness of competition between the Parties
       and  their  competitors  based on  the  distinction  between  direct  and  indirect
        connections.
(1477)  As outlined in section 6.6, the Commission considers that direct (non-stop) flights
       and indirect (one- or multi-stop) flights are part of the same product market when
        considering long-haul flights. Therefore, in the route-by-route assessment of the
         relevant long-haul routes, the Commission will include both direct and indirect
          flights in the market share as well as HHI estimates. In addition, in the competitive
        assessment, the Commission will consider the impact that indirect flights have on the
         Parties’ direct operations on a route-by-route basis bearing in mind that on some
         routes,  indirect  flights are an important competitive  constraint on the  Parties.
         Nevertheless, based on the results of the market investigation as well as based on
        passengers’ actual ticket purchasing behaviour (i.e., their revealed preferences), the
       Commission considers that  airline passengers prefer direct  flights over indirect
          flights. As outlined in more detail below, this is relevant for the assessment of
        closeness of competition on the overlapping long-haul routes.

10.1.4.1. Lufthansa and MEF’s view on the relevance of indirect connections
(1478)  Lufthansa and MEF submit that indirect connections remain a strong competitive
         constraint on routes irrespective of the number of direct operations.1449 In particular,
         the Parties have provided quantitative evidence according to which the share of
         indirect passengers  is  significant, even on  routes on which  there  are  several
        competitors with a direct connection. In addition, the Parties disagree with the view
        expressed by some market participants in the market investigation that business
        passengers prefer direct flights over indirect flights.
10.1.4.2. Evidence on passenger preferences for direct connections
(1479)  The below provides a summary of the available evidence on passenger preferences
         for direct connections compared to indirect connections.
(1480)  First, long-haul competitors consistently consider that passengers have a preference
         for direct connections over indirect connections.
(1481)  According to long-haul competitors, passengers consider the availability of direct
          flights as well as the total flight duration (which is impacted by whether the flight is
         direct or indirect) as the most important criteria when purchasing a long-haul airline
          ticket after the price of the ticket (and together with the frequencies offered per
         week).1450 In terms of factors that limit the substitutability between direct and
         indirect flights, long-haul competitors list most commonly the difference in total
         travel time, difference in price, duration of the lay-over and whether the lay-over
        happens during the night (between 12am and 6am).1451
(1482)  In addition, many long-haul competitors consider that there are certain passenger
        groups (particularly business travellers) that have a stronger preference for direct
          flights over indirect flight, whereas there are other passenger groups (particularly
       young  leisure  travellers)  that  usually  purchase  the  cheapest  available  ticket,
        independently of whether the flight is direct or indirect. For instance, LOT Polish
         Airlines explained that “[b]usiness travellers would typically choose direct flights
       when flying on short business trips” whereas “[t]he group that would typically
        choose the cheapest flight available are the passengers traveling for leisure purpose,
         for example people who entered their adulthood recently”. Air Europa, Air France-
      KLM, Air Transat, Asiana, Etihad, IAG, Japan Airlines, and Turkish Airlines
        provided similar responses during the market investigation.1452
(1483)  However, as correctly pointed out by Lufthansa and MEF in the Response to the
         SO,1453  it may not only be business passengers that have stronger preferences for
         direct flights over indirect flights. Instead, as reflected in the responses by some
        long-haul competitors, other passenger groups such as senior travellers and families
        with children may also have a stronger preference for direct flights over indirect

(1487)  The claim by Lufthansa and MEF according to which this assessment is inconsistent
        with  the Commission’s assessment  of  indirect  flights on  short-haul  routes  is
        unfounded.1461 In particular, in the assessment of short-haul routes, given the more
         limited  relevance  of  indirect  connections compared  to  long-haul  routes,  the
       Commission considers that indirect connections are not part of the same market as
         direct connections, unless more than 10% of passengers on a route fly via an indirect
        connection. Conversely,  in  the Commission’s assessment  of  long-haul  routes,
         indirect connections are always included in the same market as direct connections,
        independently of the share of passengers flying via an indirect connection on a route.
       However, the fact that most passengers choose a direct connection over an indirect
        connection, even when there is only a single airline offering a direct connection,
       shows that passengers prefer direct connections, even in long-haul, and that therefore
         the distinction between direct and indirect connections is a relevant one for the
        assessment of closeness of competition in long-haul.
(1488) A further illustration of the fact that passengers prefer direct connections over
         indirect connections is provided also in the following chart presented by the Parties.

         are 263 weekly indirect connections in S24 whereas there are only 14 weekly direct
        connections. The Parties refer to these figures to illustrate that customers have
         significant choice on this route. However, when looking at customers’ actual choices

(1489)  The fact that most passengers choose direct flights over indirect flights, even though
        customers in the passenger air services market are relatively price sensitive and the
        market is characterised by low switching costs and a relatively high degree of price
        transparency confirms, rather than contradicts, that passengers prefer direct flights
        over indirect flights.
(1490)  In conclusion, the Commission considers that the available evidence shows that
        passengers prefer direct connections over indirect connections. In addition, the
         available evidence shows that the competitive constraint imposed by competitors
        with only indirect connections on a route decreases with the number of direct
        competitors active on the route.

10.1.4.3. Relevance to the competitive assessment for long-haul routes
(1491)  Given  that  passengers  prefer  direct  connections  to  indirect  connections,  the
       Commission considers that on routes where two or more airlines offer a direct
        connection, the airlines offering a direct connection compete more closely with each
         other than with airlines that only offer indirect connections on the route.
(1492)  As noted  at the outset of  this  section, in  line with  its market  definition, the
       Commission considers that indirect connections do exert some competitive constraint
       on direct connections. Therefore, the Commission’s analysis includes both direct and
         indirect connections in its market share and HHI estimates and considers in more
          detail the relevance of the competitive constraint from indirect connections on direct
        connections on a route-by-route basis.
10.1.5.  Barriers to entry and expansion
(1493)  The Commission’s market investigation confirmed the existence of several barriers
         to entry and expansion for the long-haul routes discussed in this Decision.
(1494)  The  following  sub-sections  discuss  the most  important  barriers  to  entry and
        expansion on the long-haul routes of concern, including: i) access to feeder traffic, ii)
         availability of traffic rights, iii) availability of slots and existing large slot portfolio
         of the Parties, iv) profitability of the route, v) the strong competitive position of the
          Parties, and vi) availability of aircrafts and crews.
(1495)  The above barriers to entry apply, to a different extent, to both direct and indirect
          flights. The Parties’ argument according to which “the identified barriers to entry are
        not relevant for indirect traffic as indirect connection (i) are not really bound to
          traffic rights, (ii) do not require feeder traffic and  (iii) are in general based on
         existing slot portfolios” are vague, unsubstantiated and not supported by the overall
        evidence collected by the Commission during its market investigation, as further
          illustrated in the following sections 10.1.5.1 to 10.1.5.6.1464
10.1.5.1. Access to feeder traffic
(1496)  As  explained  in  section  10.1.2,  long-haul  routes can be  difficult  to  operate
         sustainably without access to feeder traffic, which generally constitutes a significant
        advantage, and feeder traffic is required for significant operations. Therefore, access
         to feeder traffic constitutes a significant barrier to entry and expansion on many of
         the long-haul routes covered by this Decision, although to varying degrees.
(1497)  The Transaction is likely to raise barriers to entry for competitors by limiting the
         availability of feeder traffic on the long-haul O&Ds of concern because ITA operates
        an airport hub at Rome-FCO whereas Lufthansa’s JV partners operate airport hubs at
         several of the destination airports. The destination airports where United Airlines
        (Lufthansa’s JV  partner) operates a hub include Chicago-O’Hare (ORD), Los
        Angeles International (LAX), New York-Newark Liberty (EWR), San Francisco
         International  (SFO)  and  Washington-Dulles  (IAD).  In  addition,  Air  Canada
        (Lufthansa’s  joint venture partner) operates an airport hub  at Toronto Pearson
        (YYZ).1465 Following the Transaction, the Parties (and their JV partners) will have an
         airport hub on both ends of the route on each of the three routes of concern: Rome-
        Washington,  Rome-San Francisco,  and  Rome-Toronto.  Compared   to   their
         competitors, the Parties will therefore face fewer barriers to expand on these routes

        has access to feeder traffic on either end of these routes).

10.1.5.2. Availability of traffic rights
(1501)  In order for an airline to operate flights outside  its home jurisdiction and enter
        another country’s airspace, an air-services agreement (“ASA”) for traffic rights needs
         to be in place between the two countries. In addition, the airline has to obtain the
         rights from the relevant national or regional regulatory authorities to operate services
       between the two countries. ASAs can grant different degrees of freedoms/rights to
          airlines and can limit the number of services operated between the countries, the type
         of services these carriers can provide, and the number of carriers allowed to operate
         these services.
(1502)  The market investigation shows that the availability of traffic rights granted to
         carriers according to existing ASAs may constitute a barrier to entry and expansion
       on some of the overlap routes.
(1503)  First,  air  carriers generally consider the  availability of  traffic  rights to be an
        important factor in the decision whether to enter or expand on a new route.1469 In a
         similar way, air carriers consider a lack of availability of traffic rights to be a barrier
         to entry and expansion.1470
(1504)  Second, air carriers confirm that their ability to influence the availability of traffic
         rights  is  limited  considering  that  traffic  rights  are  negotiated  between  the
        governments of the relevant countries or between supranational entities, limiting the
          ability of airlines to directly influence such negotiations.1471 Moreover, reaching such
        agreements generally takes a while as negotiations occur relatively infrequently and a
         resolution may therefore not be achieved quickly. While the airline could ask or
        lobby  its government to  initiate such negotiations,  it does not have any direct
         influence on the result of such discussions.
(1505)  In relation to the availability of traffic rights specifically on the overlapping long-
        haul routes of concern, responding long-haul competitors explain that the EU-US
       Open Skies Agreement covers traffic rights for routes between the EU and the United
          States.1472 This agreement allows airlines based in the EU or the US to operate on
       any routes between the EU and the US without restriction in terms of traffic rights.
        Therefore, traffic rights do not appear to constitute a barrier to entry or expansion on
         routes between the EU and the United States, except for airlines based neither in the
     EU nor in the US (such as the Gulf carriers).
10.1.5.3. Availability of slots and existing large slot portfolios of the Parties
(1506)  The market investigation shows that slot constraints at relevant airports constitute a
         barrier to entry and expansion on some of the overlapping long-haul routes.
(1507)  First, air carriers consider that the availability of slots for take-off and landing is
         generally one of the most important criteria when deciding to enter a new long-haul
         route or expand operations, as without access to a sufficient number of slots entry on
        a new route is not possible.1473 Access to slots therefore appears to be a necessary but
        not sufficient condition to enter a route. In a similar way, air carriers consider a lack
        of availability of slots to be a barrier to entry and expansion.1474

(1512)  The  fact  that ITA  holds  a  significant  slot  portfolio  at Rome-FCO whereas
        Lufthansa’s JV partners hold significant slot portfolios at the destination airports
       means that they both can adapt flexibly to changes in capacity and pricing and
        thereby exert competitive constraints on each other pre-Transaction. Conversely, air
         carriers without a significant number of airport slots at either the origin or destination
         airport are less able to adapt flexibly to changes in capacity in pricing on such routes
       which may in turn constitute a barrier to entry and expansion for such carriers.1476

(1513)  The market investigation carried out by the Commission did not provide any

10.1.5.4. Profitability of the route
(1514)  The market investigation shows that the profitability of the route is an important
         factor when deciding to enter a new route and therefore limited profitability could
        serve as a barrier to entry.1478 Profitability of the route is affected by various factors,
        such as the level of demand on the route, the air carrier’s ability to attract connecting
         passengers, economies of scale and scope, the share of business demand, inter alia.
       Each of these elements can serve as a barrier to entry on its own due to its effect on
         the profitability of the route.
(1515)  First, the market investigation shows that the level of demand and the traffic size on
         the route serves as an important factor in the decision to enter or expand on the
        overlap routes.1479 This means that for routes with relatively low demand significant
         barriers to entry are likely to exist for a competitor to enter the route with a direct
        connection.
(1516)  Second, as described also in section 10.1.5.1, the market investigation’s results,
       which are not contradicted by the arguments brought by the Parties in their Response
         to the SO,1480 show that having a network and the ability to offer connecting flights
         are important elements for profitability and could therefore constitute a barrier to
          entry.1481 Insufficient demand on the route means that air carriers will have difficulty
         to fill their planes. On certain routes, this may mean that a carrier can only operate
         profitably if this carrier can fill its planes on the route by relying on feeder traffic and
         transporting connecting passengers to supplement the stand-alone profitability of the
         route. Alternatively, on other routes, it may mean that, while the carrier can still be
        able to operate profitably on the route, this carrier will only be able to operate with
         significantly lower frequency on the route compared to carriers with (better) access
         to feeder traffic on the route. As described above, competitors consider that the
        frequency offered on the route is among the most important elements for passengers
       when choosing a  carrier. Therefore, having a network and the  ability to offer
        connecting traffic can serve both as a barrier to entry and expansion on a route.
(1517)  Third, the market investigation confirms that economies of scale and scope are
        important to operate the routes profitably and could serve as a barrier to entry on
         routes between the EEA and North America.1482
(1518)  Not having an airport hub at one or both ends of the route may impede rivals’ ability
         to enter and expand on these routes. This  is, among other reasons, due to the
         existence of economies of scale when operating from an airport. Generally, the more
          flights an airline operates from an airport, the lower tend to be its marginal and


      ITA at this airport means that ITA can adapt more flexibly to changes in capacity and pricing on the
        long-haul routes of concern, compared to rivals that currently do not have a significant slot portfolio at
       Rome-FCO. This also applies to those airports where Lufthansa’s JV partners hold a large slot portfolio.

        average costs of operating an additional flight from this airport. This is because
        operating from an airport requires certain fixed costs (e.g., renting airport facilities,
         hiring ground staff) that become proportionally smaller to each flight, the more
          flights an airline operates at the airport. In addition, having a larger flight schedule at
        an airport enables airlines to optimise costs more efficiently at this airport (e.g.,
         airport crews can be utilised more efficiently). This means that airlines that typically
        operate without having an airport hub (i.e., that do not rely on a dense network of
        domestic and short-haul flights which “feed” passengers onto long-haul flights) at
         either end of the route, face additional barriers to entry and expand. Similarly, having
        a hub only at one end of the route puts a carrier at a disadvantage compared to
         carriers having hubs at both ends of the route, decreasing the incentive for the carrier
         to prioritize the route within its route portfolio.
(1519)  Fourth, on routes where the share of business passengers is significant, the ability to
         offer business class/premium services  will  affect the  carriers’  profitability and
         therefore could serve as a barrier to entry on the route. The market investigation
        confirms that the potential for business or corporate customers  is an important
        element that is taken into account by air carriers when deciding to enter a new long-
        haul route.1483
(1520)  Fifth, market participants note that the opportunity costs, meaning, the profitability
         of the route compared to other routes on which the aircraft and crew are currently
        used or could be used or the higher attractiveness of other passenger routes, can
         constitute a barrier to entry or expansion when deciding to operate certain long-haul
          routes.1484
10.1.5.5. The strong competitive position of the Parties
(1521)  In previous cases, the Commission found that the strong/dominant position of a
         carrier on a route could constitute a significant barrier to entry on the market for
        passenger air services. In the Ryanair/Aer Lingus III decision, the Commission found
         that the presence of a strong competitor on a route can act as a very significant
         barrier to entry and expansion. This dynamic is caused by a number of market
         conditions, which are particular to the air passenger services market. First, a carrier
        with a strong presence (hub or base) at a particular airport has the ability to quickly
         re-allocate flights and frequencies in order to offer the most attractive schedules in
        response to new entry, for example by re-arranging departure times close to those of
         the entrant. Second, customers in the passenger air services market are relatively
         price  sensitive, and the market  is characterised by low switching costs and a
         relatively high degree of price transparency. While these market features can,
        dependent on circumstances, promote price competition, they may also allow for a
        strong incumbent to efficiently price new competitors out of the market. This is
         particularly  true  if the incumbent benefits from a frequency advantage and/or
       economies of scale associated with having a large base at the relevant airport. The
        incumbent may also be able to (partially) offset the losses associated with aggressive
         price retaliation by feeding the traffic to other, more profitable routes and/or through
         servicing the relatively profitable TS (time sensitive) segment, which typically
         requires a frequent, regular schedule that only the incumbent can provide. As such,
         the presence of a strong competitor on a route, and the risk of aggressive retaliation,
      may in itself deter new entry and thereby act as a significant barrier to entry.
