         the AA-IAG JV. Third, given the relatively low level of demand on this route, if the
         Parties were to increase prices on this route after the Transaction, competitors could
         enter  or expand on  this  route with a  relatively  small number  of  short-haul
        connections from Catania to their long-haul hubs in Europe.
(1845)  In the third place, on the route Naples-New York (winter only), where the Parties’
       combined market share  is high and the increment arising from the Transaction
         significant, the following countervailing factors apply. First, demand on this route
        during the winter seasons is particularly low (<14 000 in Winter 2022/23 and <6 000
         in Winter 2021/2022). Second, during the winter seasons, the other two  joint
        ventures have a sizeable number of connections from Naples to their long-haul hubs
         in Europe. In particular, based on Winter 2023/2024, Air France-KLM (of the Blue
        Skies JV) has 19 average weekly frequencies connecting Naples with its hubs in
       Amsterdam and Paris, whereas IAG (of the AA-IAG JV) has 15 average weekly
        frequencies connecting Naples with its hubs in Dublin, London and Madrid. Third,
        given the relatively low level of demand on this route, if the Parties were to increase
         prices on this route after the Transaction, competitors could enter or expand on this
         route with a relatively small number of short-haul connections from Naples to their
        long-haul hubs in Europe. Fourth, the Parties will continue to face competition on
         these routes from competitors with sizeable market shares. Namely, as shown in
        Table 95, the Transaction would leave, in addition to Lufthansa and its A++ JV
         partners United Airlines and Air Canada, the Blue Skies JV with markets shares over
      25% for the last two winter seasons.
(1846)  Seventh, the market investigation did not reveal any substantiated competition
        concerns for these routes.1787
(1847)  Eighth, the Commission has taken into consideration multiple exceptional factors of
          this case, namely that ITA’s long-term competitiveness as a standalone carrier is
        highly uncertain (see section 7.2.2) and that, following the Transaction, ITA will
         retain some ability and incentive to compete against Lufthansa’s A++ joint venture
         partners, in particular due to the presence of MEF as a controlling shareholder (see
         section 10.1.1).
(1848)  In conclusion, the Transaction would not significantly impede effective competition
        with respect to the 38 indirect / indirect overlapping routes identified above.

12.5.   Non-horizontal overlaps
(1857)  The Proposed Transaction gives rise to relevant vertical relationships between the
          activities of Lufthansa in the upstream markets for (i) MRO services; (ii) ground
        handling services, (iii) cargo handling services, and (iiv) flight training services, and
       ITA’s activities in the downstream market for passenger and cargo air transport
         services, as the Parties have an individual or combined market share exceeding 30%
       on certain markets. In addition, the Transaction gives rise to non-horizontal overlaps
         in relation to ITA’s provision of feeder traffic to third-party airlines, including to
        competitors that are active on routes where Lufthansa is also active on.
12.5.1. MRO
(1858)  The Proposed Transaction gives rise to vertically affected markets in relation to line
        maintenance services at FRA, MUC, STR, DUS, BRU, FCO, and FLR airports.1791
       The Proposed Transaction does not give rise to vertically affected markets in relation
         to heavy maintenance  services, engine maintenance  services and components
        maintenance services as the Parties’ individual and combined market shares on the
        upstream  and  downstream  market  (under  the  narrowest  definition)  do  not
        exceed 30%.

        with respect to these markets.
12.5.2.  Ground handling services
(1861)  The Proposed Transaction gives rise to potential vertical relationships between the
          activities of Lufthansa in the upstream market for ground handling services and
       ITA’s activities in the downstream market for passenger air transport services as the
         Parties have a market share exceeding 30% of passenger traffic at FRA and MUC
         airports (if including self-handling).
(1862)  ITA is fully sourcing ground handling services in the airports where it operates and,
        according to the Business Plan for [details of ITA’s business plan].1793  It has a
         contract with Swissport as the main provider of groundling services at the two main
         airports where ITA operates, i.e. FCO and LIN. […].1794
(1863)  Given that Lufthansa is not active in the provision of ground handling services in
     FCO and LIN airports, the Proposed Transaction cannot result in any customer
         foreclosure in the two main ITA hubs.
                     12.5.2.1. Ground handling services at FRA
(1864)  As is visible from the Table 98 below, ITA has a very limited significance as a
        customer for ground handling services at FRA airport where Swissport is currently
       empowered to provide ground handling services to it, so the Transaction could not
        give rise to customer foreclosure. Even if ITA were to switch to Lufthansa, there
       would remain a sufficiently large customer base for other ground handling providers.
(1865)  At the same time, given the limited scope of ground handling services provided to
         third parties by Lufthansa in FRA (see Table 98 below), the Proposed Transaction
        cannot affect Lufthansa’s incentive to provide ground handling services to other
          airlines and thus lead to input foreclosure. As explained by Lufthansa,1795 […].
(1866)  Although the combined market shares of the Parties on the downstream air passenger
        market are relatively high, the increment resulting from the Transaction is very
        small ([0-5]%).

                     12.5.2.3. Conclusion
(1871)  The Commission deems  that  the  Transaction would  not  significantly impede
         effective competition through input or customer foreclosure with respect to ground
        handling services.
(1872)  Even in the hypothetical scenario where Lufthansa after the Proposed Transaction
         raised its prices, this would likely have a limited impact on Air Passenger Services
        providers as ground handling services account for a small proportion of the overall
         costs for Air Passenger Services.
12.5.3.  Cargo handling services
(1873)  The Proposed Transaction gives rise to a relevant vertical relationship between the
          activities of Lufthansa in the upstream market for cargo handling services at MUC
       and ITA’s activities in the downstream market for air cargo transport services. The
        Transaction give rise to one vertically affected market with respect to cargo handling
         services at MUC, where Lufthansa estimates its market shares in landside cargo
        handling to go above 30%.
(1874)  However, this link is not material in light of ITA’s extremely limited market shares
         in air cargo transport (less than [0-5]% in intra-European air cargo transport and
       [0-5]% on intercontinental routes in 2022) and who is therefore not an important
        customer on the market for landside cargo services. As a result, even if ITA were to
        purchase  all  its cargo handling services from Lufthansa, there would remain a
         sufficiently large customer base for all competitors.
(1875)  The Transaction also does not raise any input foreclosure concerns: Lufthansa only
        provides limited cargo handling services to third-party airlines at MUC (where  it
        operates  as warehouse ground  handling  agent and  provides  airmail  handling
         services). Competitors on the market for air cargo transport services have sufficient
         alternatives to source services, such as CargoGate (the largest warehouse space in
      MUC), Swissport Cargo Services (also handling Swiss Air Lines) and LUG Cargo.
       Also located at Munich Airport Cargo area are several landside consolidation agents,
        with AHTS and AirTruck being the largest ones, providing import and export BUP-
         services (Build up Pallet) for freight forwarders.
(1876)  Consequently, the Commission deems that the Transaction would not significantly
       impede effective competition through input or customer foreclosure with respect to
        cargo handling services.
12.5.4.  Flight training services
(1877)  The Proposed Transaction does not give rise to any actual vertical link in relation to
          flight training services considering that ITA currently sources  its training needs
          internally.
(1878)  The Proposed Transaction would only give rise to vertical link between the activities
        of Lufthansa the upstream market for flight training services at European level and
       ITA’s activities in the downstream market for demand of such services should the
        market be further segmented by aircraft type, as Lufthansa’s share would exceed
      30% in relation to certain similar models (see Table 100 below).

(1880)  Given the very limited significance of ITA as a customer for flight training services –
       which is evident considering that it currently needs only three FFS to train its pilots –
       and also the limited market shares of Lufthansa in the market for the provision of
          flight training services, the Proposed Transaction cannot affect Lufthansa’s incentive
         to provide training services to other customers nor restrict Lufthansa’s competitors
       from gaining access to market opportunities.
(1881)  Moreover, Lufthansa’s lack of market power in the upstream market for flight
         training services precludes an incentive to foreclose, especially given that several
         large and  structured  operators  are  active on  that market, such  as CAE  Inc.;
         FlightSafety  International;  L3Harris;  Avenger  Flight  Group;  United  Airlines;
        Emirates; Pan AM Flight Academy, and Delta.
(1882)  Consequently, the Commission deems that the Transaction would not significantly
       impede effective competition through input or customer foreclosure with respect to
          flight training services.
12.5.5.  Online flight ticket distribution
(1883)  The Commission does not consider that the Transaction would lead to a significant
       impediment of effective competition in relation to distribution of flight tickets. Apart
       from providing air passenger services, both Lufthansa and ITA sell tickets for their
          flights through both direct and indirect channels (e.g. their own websites or OTAs).
       The Transaction would lead to vertically affected markets (i.e. passenger air travel
         services (upstream) and distribution of flight tickets (downstream)) only under the
        narrowest plausible market definition, assuming that the relevant online flight ticket
         distribution markets are national in scope. The affected markets would be Austria,
        Belgium, Germany, Italy, and Switzerland.
(1884)  Even under  this  narrowest  understanding  of  the  relevant  geographic  market,
        however, the Parties would not have the ability of incentive to foreclose third-party
         indirect  distributors. In no case the combined market shares of the Parties in
        passenger tickets sold would exceed 50% and the increment would be minimal or



                                    458

[PÁGINA PDF 461]
        next to non-existent (below 1%),1796 so the Transaction would not bring about a
         material change in the market conditions. Moreover, as both Parties currently have a
         similar mix of distribution channels and currently distribute the majority of their
         tickets (>50%) via indirect channels,1797 there is no reason to suspect that they would
       change  their  distribution  strategy  and  withhold  their  content  from  indirect
          distributors. In fact, foreclosing intermediaries from access to their flight tickets
        could harm their own business model, as it heavily relies on this distribution channel.
12.5.6.  Feeder traffic
12.5.6.1. Introduction
(1885)  In the air transport sector, there are various types of agreements between independent
          airlines that allow passengers to purchase a single ticket for an indirect route
        including two or more legs where each leg is operated by one of the airlines that is
         party to the agreement. Interlining agreements are commercial agreements between
          airlines to enable one airline to book passengers on another airline’s flights and allow
        passengers to travel on one ticket despite their journey being on flights operated by
        multiple airlines. Such agreements also enable passengers to check their bags from
         the point of origin through to their final destination. Codeshare agreements are an
       enhanced form of interline agreements which allow flights operated by one airline
         also to be marketed by its codeshare partner under that carrier’s own code, which
       means that airlines publish and market flights of their code-sharing partners under
          their own airline designator and the flight number as part of their published timetable
        or schedule.
(1886)  Interlining and codeshare arrangements are in principle mutually beneficial to the
          airlines participating in such agreements as they give each party the opportunity to
         increase its load factors. In principle, they also benefit passengers as they increase
        connection opportunities, allow passengers to be compensated in case of missed
        connections and spare them from having to take back luggage and re-check it at the
        connection airport.
(1887)  As part of their cooperative efforts, some carriers have formed global alliances. An
         alliance is an agreement between two or more airlines to link each of the airlines’
         route networks and coordinate on specified activities (e.g., marketing and sales;
        coordination of airport operations).
(1888)  ITA  is currently a member of the SkyTeam alliance, together with Aerolíneas
        Argentinas, Aeroméxico, Air Europa, Air France-KLM, China  Airlines, China
         Eastern, Czech Airlines, Delta, Garuda Indonesia, Kenya Airways, Korean Air,
       Middle East Airlines, Saudia, TAROM, Vietnam Airlines, Virgin Atlantic, and
       Xiamen Air. As part of its membership in the SkyTeam alliance, ITA has extensive
          interline and codeshare agreements with most members of the SkyTeam alliance and
        hence provides extensive feeder traffic to these airlines.
(1889)  Lufthansa  is a member of Star Alliance, which includes Aegean Airlines, Air
        Canada, Air China, Air India, Air New Zealand, All Nippon Airways, Asiana,
        Austrian  Airlines, Avianca, Brussels  Airlines, Copa  Airlines, Croatia  Airlines,
        EgyptAir, Ethiopian Airlines, EVA Air, LOT Polish Airlines, Scandinavian Airlines,
       Shenzhen Airlines, Singapore Airlines, South African Airways, SWISS International
        Air Lines, TAP Portugal, Thai Airways, Turkish Airlines and United Airlines.

1796     Reply to RFI65B.
1797     Reply to RFI 65.


                                    459

[PÁGINA PDF 462]
(1890)  The theory of harm examined in relation to feeder  traffic relates to a risk of
         foreclosure whereby the Parties would deny competing air carriers access or hamper
          their access (e.g., by raising the price charged for such access) to feeder traffic. The
        concern is that the Parties may have the ability and incentive to foreclose rivals’
        access to feeder traffic on such routes where the other merging party also operates in
        order to divert passengers from the rival to whom feeder traffic has been provided to
         the other merging party.
(1891)  As regards the Transaction, the Parties may foreclose rivals’ access to feeder routes
        flown by ITA between Rome and smaller destinations in and around Italy with the
       aim of diverting these passengers onto flights that connect through Lufthansa’s hubs
       which equally allow these passengers to reach their final destinations.1798
(1892)  For example, according to this theory of harm, the Parties could deny or hamper
        access to ITA’s flights connecting Rome-Fiumicino (FCO) with various smaller
         locations in Italy and neighbouring countries for passengers connecting to/from a
          flight operated by another carrier between Rome-FCO and a destination in Asia
       where Lufthansa also operates. As a result, prices may increase on the various air
         transport markets between smaller destinations in Italy and neighbouring countries at
       one end of the route and the destination in Asia at the other end, as the competitive
        pressure on Lufthansa on  these  routes would be reduced  as a  result  of  the
         Transaction. In addition, the foreclosure strategy may also result in increased prices
       on the stand-alone “trunk route” between Rome-FCO and the destination in Asia, as
         the restricted access to feeder traffic may cause the airlines relying on such access to
        decrease capacity on the “trunk route” or (in the extreme) decide to exit the “trunk
        route” altogether.
(1893)  The Commission has focussed its investigation on the impact of the Transaction on
       ITA’s feeder  traffic. This  is because of a lack of concern  raised by market
         participants on the impact of the Transaction on Lufthansa’s pre-existing feeder
        arrangements and because Lufthansa has a significantly larger long-haul network
        than ITA. The Parties therefore stand to benefit more significantly from a strategy of
        reducing ITA’s feeder traffic to  its rivals than vice versa (reducing Lufthansa’s
         feeder traffic in order to benefit ITA’s long-haul operations).
                     12.5.6.2. Overview of feeder traffic provided by ITA

12.5.6.3. Lufthansa and MEF’s view
(1901)  As discussed in section 6.9, Lufthansa and MEF consider that there is no separate
         feeder market since Lufthansa and ITA do not actively engage in feeder traffic as an
        independent commercial activity. Nevertheless, Lufthansa and MEF have assessed
        whether  the Transaction may  result  in  foreclosure  of ITA’s  feeder  traffic  to
        Lufthansa’s rivals on long-haul routes.
(1902)  According to Lufthansa and the MEF, the Transaction does not raise such foreclosure
        concerns related to feeder traffic for the following reasons.
(1903)  In the Form CO, Lufthansa and MEF focussed on the 10 most important short-haul
         routes on which ITA transported passengers on behalf of another carrier in IATA
      Summer 2022 season (in terms of number of passengers transported by ITA as feeder
           traffic).1803 According to the Parties, no foreclosure concerns arise on these routes for
         several reasons. First, on two of these routes (Madrid-Rome and Amsterdam-Rome),
         direct flights are also operated by third-party carriers that could replace ITA as a
        provider of feeder traffic on these routes. Second, for routes feeding traffic into long-
        haul connections from Rome to Naples and Venice, direct long-haul connections
       from Rome-FCO for many North American destination are available and therefore
        passengers can choose these direct connections rather than flying via Naples or
        Venice. Third, for routes ending in Rome-FCO, various third-party carriers fly into
          this airport from across Europe and therefore any foreclosure strategy involving this
         airport as the final destination would be ineffective.
(1904)  In addition, the Parties claim that during the summer season, most small Italian
         airports are not only connected to Rome-FCO (for which ITA provides the main
         feeder traffic option) but also to other European hubs. For example, according to the
          Parties, Catania airport (CTA) is connected not only with Rome-FCO, but also with
       Amsterdam-Schiphol (AMS), Barcelona-El Prat (BCN), Paris-Charles de Gaulle
       (CDG), Copenhagen Airport (CPH), Madrid-Barajas (MAD) and London-Heathrow
        (LHR).1804 Similarly, during the winter season, most small Italian airports remain
        connected to at least one other European hub, in addition to Rome-FCO. In any
         event, according to Parties, if ITA were to restrict its feeder traffic to these small
          Italian airports, independent European carriers (such as Air France-KLM) could

        Naples (NAP), Venice (VCE), LIN and Genoa (GOA) are connected to various European hubs other
        than FCO. However, Lufthansa and MEF do not substantiate this view and/or explain why exactly these
          Italian airports were selected for this analysis.

        operate additional flights to these small Italian airports during the winter season to
         replace the traffic lost from ITA’s feeder network.1805
(1905)  Finally, the Parties focus on the 10 most important carriers to which ITA provides
         feeder traffic (based on number of passengers transported by ITA during the IATA
      Summer 2022 season).1806 According to the Parties, no foreclosure concerns arise in
         relation to these carriers for the following reasons. First, Delta (the carrier to which
      ITA provided the most feeder traffic) has already been able to reduce its feeder
          traffic from ITA since the Transaction was announced while still expanding capacity
        to/from FCO. Second, Air France-KLM (the carrier to which ITA provided the
        second most feeder traffic) has a large short-haul network in Europe, including to
        various destinations in Italy and therefore does not rely on ITA’s feeder traffic to
       compete effectively. Third, the remaining 8 carriers could turn to various alternative
         carriers with a large network in Europe (including Italy) that could provide them with
         feeder traffic instead of ITA.1807
(1906)  In an RFI submission during the Phase II investigation, Lufthansa and MEF further
        argued that ITA’s feeder traffic typically only accounts for a small proportion of the
          total traffic of long-haul routes operated by third-party airline carriers to/from Rome-
     FCO and that, for the limited number of long-haul routes operated by rivals where
       ITA’s feeder traffic accounts for a higher share, either ITA will have no incentives to
        stop providing feeder traffic post-Transaction due to these rival carriers being part of
         the Star Alliance (of which Lufthansa is also a part) or because Lufthansa does not
       compete with these third-party carriers on these routes.1808
12.5.6.4. The Commission’s assessment
(1907)  As outlined in more detail in section 6.9, the Commission considers that there is a
         separate market for feeder traffic. The following sections assess the Parties’ ability
       and incentive to engage in vertical foreclosure strategies and what impact such
         strategies would likely have on effective competition on the relevant routes.
12.5.6.4.1.    Ability to foreclose
(1908)  As outlined in section 10.1.2, having access to a wide network of short-haul flights at
       an airport in order to feed the long-haul flights can constitute an important input for
        long-haul competitors. Therefore, given that the provision of feeder traffic to third-
         party carriers (i.e., the upstream market) can constitute an important input for the
        provision of long-haul flights of these third-party carriers  (i.e., the downstream
        market), the restriction of access to that input can potentially raise competition
         problems.1809
(1909)  From a practical perspective, ITA would have the ability to restrict access to its
         feeder traffic to third-party carriers, either by terminating existing feeder agreements,
       by demanding higher prices for continuing such existing feeder agreements and/or
        through other means (e.g., by limiting the routes on which ITA continues to provide
         feeder traffic). In particular, Special Prorate Agreements ("SPAs") support interlining
       and code-sharing and specifically define the distribution of the revenues and the
         settlement of ticket costs between carriers and may include a commission in favour


1805    Form CO, paragraph 2165.
1806    Form CO, paragraph 2167.
1807    Form CO, paragraph 2167.
1808     Lufthansa and MEF’s response to RFI 42, Q1.
1809     Non-horizontal Merger Guidelines, paragraph 34.


                                    464

[PÁGINA PDF 467]
        of the ticketing carriers. SPAs have varying terms with an end date (typically
         requiring annual extension) or with an open end. It is also customary for SPAs to
       have a 30-day prior written notice termination clause that can be exercised by either
         carrier at any time, without cause. Codeshare agreements are typically open-ended
       and have varying termination clauses.1810
(1910)  However, while ITA would, from a practical perspective, have the ability to limit the
        access of feeder traffic to third-party air carriers post-Transaction, it seems unlikely
         that such a strategy would result in an effective foreclosure of these rivals. Table 101
       above shows that feeder traffic provided by ITA generally represents a relatively
        small share of the total of passengers on the third-parties’ long-haul flights on each
         relevant route. Out of the 39 long-haul routes identified in Table 101, ITA’s feeder
          traffic on average accounted for only around 8% and 9% of total traffic in Winter
        2022/23 and Summer 2023, respectively.1811
(1911)  There are only six routes where ITA’s feeder traffic accounted for at least 20% of
          total traffic in Winter 2022/23 or Summer 2023 (ROM-AMM, ROM-HGH, ROM-
      CKG, ROM-SZX, ROM-WNZ, ROM-BJS) and only three routes (ROM-AMM,
      ROM-HGH, ROM-CKG) where it accounted for more than 30% in at least one of the
          last two seasons.
12.5.6.4.2.    Incentive to foreclose
(1912)  The Parties’ incentive to foreclose rivals on certain long-haul routes from ITA’s
         feeder traffic depends on the Parties’ downstream market share (i.e., the market share
         of the Parties on the routes on which ITA provides the feeder traffic). The table
       below summarises the Parties’ combined market share on each of the six long-haul
         routes on which ITA provides at least 20% feeder traffic to at least one competitor
         active on these routes.
Table 102: Parties’ combined market shares on selected long-haul routes

                                            W22/23                           S23
ROM-AMM                               <1%                       <1%
ROM-BJS                                  23%                        70%
ROM-CKG                               1%                        13%
ROM-HGH                                 93%                        89%
ROM-SZX                                  18%                        12%
ROM-WNZ                               3%                        16%
Source: RFI 63, Annex Q1.
(1913)  The table shows that on four of the six routes (ROM-AMM, ROM-CKG, ROM-SZX,
      ROM-WNZ), the Parties’ combined market share is low to moderate. Therefore, on
         these routes, the Parties’ incentive to foreclose competitors from access to ITA’s
         feeder traffic appears low. On the other two routes (ROM-BJS, ROM-HGH), the
         Parties have high combined market shares and therefore have, prima facie, a higher
         incentive to foreclose rivals from ITA’s feeder traffic.
(1914) On these two routes, ITA provides feeder traffic to Air China, as shown in Table 101
        above. Air China is a Star Alliance partner of Lufthansa.1812 In addition, Air China
       and Lufthansa are part of the C+ joint venture, covering routes between Europe and

         China.1813 Since feeder arrangements between Star Alliance members are offered on
        a reciprocal basis, the Parties’ incentives to maintain access to the network of Star
        Alliance carriers post-merger would work against any potential incentive to foreclose
        competitors post-merger by preventing access  to ITA feeder  flights.1814 More

12.5.6.4.3.    Likely impact on effective competition
(1915)  As discussed above, the Commission considers that Lufthansa would probably not
       have the ability or the incentives to foreclose rivals from ITA’s feeder traffic on any
        long-haul route. Therefore, the Commission has not further assessed whether such
         foreclosure strategies would have any effect on the long-haul routes.
12.5.6.5. Conclusion
(1916)  In light of the above, the Commission considers that the Transaction does not result
         in a significant impediment of effective competition in relation to the provision of
         feeder traffic to long-haul services operated by other carriers.

13.    CONCLUSION
(1917)  For the reasons set out above, the Commission concludes that the Transaction would
         significantly impede effective competition with respect to passenger air services on
         the following routes in both the Winter and Summer IATA Seasons and under any
         plausible market  definition, as a result of a creation or strengthening of a
       dominant position in the relevant markets:
          (a)   Direct Short-haul routes: Milan – Brussels, Milan – Düsseldorf, Milan –
               Frankfurt, Rome – Frankfurt, Rome – Munich, Rome – Zurich, Rome –
            Hamburg.
         (b)   Direct/indirect short-haul routes: Bari – Munich, Naples – Frankfurt.
          (c)   Direct long-haul routes: Rome – Washington, Rome – San Francisco.
(1918)  For the reasons set out above, the Commission concludes that the Transaction would
         significantly impede effective competition with respect to passenger air services on

        dominant position in the relevant markets:
          (a)   Direct Short-haul routes: Milan – Hamburg.
         (b)   Direct/indirect  short-haul  routes:  Brindisi –  Düsseldorf (Summer IATA

          IATA  Season),  Naples –  Düsseldorf  (Winter IATA  Season),  Naples –

14.    COMMITMENTS
14.1.   Introduction
(1922)  As further described in section 4, in order to render the Transaction compatible with
         the internal market, the Parties submitted a first set of commitments in the Phase II
         investigation, pursuant to Article 8(2) of the Merger Regulation, on 11 April 2024
         (“the Initial Commitments”), which the Commission decided not to market test.
       These Initial Commitments were followed by updated commitments on 6 May 2024
         (the “Second Commitments”). The Parties submitted a final set of commitments on
       18 June 2024 (the “Final Commitments”).
(1923)  Both the Initial Commitments and the Second Commitments included:
          (a)   commitments to address the competition concerns on certain overlapping short-
              haul routes by entering into an agreement with one or more remedy takers and
            by making available slots and possibly other elements to those remedy takers;
         (b)  commitments to address the competition concerns at LIN airport by divesting
                slots at LIN airport; and
          (c)   commitments to address the competitions concerns on certain overlapping
              long-haul routes by committing to procure the operation at a minimum weekly
             frequency  for the summer and/or the winter IATA seasons (“Long-Haul
             Capacity Remedy”).
(1924)  In addition, the Second Commitments included:
          (a)   commitments to address the competition concerns on certain overlapping
                direct/indirect short-haul routes by entering into a special prorate agreement
              (“Special Prorate Agreement” or “SPA”) in relation to ITA’s domestic network
             with one or more of the remedy takers for the overlapping short-haul routes;
         (b)  commitments to address the competitions concerns on certain overlapping
              long-haul routes by separating ITA’s operations on long-haul routes between


                                    467

[PÁGINA PDF 470]
                Italy and North America, where ITA’s activities overlap (directly or indirectly)
             with the operations of the A++ JV (“Long- Haul North Atlantic Business”)
            from  the  rest  of DLH’s  organisation and by implementing  ringfencing
             measures “Hold-Separate and Ringfencing Commitment”); and
          (c)   commitments to address the competitions concerns on certain overlapping
              long-haul routes by concluding agreements (such as interlining or code share
             agreements) with other airlines on flights to/from Rome Fiumicino to other
            European airports (“Long-Haul Connectivity Remedy”).
(1925)  As further explained in section 14.5, the Final Commitments introduced further
       improvements to address the competition concerns on specific short-haul routes. As
         to the long-haul routes of concern listed in this Decision, the Final Commitments
        replaced  the  Initial and Second Commitments, namely  the Hold-Separate and
        Ringfencing Commitment, the Long-Haul Capacity Remedy, and the Long-Haul
        Connectivity Remedy, with a commitment to enter into agreements with one or more
         competitors, in order to establish either (a) a certain number of direct weekly
         frequencies, (b) a certain number of weekly additional and/or improved one-stop
        connections, or (c) a combination of frequency increase of direct weekly frequencies
       and additional one-stop weekly connections (“Long-Haul Remedy”).
(1926)  Neither of the Initial Commitments or the Second Commitments had an upfront
        buyer or fix-it first structure while the Final Commitments added an upfront buyer
         structure  for the commitments  to address the competition concerns on  certain
        overlapping short-haul and long-haul routes and with respect to Linate airport. The
         Parties did not formally put forward any remedy  takers  for approval by  the
       Commission for any of the commitments of the Initial Commitments, the Second
       Commitments, or the Final Commitments, but included in their submissions in the
       Form RM accompanying the commitments a list of potential remedy takers for each
         of the components of the Final Commitments.
14.2.   Framework of assessment
14.2.1.  Overview
(1927) When a concentration raises competition concerns because  it would significantly
       impede effective competition, in particular as a result of the creation or strengthening
         of a dominant position, the parties may seek to modify the concentration in order to
         resolve the competition concerns and thereby gain clearance of their merger. The
       commitments have to eliminate the competition concerns entirely and have to be
        comprehensive  and  effective  in  all  respects.  In  assessing  whether  proposed
       commitments  are  likely  to  eliminate  the  competition concerns  identified,  the
       Commission considers all relevant factors including inter alia the type, scale and
        scope of the proposed commitments, judged by reference to the structure and
         particular characteristics of the markets in which the competition concerns arise,
        including the position of the parties and other participants on the markets.1815
(1928)  Commitments must be put forward by the parties and the Commission has the power
         to accept only such commitments as are capable of rendering the Transaction
        compatible with the internal market.




1815    Remedy Notice, paragraphs 5, 9, and 12.


                                    468

[PÁGINA PDF 471]
(1929)  Commitments in Phase II must be submitted to the Commission within not more than
       65 working days from the day on which proceedings were initiated.1816 Where the
         parties submit commitments before such legal deadline, but subsequently modify
        such commitments after the deadline, the Merger Regulation does not impose any
         obligation on the Commission to accept such commitments.1817 The Commission will
        only accept these modified commitments where it can clearly determine – on the
         basis  of  its assessment of information already received  in  the course  of  the
         investigation, including the results of prior market testing, and without the need for
       any other market  test –  that such commitments, once implemented,  fully and
       unambiguously resolve the competition concerns  identified and where there  is
         sufficient time to allow for an adequate assessment by the Commission and for
        proper consultation with Member States.1818 The Commission will normally reject
        modified commitments which do not fulfil those conditions.1819
14.2.2.  Elimination of all identified competition concerns
(1930)  The commitments have to eliminate the competition concerns entirely and have to be
        comprehensive and effective from all points of view.
(1931)  Regarding the exact form of the commitments, the General Court has pointed out
          that, while the Merger Regulation lays down the principle whereby the Commission
      may authorise a merger only if the proposed commitments address the competition
        concerns  identified,  it “leaves  it a wide  discretion as  to the form which the
       commitments in question may take.”1820 Commitments may be structural in nature,
        such as the commitment to divest a certain business unit. It may also be however,
         that  other  types  of  commitments  are  capable  of  preventing  the  significant
       impediment to effective competition.1821 In  particular, other types of  structural
       commitments may be suitable to resolve all types of concerns if they are equivalent
         to divestitures in their effects.1822
(1932)  As regards divestitures, the Remedy Notice sets out that the divested activities must
         consist of a viable business that, if operated by a suitable purchaser, can compete
         effectively with the merged entity on a lasting basis and that is divested as a going
        concern. For the business to be viable, it may also be necessary to include activities
       which are related to markets where the Commission did not identify competition
        concerns  if  this  is  required  to  create an  effective competitor  in  the  affected
         markets.1823 The business has to include all the assets which contribute to its current
        operation or which are necessary to ensure its viability and competitiveness and all
        personnel which is currently employed or which is necessary to ensure the business’

[PÁGINA PDF 472]
          viability and competitiveness.1824 In the description of the business, the Parties also
        have to set out the arrangements for the supply of products and services by them to
         the  divested  business  or by  the  divested  business  to  them. Such  on-going
         relationships of the divested business may be necessary to maintain the full economic
          viability and competitiveness of the divested business on a transitional basis.1825
(1933)  The business to be divested has to be viable as such. Therefore, the resources of a
         possible or even presumed future purchaser are not taken into account, in principle,
       by the Commission at the stage of assessing the remedy. The situation is different if
        already during the procedure a sale and purchase agreement with a specific purchaser
           is concluded whose resources can be taken into account at the time of the assessment
         of the commitments.1826 A divestiture consisting of a combination of certain assets
       which did not form a uniform and viable business in the past creates risks as to the
          viability and competitiveness of the resulting business. Such an approach may be
        accepted by the Commission only  if  the  viability of the business  is ensured
        notwithstanding the fact that the assets did not form a uniform business in the
          past.1827
(1934)  The intended effect of the divestiture will only be achieved if and once the business
           is transferred to a suitable purchaser in whose hands  it will become an active
        competitive force in the market.1828 In general, there are three ways to ensure that the
        business is transferred to a suitable purchaser. First, the business is transferred within
        a fixed time-limit after adoption of the decision to a purchaser which is approved by
         the Commission on the basis of purchaser requirements set out in the commitments.
        Second, in addition to the conditions set out for the first category, the commitments
      may foresee that the parties cannot complete the notified operation before having
        entered into a binding agreement with a purchaser for the business, approved by the
       Commission (so-called ‘upfront buyer’). Third, the parties identify a purchaser for
         the business and enter into a binding agreement already during the Commission's
        procedure (so-called ‘fix-it-first’ remedy).1829 The choice of the category depends on
         the risks involved in the case and therefore on the measures which enable the
       Commission to conclude with the requisite degree of certainty that the commitment
         will be implemented. Among others, this will depend on the nature and the scope of
         the business to be divested and any uncertainties inherent in the transfer and
        implementation, in particular the risks of finding a suitable purchaser.1830
(1935)  The Commission welcomes up-front buyer remedies in particular in cases where
         there are considerable obstacles for a divestiture, such as third party rights, or
         uncertainties as to finding a suitable purchaser.1831 In such cases, an up-front buyer
         will allow the Commission to conclude with the requisite degree of certainty that the
       commitments will be implemented, as such a commitment creates greater incentives
         for the parties to close the divestiture in order to be able to complete their own
         concentration.1832

(1936)  The Commission welcomes  fix-it-first remedies in particular in cases where the
         identity of the purchaser is crucial for the effectiveness of the proposed remedy. This
        concerns cases where, given the circumstances, only very few potential purchasers
        can be considered suitable, in particular as the divested business is not a viable
        business in itself, but its viability will only be ensured by specific assets of the
         purchaser, or where the purchaser needs to have specific characteristics in order for
         the remedy to solve the competition concerns.1833 The Court has clarified in that
        regard that it does not follow from the last sentence of paragraph 57 of the Remedy
        Notice that an ‘up-front buyer’ solution containing specific requirements as to the
          suitability of a purchaser should systematically be regarded as equivalent to the ‘fix-
           it-first’ solution and as generally acceptable.1834 In particular, such equivalence
        cannot be recognised where the divestment business is structurally inadequate for the
        purpose of addressing the anticompetitive effects of the concentration. The ‘up-front
        buyer’ solution is intended above all to put pressure on the transferee to accelerate
         the divestiture, in situations where the feasibility of the divestiture or the viability of
         the divestment business depends on external constraints, which must be removed
         quickly, such as obtaining authorisation from the authorities or access to certain
         assets held by the potential purchasers of that business.1835
(1937)  As regards the removal of links with competitors, the Remedy Notice explains that
       where competition concerns result from agreements with companies supplying the
       same products or providing the same services, a suitable remedy may be the
        termination of  the  respective agreement, such as  distribution agreements with
        competitors or agreements  resulting  in the coordination of  certain commercial
         behaviour.1836
(1938)  As  regards  access commitments,  the Remedy  Notice  specifies  that  if  those
       commitments actually make the entry of sufficient new competitors timely and
          likely, they can be considered to have a similar effect on competition in the market as
        a divestiture.1837 This principle that the likely entry of a new competitor is necessary
         in order for access commitments to be considered suitable has also been established
         in previous Commission decisions, specifically in the assessment of airline mergers:
        “In  airline cases, commitments are acceptable to the Commission where  it  is
          sufficiently likely that actual entry by new competitors will occur and where such
         entry would eliminate any serious doubts as to the compatibility of the concentration
        with the internal market.”1838
(1939)  This principle corresponds to the assessment of entry as a competitive constraint on
         the merging parties. As stated in paragraph 68 of the Horizontal Merger Guidelines,
         “for entry to be considered a sufficient competitive constraint on the merging parties,
             it must be shown to be likely, timely and sufficient to deter or defeat any potential
         anti-competitive effects of the merger.”1839
(1940)  For mergers in the air transport sector, the Commission has previously clarified that
         “in air transport mergers, a mere reduction of barriers to entry by a commitment of
         the parties to offer slots on specific airports may not always be sufficient to ensure

(1941)  Concerning the sufficient likelihood of entry, in the case of air transport mergers, the
        Court previously held that “the mere threat of an entry […] is not sufficient. […]
       What counts is the prospect of an entrant which offsets the anti-competitive effects
         specifically established in the contested decision […].”1841 The likelihood of an entry
           is further dependent, among several considerations, on the profitability of the entry,
         the attractiveness of the route and the level of possible barriers to entry.
(1942)  As to a timely entry, as previously stated, what constitutes an appropriate time period
      may depend on the characteristics and dynamics of the market, as well as specific
         capabilities of potential entrants.1842 While in its past airline cases, the Commission
        held that an entry occurring within the next two years may be considered as
         timely,1843 what constitutes a “timely entry” has to be assessed for each case
         individually.
(1943)  Commitments  relating  to  the  future behaviour  of  the merged  entity may be
        acceptable only exceptionally in very specific circumstances. Such commitments, for
         instance in the form of undertakings not to raise prices, to reduce product ranges or
         to remove brands, will generally not eliminate the competition concerns resulting
       from horizontal overlaps. In any case, those types of remedies can only exceptionally
        be accepted if their workability is fully ensured by effective implementation and
        monitoring, and if they do not risk leading to distorting effects on competition.1844
14.2.3.  Capable of being implemented effectively within short period of time
(1944)  Commitments must be capable of being implemented effectively within a short
        period of time as the conditions of competition on the market will not be maintained
          until the commitments have been fulfilled.1845
(1945)  The Commission has to be able to conclude with the requisite degree of certainty that
             it will be possible to implement the commitments and that it is likely that the new
        commercial structures resulting from them will be sufficiently workable and lasting
         to  ensure  that  the  significant  impediment  to  effective  competition  will  not
         materialise.1846
(1946)   If the parties submit remedy proposals that are so extensive and complex that it is not
         possible for the Commission to determine with the requisite degree of certainty, at
         the time of its decision, that they will be fully implemented and that they are likely to
        maintain effective competition in the market, an authorisation decision cannot be
         granted. The Commission may reject such remedies in particular on the grounds that
         the implementation of the remedies cannot be effectively monitored and that the lack
         of effective monitoring diminishes or eliminates the effect of the commitments
         proposed.1847

(1947)  The Court has clarified that  “it must be held in that regard that commitments

         the Commission  is able to conclude, with certainty, that  it will be possible to

       commitments may in particular be affected by risks in relation to the transfer of a
        business to be divested, such as conditions attached by the parties to the divestiture,
         third party rights in relation to the business or the risks of finding a suitable
         purchaser, as well as risks in relation to the degradation of the assets in the time
        before the divestiture has taken place.1849
14.2.4.  Case-by-case approach
(1949)  The Commission notes that whether a remedy is suitable to eliminate the competition
        concerns identified can only be examined on a case-by-case basis.1850
(1950)  The fact that similar remedies have been accepted or rejected in previous airline
        cases is not sufficient to conclude that those remedies solve or do not solve the
        competition concerns in the present case. The Commission must assess the proposed
       commitments taking into account the specificities of the transaction under review in
         line with the legal standards set out above.

14.3.1.  Description of the Initial Commitments

             agreement with one or more remedy takers (“Short Haul Remedy Taker(s)”)
            and by making available slots and possibly other elements to those remedy
               takers (“New Entrant Remedy”);
         (b)  Commitments to address the competition concerns on two overlapping short-

               to remedy takers upon request (“Slot Remedy”; together with the New Entrant

          (c)  Commitments to address the competition concerns at LIN airport by divesting
                slots (“LIN Slots Remedy”); and
         (d)  Commitments to address the competitions concerns on three overlapping long-
              haul routes (where both Parties offer direct services) by committing to procure
              the operation at a minimum weekly frequency for the summer and/or the winter
          IATA seasons (“Long-Haul Capacity Remedy”).
(1952)  The Initial Commitments also foresaw the appointment of a Monitoring Trustee to
        monitor the Parties’ implementation of the Initial Commitments.

          “New Entrant Remedy Short-haul Route(s)”).
(1954)  For the above-mentioned routes, the Initial Commitments provided that the Parties
       and the remedy taker(s) would enter into an “Entry Commitment Agreement” which
       would impose the obligation on the remedy taker(s) to enter the routes and operate
       them until the end of the Minimum Period, that is to say for four consecutive IATA
         seasons. According to the text of the Initial Commitments, during the Minimum
         Period, the slots should only be used for scheduled passenger air transport services
       on the six routes and the remedy taker would not be entitled to “transfer or assign”
         these slots.
(1955)  Before the Parties provided the remedy taker(s) with the necessary slots, the Initial
       Commitments provided that the remedy taker(s) would need to apply for the slots
        under the general slot allocation procedure. If the remedy taker(s) is/are able to
        obtain necessary slots, the number of slots to be made available by the Parties would
        be reduced accordingly.
(1956)  To be approved by the Commission, the Initial Commitments provided that the
       remedy taker(s) would need to meet the following conditions:
          (a)  The remedy taker(s) must be independent of and unconnected to the Parties;
         (b)  The remedy taker(s) must have the financial resources, proven expertise and
              incentive to act as a viable and active competitive force;
          (c)  The operations on the routes by the remedy taker(s) must neither be likely to
               create prima facie competition concerns nor give  rise to a  risk  that the
             implementation of the Commitments will be delayed.
(1957)  According to the proposed New Entrant Remedy, the Parties were not obliged to find
        a remedy taker within a specific timeline and were allowed to close the Transaction
         as soon as the Commission decision is adopted.
(1958)  The Parties explained in the Form RM that they considered that there were several
         interested and suitable potential remedy takers for all or parts of the New Entrant


                                    474

[PÁGINA PDF 477]
       Remedy, namely Volotea, EasyJet, Wizz Air, Ryanair, Neos, Transavia, Aeroitalia,
        Vueling and Air France.1851
14.3.1.2. Slot Remedy
(1959)  The Parties also committed to make available under the Initial Commitments the
        following number of slots to an interested remedy taker on the Rome-Brussels and
        Milan-Brussels routes, however without committing to find a suitable remedy taker:
          (a)  Rome FCO-Brussels: 14 weekly frequencies  in the summer seasons and
            14 weekly frequencies in the winter seasons; and
         (b)   Milan-Brussels: 14 weekly frequencies in the summer seasons and 14 weekly
              frequencies in the winter seasons to/from LIN/MXP airport.
(1960)  Other provisions of  this  part of the  Initial Commitments were  similar  to the
         provisions in connection with the New Entrant Remedy: the slots should be used
        only on the two routes to Brussels for a duration of four consecutive IATA seasons;
         the remedy taker would  first need to apply for the slots under the general slot
         allocation procedure and, in the case of a successful application, the number of slots
         to be made available by the Parties would be reduced accordingly; the remedy taker
       would need to meet the same conditions as set out in paragraph (1952) (1952)above
         to be approved by the Commission. The Parties also identified the same potential
       remedy takers as those listed in paragraph (1954)(1954) above.
14.3.1.3. LIN Slots Remedy
(1961)  The Transaction would result in an increment in slot holdings at LIN (“LIN Total
         Slot Increment”). According to the Parties, this concerned:
          (a)   148 weekly slots, equalling 74 weekly frequencies in the summer; and
         (b)  136 weekly slots, equalling 68 weekly frequencies in the winter.
(1962)  The Parties offered to divest slots equal in number to the LIN Total Slot Increment in
         the following ways: First, the Parties would transfer slots to the remedy taker(s) on
         the three routes to/from Milan as described in paragraph (1949) above (the “LIN
       Route Remedy Slots”). Second, if any of the LIN Increment remained, the Parties
       would transfer additional slots to the same remedy taker(s) on the three routes
        to/from Milan or the remedy taker on the two routes to/from Brussels (“LIN Remedy
        Taker Slots”). Third, if any of the LIN Total Slot Increment remained after those
          transfers, the Parties would transfer  all remaining  slots of the LIN Total Slot
        Increment to the slot coordinator at LIN. The Initial Commitments provided that the
         divested slots were to be spread across all traffic days and LIN’s operating hours.
14.3.1.4. Long-Haul Capacity Commitment
(1963)  The Long-Haul Capacity Commitment covered the following three direct/direct long-
        haul  overlap  routes:  Rome-Washington  (both  seasons), Rome-San  Francisco
       (summer season) and Rome-Toronto (summer season).
(1964)  For these routes, the Parties committed to procure that at least a minimum number of
        seasonal widebody frequencies were offered for the duration of six consecutive
      IATA seasons, the first such season being from the beginning of the season in which
         the Parties have received approval from the US DoT to integrate ITA into the A++
      JV agreement.

(1965)  The minimum number of frequencies for the three routes were as follows:
          (a)  Rome FCO-Washington: 14 weekly frequencies in the summer seasons and 7
            weekly frequencies in the winter seasons:
         (b)  Rome FCO-San Francisco: 12 weekly frequencies in the summer seasons; and
          (c)  Rome FCO-Toronto: 14 weekly frequencies in the summer seasons.
(1966)  The Long-Haul Capacity Commitment would have ended on the relevant route if a

         period. Furthermore, the Long-Haul Capacity Commitment would have been without
         prejudice to the Parties cancelling flights due to Operational Risks, defined in the
          Initial Commitments as risks outside the Parties’ area of influence.
14.3.2.  Assessment of the Initial Commitments
(1967)  The Commission decided not to market test the Initial Commitments as it considered
         that they suffered from several deficiencies affecting their comprehensiveness and/or
         effectiveness. Amongst others:
          (a)   with respect to the Short-Haul Remedy Package, the Parties did not offer
             remedies with respect to 18 short-haul routes of concern;1852
         (b)   with respect to the New Entrant Remedy, (i) the Initial Commitments were
              unclear as to whether the Short-Haul Remedy Taker(s) would need to operate
                  all of the frequencies offered on each route or whether they could operate
             fewer  frequencies,  (ii)  the  Initial Commitments  did  not  include  e.g., a
               divestiture period, or any timeframe within which an entrant would need to be
              found, the Entry Commitment Agreement signed, the slots divested, or any
             timeframe within which the chosen entrant would need to start operations on
              the relevant routes; (iii) it was unclear how many Short-Haul Remedy Takers
               there would be; (iv) specifically for the Milan-Düsseldorf and Milan-Hamburg
               routes, the Initial Commitments appeared to leave the choice of slots at either
        MXP or LIN entirely to the discretion of the Parties; (v) similarly, the Initial
           Commitments appeared to leave the choice of the exact date and time of the
                slots  entirely  to the  discretion of the  Parties;  (vi)  the Commission was
             concerned that the Minimum Period of two years was too short; (vii) the Initial
           Commitments provided that the Parties would provide the Short-Haul Remedy
              Taker(s) in addition to the slots themselves, with “other necessary elements (if
             any)” to be defined based on the new entrant’s needs), without explaining for
            example what these elements might be, whether the Parties would provide
              these elements at cost or other commercial conditions, or if there would be a
               time-limit on providing these elements;
          (c)   with respect to the Slot Remedy, it aimed at fostering potential entry in the
               future rather than immediately reducing the market power of the Parties by
               transferring the share of their business to an independent competitor, although

1852    The direct/direct short-haul overlap on the route Milan-Stuttgart, the three future direct/direct short-haul
        overlaps on the routes Rome-Hamburg, Rome-Vienna, and Milan-Vienna, and the fourteen current
         short-haul direct/indirect overlaps. This reflects the scope of the Commission’s preliminary competition
        concerns as set out in the Statement of Objections of 25 March 2024 and as still relevant at the time of
        submission of the Initial Commitments on 11 April 2024. In any event, the Short-Haul Remedy Package
         of the Initial Commitments also did not cover the final scope of competition concerns as set out in this
        Decision as it did not cover the two future direct/direct short-haul routes Rome-Hamburg and Milan-
       Vienna as well as the eight current short-haul direct/indirect overlaps.


                                    476

[PÁGINA PDF 479]
             evidence collected in this case suggested that the likelihood that there would be
                insufficient interest would have been high;
         (d)   with respect to the LIN Slots Remedy, while the scope of the proposed transfer
              of slots fully covered the increment stemming from the Transaction, and in
               principle the type of remedy offered was appropriate to address the competition
             concerns identified by the Commission with respect to airport dominance at
            LIN, the LIN Slots Remedy under the Initial Commitments suffered from
               certain shortcomings in terms of modalities of implementation that could have
             rendered it ineffective; for example, (i) the 3-step transfer process gave rise to a
              possible risk of fragmentation of the slot portfolio at LIN which in turn gave
                rise to a risk that the minimum scale required to operate the LIN Slots Remedy
              sustainably would not be achieved by  the remedy  taker,  (ii)  the  Initial
           Commitments appeared to leave the exact choice of the date and time of the
           LIN  slots  entirely  at  the  discretion  of  the  Parties, and  (iii)  the  Initial
           Commitments  did  not  foresee any  divestment  closing  deadlines  or any
             timeframe within which a legally binding agreement would be signed with the
            remedy taker or the slots would be divested;
          (e)   with respect to the Long-Haul Capacity Commitment, among others, (i) the
              type of remedy seemed inappropriate, (ii) the scope of the commitment was
                insufficient  in  terms  of  frequencies and  duration;  (iii)  the Commission
              considered that the Parties had the ability and incentives to circumvent the
            commitment; and (iv) the Commission considered that the remedy included too
             broad exit clauses.
14.4.   The Second Commitments
14.4.1.  Description of the Second Commitments
14.4.1.1. Short-Haul Commitments
(1968)  As regards the competition concerns arising on specific short-haul routes, the Second
       Commitments  removed  the  Slot Remedy  originally  contained  in  the  Initial
       Commitments. Instead it contained a modified version of the New Entrant Remedy,
        with the content as described in section 14.4.1.1.1, and added a new commitment
        concerning  a  special  pro-rate  agreement,  with  the  content  as  described  in
         section 14.4.1.1.2.
14.4.1.1.1.   New Entrant Remedy
(1969)  In the Second Commitments, the Parties extended the scope of the New Entrant
      Remedy to include the two Brussels routes, Milan – Brussels and Rome – Brussels.
       The New Entrant Remedy in the Second Commitments therefore covered eight of the
        twelve  direct/direct short-haul routes of concern.1853 The Second Commitments
         specifically provided for the possibility that the Brussels routes could be taken up by
        a different remedy taker than the six short-haul routes already included in the New
        Entrant Remedy under the Initial Commitments.1854


1853     Second Commitments, clause 15. The number of 12 direct/direct short-haul routes of concern reflects

       Second Commitments on 6 May 2024. In any event, the New Entrant Remedy of the Second
       Commitments also did not cover the final scope of competition concerns as set out in this Decision as it
        did not cover all ten routes of concerns as the two future direct/direct short-haul routes Rome-Hamburg
       and Milan-Vienna were not included.

(1970)  In addition, the Parties committed to enter into the Entry Commitment Agreement
        with the remedy taker(s) for the New Entrant Remedy as early as possible, but in any
        event no later than within a certain time frame  after the Commission clearance
         decision, which however did not constitute a sufficiently specific deadline.1855 The
        Entry Commitment Agreement would provide for the entry of the remedy taker in a
         specific IATA season and impose the obligation on the remedy taker(s) to enter the
         routes and operate them until the end of the Minimum Period, which the Parties
        extended in the Second Commitment to six consecutive IATA seasons (i.e., three
         years, or three summer and three winter seasons), from four under the  Initial
        Commitments.1856
(1971)  The Second Commitments also provided that if the remedy taker(s) ceases to operate
         the slots during the first or second year of the three-year period, all slots would
        automatically  fall back  to the  Parties. The  Parties committed  to subsequently
        “procure the divestment to a new taker through the conclusion of a new Entry
       Commitment Agreement for the remaining part of the Minimum Period.” If the
       remedy taker(s) cease to operate the slots during the third year of the three-year
         period, the Parties committed to release the slots to the relevant slot coordinators.1857
(1972)  Other changes notably included specifying that the exact traffic days and hours of the
          slots to be divested would be agreed as part of the Entry Commitment Agreement
        with the remedy taker with the aim to reflect the current offering on the market,
        defined as the traffic days and hours currently being offered by the Parties on the
         route.
14.4.1.1.2.    Special Pro-Rate Agreement
(1973)  In  order  to  address  the  competition  concerns  on  the Remedy  Short-Haul
         Direct/Indirect  Routes,1858  the  Parties included  in  the Second Commitments a
       commitment to enter into a Special Pro-Rate Agreement (“SPA”) with the remedy
         taker in relation to ITA’s domestic network. The SPA would connect the remedy
         taker(s) with all intra-Italian routes served by ITA from Milan Linate and Rome
        Fiumicino  airport.1859 This would enable the remedy  taker(s)  to  offer  indirect
        connections on the Remedy Short-Haul Direct/Indirect Routes and allow  it to
         replicate ITA’s activities pre-merger beyond those routes as it offered the remedy
         taker(s) access to all of ITA’s domestic network. Therefore, the SPA would also
        allow the remedy taker to enhance the connectivity of its operations to and from
       Milan Linate airport and Rome Fiumicino airport beyond the Remedy Short-Haul
         Direct/Indirect Routes.
(1974)  The SPA would be based on a so called Straight-Rate Proration (“SRP”) with
      minimum prorates to be paid by the remedy taker to ITA. The Second Commitments

14.4.1.3. Long-Haul Commitments
(1977)  As regards the competition concerns arising on specific long-haul routes, the Second
       Commitments maintained the Long-Haul Capacity Commitment, with the content
        described in section 14.3.1.4 and complemented it with additional commitments to
         hold-separate and ring-fence certain parts of ITA’s long-haul business, as described
         in section 14.4.1.3.2, and introduced a new commitment to offer the conclusion of
        cooperation agreements with one or more remedy taker(s), as described in section
         14.4.1.3.3.
(1978)  The remedy would have been split between two phases: in a first phase, from closing
         of the Transaction  until the receipt of the US Department of Transportation’s

        approvals by  other  antitrust  authorities  (“Antitrust  Approvals”),1863  only  the
       commitment to hold-separate and ring-fence would have applied; in a second phase
         as of receipt of the Antitrust Approvals, only the Capacity Commitment and the
       commitment to offer cooperation agreements to competing airlines to strengthen
          their own operation on some specific long-haul routes would have applied.

14.4.1.3.2.    Hold-Separate and Ring-Fencing Commitment
(1980)  In the Second Commitments, in addition to the Long-Haul Capacity Commitment,

       implement all necessary measures to ensure that Lufthansa does not, after closing of
         the Transaction, obtain any confidential information relating to the Long-Haul North
         Atlantic Business (together “the Hold-Separate and Ring-Fencing Commitment”).1867
       The Parties argued in the Form RM that this was to ensure that there would not have
        been coordination between ITA on the one hand and the A++ JV on the other hand
         prior to receipt of the Antitrust Approvals.1868

         structure  to  ensure  implementation  of  the  Hold-Separate  and  Ring-Fencing
       Commitment. This was meant to be achieved by:1869

         (b)   ensuring that management and staff of Lufthansa would have no involvement

          (c)   ensuring that personnel of ITA would not report to any individual at Lufthansa
               in relation to the Long-Haul North Atlantic Business;
         (d)   appointing (by MEF) a Hold Separate Manager to manage ITA’s Long-Haul
             North Atlantic Business and to report directly to ITA’s Chairman. The Hold
              Separate Manager were to be granted the necessary power for decisions and
              processes related to ITA’s Long-Haul North Atlantic Business, such as pricing,
               capacity, revenue management and network;
          (e)   creating a Long-Haul North Atlantic Committee responsible for all decisions
             concerning the network and capacity planning of ITA’s Long-Haul North
               Atlantic Business, including the opening and closing of long-haul routes. The
            Committee would consist of three members of ITA’s Board of Directors
              representing the MEF as well as the Hold Separate Manager;
           (f)   ensuring that all relevant systems, processes and IT tools pertaining to ITA’s
            Long-Haul North Atlantic Business would be kept separate from the rest of
              Lufthansa’s organisation;
         (g)   ensuring that any Lufthansa representatives serving in any committees or
              functions  of ITA  or  otherwise  potentially having  access  to  confidential

14.4.2.  Assessment of the Second Commitments
(1987)  As set out in further detail in the sections below, the Commission considered that the
         Parties made some progress in addressing some of the concerns expressed with
         respect to the  Initial Commitments. Several issues were  still not addressed, or
          insufficiently, and certain new issues arose as a result of changes made to the Initial
       Commitments. However,  the Commission decided  to market  test  the Second
       Commitments, in order to base  its decision on the best available evidence. The
       Commission took these results into consideration in  its final assessment of the
       Second Commitments.
14.4.2.1. Short-Haul Commitments
(1988)  Despite  some  improvements,  the  Commission  considered  that  the  Second
       Commitments did not entirely or comprehensively address its concerns in scheduled
          air passenger transport on short-haul routes arising as a result of the Transaction.

(1990)  With respect to the New Entrant Remedy specifically, first, the Parties addressed in
         the Second Commitments some of the deficiencies identified by the Commission in
         section 14.3.2. By way of example, the Parties clarified that:  (i) the Short-Haul
      Remedy Taker would either be one entity or there would be one Short-Haul Remedy
        Taker  for the two Remedy Short-Haul Routes from/to BRU and one  for the
        remaining Remedy Short-Haul Routes; (ii) the slots to be divested for the operation
         of the Remedy Short-Haul Routes and the LIN Remedy Slots would be agreed as
         part of the Entry Commitment Agreement with the Short-Haul Remedy Taker with
         the aim to reflect the current offering on the market (i.e. the traffic days and hours
         currently being offered by the Parties on the route), and, in addition, the Second
       Commitments refer to the relevant slots as those within the Relevant Time Window,
        defined in Section A. of the Second Commitments, as the period of 20 minutes on
         either side of the Slot time requested by the Short-Haul Remedy Taker;1877 and
            (iii) the Minimum Period was extended from 4 to 6 consecutive IATA seasons
            (i.e., from 2 to 3 years).1878
(1991)  Second, the Parties simultaneously extended the scope of the New Entrant Remedy
       and addressed the Commission’s concerns with respect to the Slot Remedy by
        including the LIN/MXP-BRU and FCO-BRU  direct/direct short-haul routes of
        concern into the Remedy Short-Haul Routes. However, in the first place, the Second
       Commitments provided in Section A that the Short-Haul Remedy Taker would be
        “the entity or, in case the Remedy Short-Haul Routes from/to BRU on the one hand

         different airlines". In other words, there was built-in flexibility to allow for the routes
        Milan-Brussels and Rome-Brussels to be taken up by a separate remedy taker than
         the other Remedy Short-Haul Routes. In the second place, the Parties still did not
         offer remedies with respect to 4 direct/direct short-haul routes of concern, namely the
         current direct/direct short-haul overlaps on the routes Milan-Stuttgart and the three

14.4.2.1.2.   SPA Commitment
(2002)  As indicated in section 14.4.1.1.2 above, the SPA generally went beyond the scope
         of concerns identified by the Commission on the short-haul direct/indirect overlaps
         as it offered the remedy taker(s) access to all of ITA’s Italian domestic network, and
        not just on the Italian domestic leg of the routes identified in sections 9.4.5 and 9.4.6
        above. In this context, the Commission considered that the scope of the SPA’s
        agreement as such could be sufficient and adequate. However, as set out below, the
       Commission considered that the SPA Commitment suffered from certain deficiencies
         that would have affected its effectiveness.
(2003)   First, the New Entrant Remedy left the flexibility to the remedy taker(s) whether they
        choose to operate the routes Milan-Düsseldorf and Milan-Hamburg from Linate or
        Malpensa. To the extent that the remedy taker would choose Malpensa, the remedy
         taker would not be able to offer connecting flights to destinations in Italy as the SPA
       would apply only  to connections through Milan Linate and Rome Fiumicino.
        Considering that the Rome-Düsseldorf or Rome-Hamburg routes were not part of the
      New Entrant Remedy and therefore that connections through Rome were not an
         option, this meant that the SPA would not have been applicable for connections to

        unaddressed. This was a flaw in the design of the remedies, which left a loophole

(2004)  Second, the Commission considered that the duration of the SPA was likely to be too
         short. More specifically, the agreement was limited in duration to three years,1909
          after which there would not be a remedy in place for the direct/indirect overlaps. In
         the Commission’s past decisional practice, it is on the one hand acknowledged that
       “SPAs are generally valid for one year and are renegotiated thereafter”,1910 but, on
         the  other hand  the  duration  of SPAs concluded pursuant  to commitments  in
        competition cases in the airline industry by the Commission exceeded, in most cases
         three years. More specifically, the special prorate agreements concluded in M.7333 –
         Alitalia / Etihad1911 and in M.7541 – IAG / Aer Lingus1912 had a duration of up to five
        years at the choice of the requesting carrier. Furthermore, in the former case, the
        agreement could be renewed for a further period of one year, whereas in the latter
         case, for a further period of two years.1913 In addition, in the antitrust case AT.39964
       – Air France  / KLM  / Alitalia  / Delta, the special prorate agreement concluded
        pursuant to the commitments had a duration of up to ten years.1914 The results of the
       Commission’s market test were mixed and inconclusive regarding the suitability of
         the duration of the SPA Commitment. 4 out of ten competitors that expressed a view
        considered the duration as suitable whereas 4 others considered it unsuitable, and 2
        responded “Other”.1915
(2005)  Third,  the  Commission  considered  that,  although  the  concept  of  the SPA
       Commitment was  acceptable  as a remedy  for  the concerns  arising from  the
         direct/indirect short-haul overlaps in this case (taking into account the degree of
        competitive constraint ITA’s indirect connections imposed on Lufthansa’s direct
          flights before the Transaction as well as the number of routes of concern), the SPA
       Commitment did not specify in sufficient detail the access conditions and that certain
         conditions or terms that were specified gave rise to certain issues that could affect its
         effectiveness.
(2006)  This view was supported by the results of the market test. Indeed, on the one hand,
