         entrant  to  establish  viable  operations  while  relying on  the  flights  of  their
         competitor1916 and that this is common industry practice. On the other hand, many
        explained that this would depend on the content of the SPA. For example, according
         to Air Europa, “it depends on the content of the SPA. If it is a good SPA for both
         parties and Lufthansa has an incentive to offer the necessary feed (and there is
          sufficient demand) then the interest[s] are aligned and the remedy taker can stablish

1921     Reservation Booking Designators (‘RBDs’) are alphabetic or alpha-numeric codes used by airlines to
         identify a fare type and allow airline staff and travel agents to find the rules applicable to that fare.
        Thus, the flight's booking class, is determined by its RBD and is utilised in reservation procedures to
         specify which booking class is being chosen by the passenger. Additionally, the RBD correlates to the
        type of cabin or service class provided on the plane by the airline operating the flight.

        with the selected remedy taker(s), carried strong implementation risks.
(2013)  Fourth, the Commission was concerned that the SPA Commitment was not suitable
         to be taken up by either of the potential remedy takers Volotea and easyJet, which
       would leave the Commission with the risk that no remedy taker would be found or
         that only an unsuitable remedy taker would sign a deal.
(2014)  In the first place, the Commission was concerned that the remedy offer would not fit
         the business model of the potential remedy takers as both Volotea and easyJet are
     LCC carriers. The incompatibility of the remedy takers’ point-to-point business
       model with the nature of the SPA Commitment  (i.e., the fact that point-to-point
      LCCs do not enter into interlining agreements such as the proposed SPA) was
         identified by several competitors in their responses to the Commission’s market test.

14.4.2.3. Long-Haul Commitments
(2021)  For the reasons set out below, the Commission considered that the Long-Haul
       Commitments were insufficient and inadequate and therefore incapable of rendering
         the concentration compatible with the internal market in connection with scheduled
          air passenger transport on the long-haul routes of concern.
14.4.2.3.1.    Deficiencies common  to  the  different  components  of  the  Long-Haul
           Commitments
(2022)  The  Commission  considered  that   all  the  components  of  the  Long-Haul
       Commitments, as described in section 14.4.1.3, suffered from common deficiencies.
(2023)  First, most of the components of the Long-Haul Commitments were inadequate as
        they were largely behavioural in nature, without obligations for the Parties to make
       any  significant  structural  divestments  or  otherwise  commit  to  maintaining
        competition between separate undertakings. This was in contrast to the nature of the
       Commission’s preliminary competition concerns on the 8 problematic long-haul
          routes,1949 which (i) arose as a result of the structural link created between Lufthansa,

         event, the behavioural nature of the Long-Haul Commitments contained in the Second Commitments is
         also  in contrast to the nature of the Commission’s preliminary competition concerns on the 3
        problematic long-haul routes, as outlined in Section 10 of this Decision, which (i) arise as a result of the
          structural link created between Lufthansa, on the one hand, and ITA, on the other hand, and which (ii)
         are related to horizontal overlaps.

[PÁGINA PDF 497]
       on the one hand, and ITA, on the other hand, and which  (ii) were related to
         horizontal overlaps (rather than overlaps arising from vertical or conglomerate links
         created  by  the  Transaction). As  explained  further  above,  according  to  the
       Commission’s Remedy Notice, behavioural remedies will “generally not eliminate
        competition  concerns  resulting  from  horizontal  overlaps”.1950  Therefore,  the
       Commission “may examine  other  types  of  non-divestiture  remedies, such  as
        behavioural  promises,  only  exceptionally  in  specific  circumstances  [emphasis
        added], such  as  in  respect  of  competition concerns  arising  in conglomerate
         structures”.1951
(2024)  In  contrast  to what should happen  after  the successful  divestiture of remedy
        businesses under effective divestiture remedies, the Second Commitments proposed
       by Lufthansa and MEF relied on the Parties acting against their own best interest in
        order to  fulfil these commitments. As further explained in section 14.4.2.3.2 to
         14.4.2.3.3, the Long-Haul Commitments would have required ITA to act against the
          interests of its controlling shareholder Lufthansa while simultaneously depending on
        Lufthansa for financing and requiring  it to integrate with Lufthansa’s business,
        systems and operations to realise deal synergies.
(2025)  Moreover, the Commission was of the view that there were significant challenges to
        ensuring effectiveness and enforcing most of the Long-Haul Commitments, arising
       from the fact that they were, in essence, behavioural remedies, as well as due to their
        complexity.
(2026)  In the first place, the remedies, which mostly related to the future behaviour of ITA
       and Lufthansa, were unsuitable to address the structural effects of the Transaction on
         transatlantic long-haul routes. These concerns were echoed in the replies to the
       Commission’s market test,1952 with one competitor indicating that “the commitments
        proposed by the parties cannot effectively address the long-haul issues because they
        are ill-designed and non-structural”.1953 Similarly, Air Transat explained that “the
        absence of structural remedies from Lufthansa severely undermines the effectiveness
         of the proposed Commitments”.1954 Air Europa further noted that “there are more
        straightforward remedies. For example, it would be significantly more effective to
        have a remedy taker taking over ITA LH operations on these routes or part
         thereof”.1955  In  addition,  Air  Europa  explained  that  “the  structure  of  these
       commitments relies heavily on the powers of the monitoring trustee as it has to be
         carefully and regularly monitored with clear enforcement power in case in case (sic)
         the Hold Separate (sic) and Ring Fencing is breached”.1956 In the second place, as
         further explained in Sections 14.4.2.3.2 to 14.4.2.3.3, the behavioural nature of most
         of the Long Haul Commitments made  it extremely difficult, if not impossible, to
        monitor and enforce these remedies. This  is in line with paragraph 69 of the
       Commission’s Remedy Notice according to which  “competitors may also not have
       an incentive to alert the Commission [of any breaches of the behavioural remedies]
        as they do not directly benefit from the commitments”.1957 Overall, it “may [therefore]

(2027)  Third, the Commission considered that the duration of the Long-Haul Commitments
       was  limited  and  insufficient.  Notably,  the  Hold-Separate  and  Ring-Fencing
       Commitment would have applied only until receipt of the Antitrust Approvals which
           is expected within about 2 years from this Decision. In the second place, the Long-
       Haul Capacity Commitment would only have applied from receipt of the Antitrust
        Approvals and at most for six IATA seasons (three years). There were, however, no
         indications available to the Commission that indicate that the identified competition
        concerns would have been automatically resolved by these commitments by that
         time. Therefore, the Long-Haul Commitments did not represent sufficiently long-
         lasting solutions, but at best interim remedies.
(2028)  Fifth, as explained in further detail below, the Long-Haul Commitments included
         limitations, exemptions or other similar clauses affecting their effectiveness and
         enforceability. By way of example, clause 74 of the Second Commitments envisaged
         that “at the request of the Parties, any or all of the Commitments […] may be
        reviewed, waived  of modified by the Commission based on long-term market
         evolution. […] the Commission shall in particular: a. waive without delay the Hold
        Separate and Ringfencing Commitment following the issuance  of the  Antitrust
        Approval, as any merger control or antitrust concerns of the Commission would be
        resolved in such circumstances”. Such clause would have not only illegitimately
         limited the Commission’s discretion in deciding whether to waive or not a specific
       commitment, thus preventing a thorough assessment of the market conditions, but
         also meant that the mere fact that a third country’s authority issues a decision under a
         separate regulatory regime (which includes other considerations than the preservation
         of competition) would automatically prevent the Commission from carrying out a
        thorough assessment of the effectiveness of those remedies.
(2029)  Sixth, the results of the market test further showed that the Long-Haul Commitments
         as a whole could not be considered suitable to remove all the competition concerns
         identified by the Commission in scheduled air passenger transport on the long-haul
        overlap routes of concern.
(2030) A clear majority of the competitors that provided a clear view (Yes/No) in the market
          test supported this conclusion.1959 In addition to the concerns illustrated above as to
         the ineffectiveness of the remedies to address the structural effects of the Transaction
       on transatlantic long-haul routes, almost all competitors indicated that the Long-Haul
       Commitments as a whole would not make it likely for them to enter or expand on at
          least one of the routes of concern.1960 Among customers and third parties, a majority
         of  the respondents  did  not  express a view concerning  the  suitability  of  the

14.4.2.3.2.    Hold-Separate and Ring-Fencing Commitment
(2031)  For the reasons set out below, the Commission considered that the Hold-Separate and
        Ring-Fencing Commitment was inadequate and ineffective.
(2032)  First, the Hold-Separate and Ring-Fencing Commitment suffered from the common
         deficiencies described in section 14.4.2.3.1.
(2033)  Second,  the Commission considered  that  the Hold-Separate and Ring-Fencing
       Commitment would not have addressed the root cause for the competition concerns,
       namely the structural link created between Lufthansa/the A++ JV on the one hand
       and ITA on the other hand and therefore would not have had any effect.
(2034)  Lufthansa would have had extensive rights in the A++ JV, including in terms of
         setting prices and capacity for the flights of the A++ JV on each of the relevant
         routes of concern, while simultaneously owning ITA and benefitting from its profits.
       The A++ JV is a metal-neutral joint venture. That means it is set up in a way that
        each JV member will be incentivised to treat all flying within the scope of the
         provisions of the joint venture agreement, regardless of the operating airlines.1964 The

(2039)  Third, the Commission considered that it would have been extremely complex, if not
        impossible, to hold separate ITA’s Long-Haul North Atlantic Business from the rest
         of ITA’s business.
(2040)  In the first place, the Long-Haul North Atlantic Business would have still relied on
         basic shared functions and strategies decided together at ITA’s corporate and at
        Lufthansa’s group level, such as financing, human resources management and hiring
         of crew and other personnel, operational planning (including connections with other
          flights), purchasing of all inputs (including aircraft and fuel), fleet management,
        revenue management systems, ticket distribution through the Parties’ websites and
         relationships with third-party distributors, relationships and contracts with customers
         (including namely corporate customers), frequent  flyer programmes, marketing
       campaigns and strategies, brand strategy, IT systems, and others. In this regard,
        Lufthansa and MEF themselves confirmed that the Hold-Separate and Ring-Fencing
       Commitment “would allow to keep  all supporting and administrative functions
         related  to  the Long-Haul North  Atlantic Business with  the  rest  of  the DLH
         organisation, namely IT, HR, procurement as well as sales” […]”.1981
(2041)  In the second place, there are operations that are particularly complex to  split
       between certain long-haul flights and other flights, for instance ground handling,
          traffic management and slot management at Rome Fiumicino airport.
(2042)  In the third place, the operation of flights between Italy and North America is closely
        linked with connecting traffic originating or going to destinations outside of Italy;
       and with the operation of domestic and short-haul flights more generally. Sustainable
       and profitable long-haul operations rely on domestic and short-haul feeder traffic;
       and  successful  capacity,  capacity  steering and  pricing  decisions  rely on  the
        interconnected nature of these flights. It was unclear under the Second Commitments
      how the North-Atlantic Long-Haul business that would have been held separate
       would have been able to have sufficient access to such connecting traffic and how
         the Hold-Separate and Ring-Fencing Commitment could, even in theory, have been
        applied for pricing, capacity, capacity steering and network decisions on such
          intrinsically integrated operations and businesses.
(2043)  These concerns were generally supported by the responses of competitors to the
        market  test. Among those competitors that expressed a view  (i.e., that did not
        respond “I do not know”), only 3 out of 13 competitors considered that the Hold-
        Separate and Ring-Fencing Commitments would make  it possible to keep ITA’s
        long-haul business between Italy and North America separate and ringfenced from
         the rest of ITA’s business.1982 Among the remaining 10 competitors, half responded
         in the negative and half responded “[i]t depends/Other”.1983

         highlighted by the European Commission, particularly regarding long-haul routes
        between Italy and North America. First and foremost, tying the duration of these
       commitments to the receipt of Antitrust Approvals from the US Department of
        Transportation effectively cedes control over the regulatory framework and oversight
         to American authorities; the adequation between the duration of the commitments
       and  Antitrust Approvals  implies  that once  these approvals are  obtained,  all
        competition  concerns  identified  by  the  Commission  would  be  permitted  to

        Lufthansa Group following the  integration  of ITA  into the A++ JV. Without
       permanent safeguards in place, there is a heightened risk of reduced competition on
        long-haul routes between Italy and North America. To address these deficiencies and
        uphold the principles of fair competition, it is imperative to revise the duration of the
       commitments to ensure their effectiveness beyond the receipt of Antitrust Approvals.
       The Commission should seek remedies that establish permanent separation and ring-
        fencing of ITA from the A++ JV, thereby preventing anti-competitive practices and

        Air France-KLM echoed these concerns noting that “[t]he issues will arise after the

(2050) Among those competitors that responded  “[i]t depends/Other”, LOT and Norse

(2051)  Sixth, as explained in paragraphs (2030) and (2031) above, the Parties would have
       had incentives to circumvent the Hold-Separate and Ring-Fencing Commitment to
        bring about the effects of the planned integration of ITA into the A++ JV as soon as
         possible. This was due to the myriad contacts between ITA’s Long-Haul North
         Atlantic Business and the remainder of the ITA business and the Lufthansa group,
        following from the intrinsically intertwined nature of the business as outlined above.
(2052)  Seventh,  the Hold-Separate and Ring-Fencing Commitment would have been
        extremely complex – if not impossible – to monitor. This was particularly the case
        considering that under Clause 42 of the Second Commitments, ITA would still have
        been allowed to enter into partnership agreements (such as interline, special prorate
       and codeshare) with Lufthansa and  its A++ JV partners. Under such potential
        extensive cooperation, the Commission considered that it would have been extremely
          difficult to clearly distinguish (i) between decisions that concern the O&D operations
         or the connecting operations and (ii) between on one side, legitimate exchanges of
        information related to the abovementioned cooperation agreements and, on the other
          side, sharing of confidential information and/or collusive practices. Therefore, the
        implementation of this remedy could not have been effectively monitored and the
        lack of effective monitoring had the potential to significantly diminish the effect of
         the commitments proposed.

14.4.2.3.3.    Long-Haul Capacity Commitment
(2056)  Lufthansa and MEF made only few and immaterial changes to the Long-Haul
        Capacity Commitment  in  the Second Commitments compared  to  the  Initial
       Commitments, which the Commission considered to be insufficient for the reasons
        explained in section 14.3.2. Furthermore, the Commission considered that the Long-
       Haul Capacity Commitment did not address the concerns raised in this decision for
         the following reasons.
(2057)  First, the Long-Haul Capacity Commitments suffered from the common deficiencies
        described in section 14.4.2.3.1.
(2058)  Second, the Commission considered that the type of remedy was inappropriate as it
       would have constituted, at best, a weak behavioural measure to address structural
        concerns by committing to procure that the Parties and/or Lufthansa’s JV partners fly
        a pre-determined minimum number of frequencies on certain routes.
(2059)  According  to  the  Commission’s Remedy  Notice,  behavioural  remedies  will
        “generally not eliminate competition concerns resulting from horizontal overlaps”,
       and “[i]n any case, it may be difficult to achieve the required degree of effectiveness

         of  such  a  remedy  due  to  the  absence  of   effective  monitoring  of   its
         implementation”.1997 Therefore, the Commission “may examine other types of non-
         divestiture remedies, such as behavioural promises, only exceptionally in specific
        circumstances [emphasis added], such as in respect of competition concerns arising
         in conglomerate structures”.1998
(2060)  In  this  specific case, the Commission considered  that the behavioural remedy
        proposed was  insufficient,  such  that  the  assessment  of  whether  there were
         exceptionally any specific circumstances was unnecessary.
(2061)  In the first place, the remedy did not address the loss of direct price competition
       between the Parties and their JV partners resulting from the Transaction. Even under
        a static model of price competition without any changes in demand compared to the
      Summer 2023 scenario, the Parties would have had an incentive to raise prices post-
        Transaction due to the loss of price competition. This would have involved the
         Parties flying with less than full capacity in order to sustain higher prices (similar to
         regular unilateral horizontal effects without capacity commitments); to mitigate the
         effects of flying at lower capacity, the Parties could also have tried to sell more
         tickets to connecting passengers, rather than O&D passengers, further reducing the
        need to fill the planes with passengers travelling on the O&D.
(2062)  In the second place, to the extent that demand on these routes increases post-
         Transaction, the remedy would have become entirely insufficient, as, under such
        circumstances, the Parties would have an incentive to raise capacity above the
      minimum  level  agreed  to  in  these commitments  both  with and  without  the
         Transaction. However, with the Transaction, the Parties would have had an incentive
         to raise their capacity by less than they would absent the Transaction (and prices
       would  increase more compared  to  the  counterfactual absent  the  Transaction).
        Therefore, the minimum frequency agreed to in the remedy would have become
         effectively non-binding as the capacity offered by the Parties would have been above
          this minimum level both with and without the Transaction.
(2063)  The Commission also noted that there have been no precedents involving mergers in
         the  airline industry where the Commission has accepted a commitment to  fly
      minimum capacity on certain routes.1999
(2064)  Third, the Commission considered  that the scope of the proposed Long-Haul
        Capacity Commitment was insufficient.
(2065)  In the first place, the remedy offer was below the frequencies currently offered (in
        Winter 2023/2024 and Summer 2024) and/or did not account for ITA’s growth plans
         in future seasons. On each of the three routes within the scope of the Long-Haul
        Capacity Commitment, [details of ITA’s long-haul expansion plans] such that the
         Parties’ combined frequencies are above the levels to which the Parties were
        committing in this remedy offer. This means that the minimum capacity to which the
         Parties committed in this remedy offer did not provide a suitable benchmark on the
         level of capacity that the Parties (and in particular ITA) would fly on these routes
        absent the Transaction (which would be the relevant comparison). In other words, by

         that the competition concerns would automatically have lapsed by that time.
(2067)  Fourth, the Commission further concluded that the proposed Long-Haul Capacity
       Commitments were ineffective.
(2068)  In the first place, the remedy offer would only have taken effect upon ATI approval
       by the US DoT, which is needed for ITA joining the A++ JV. In the Commission’s
        view, this was insufficient, as the Commission’s concerns on long-haul are not
         conditional on the US DoT granting ATI to ITA, as further explained in Section
         10.1.1 above. This means that the remedy offer would not have addressed the
       Commission’s concerns until ATI is granted. Also, the Parties themselves argued,
         that Antitrust Approvals may not be granted to the Parties. Thus, according to the
         Parties’ own reasoning, the remedy may have never become effective, and the Parties
       would never have had an obligation to address the Commission’s concerns on the
        problematic long-haul routes.
(2069)  In the second place, the Parties had the ability and incentive to circumvent the
        remedy. The remedy involved the Parties committing to act against their own best
          interest, rather than changing the structure of the relevant markets in such a way that
         aligns the  Parties’ best  interests with the Commission’s objective of  effective
        competition. This means  that the  Parties could have had strong incentives  to
        circumvent the proposed remedies. Examples of how the Parties would have had the
          ability to circumvent this behavioural remedy include the following:
          (a)  Type of aircraft used: The remedy offer only specified that the Parties would
             use widebody, rather than narrowbody, aircraft for the committed frequencies.
            However, the Parties would have been able to reduce capacity on these routes
            by using widebody aircraft with lower capacity than those currently used on

              the proportion of tickets sold on these routes to connecting passengers (e.g., by
              increased marketing for these indirect routes) in order to artificially decrease
              spare capacity on the trunk routes where the Commission  identified the
              competition concerns.
(2070)  In the third place, the remedy offer could only have been implemented via third
          parties. The remedy offer specified that the committed frequencies would need to be
       implemented by “Lufthansa, ITA, one of Lufthansa’s A++ JV partners, or any
        combination thereof”. However,  it was unclear whether Lufthansa and ITA have
         sufficient capacity to implement the committed frequencies on these routes without
         the support of Lufthansa’s A++ JV partners. More specifically, even following its
        expansion plans on these routes, ITA’s standalone frequency on these three routes
       would have been significantly lower than the frequencies to which the Parties would
       commit to under this remedy proposal.2004 To the extent that Lufthansa and ITA
         relied on frequencies by Lufthansa’s JV partners in order to implement the remedy,
          this would have meant that the commitments depended on actions by third parties to
         the Transaction (United Airlines and Air Canada). Therefore, the commitment was
         limited to “procuring” the frequencies rather than flying the frequencies themselves.
        This raised questions of enforceability as it was unclear how the Commission could
        have enforced these remedies vis-à-vis these third parties and what specifically the
         obligation to “procure” entailed.
(2071)  In the fourth place, the remedy offer included too broad exit clauses under which the
       remedy would no longer be effective.

          trip”. The Commission considered this to be problematic for several reasons:
          (a)  The exit clause did not specify a minimum number of scheduled weekly
              frequencies that a new entrant would need to have on these routes for the exit
              clause to hold. Under the current formulation, the  exit clause would be

14.4.2.3.4.    Long-Haul Connectivity Commitment
(2079)  The Commission considered that the Long-Haul Connectivity Commitment under the
       Second Commitments was insufficient and inadequate and therefore incapable of
        rendering the concentration compatible with the internal market for the following
         reasons.
(2080)  First,  the  Connectivity Commitment  suffered from  the common  deficiencies
        described in section 14.4.2.3.1.
(2081)  Second, the Connectivity Commitment did not include a straightforward obligation
       by the Parties to actually enter into any such agreements. Instead, the Commitments
        merely stated that the Parties would “offer [emphasis added] the conclusion of
        cooperation agreements”. Therefore, there was no sanction for not implementing any
         connectivity improvements, which increased even further the risks of the remedy
        remaining devoid of any effect.
(2082)  Third, the Commission found that the terms and conditions of the Connectivity
       Commitment were not specified in sufficient detail in the Second Commitments to
        allow the Commission to fully assess the likely impact of this commitment. The
        Connectivity Commitment did not specify at what terms the Parties would offer such
         connectivity agreements to third-parties. The Parties themselves explained in the
       Second Commitments that the “[d]etails will be negotiated and agreed upon in the
        Connectivity  Agreements”.2022  Therefore,  the  Parties  could  have made  these
        agreements unattractive to existing or potential competitors on these routes by
         requesting high prices for the cooperation agreements or by offering access only to
         limited booking classes or limited numbers of seats. The Commission’s view that the
        Connectivity Commitment did not provide sufficient detail was echoed in the market
          test with most competitors expressing a view (10 out of 17) indicating that it was not
        adequate that the Parties did not provide further details on this Commitment.2023 One
        competitor that provided a negative response, LOT, submitted that “the merging
         parties [would] have the ability to propose any conditions for such contracts […]
       and ITA, in spite of having met the obligation of having offered interline cooperation,
       would still be able to block access to the transits of long haul operator”.2024 Even
       among the competitors that replied “other”, one highlighted that “[n]ot including

(2083)  Fourth, the Commission was unable to conclude with sufficient likelihood that the
        Connectivity Agreements would be entered into by any rivals.
(2084)  In the market test, almost half of all competitors expressing a view (6 out of 14)
        submitted that the Connectivity Commitment would not make it likely that new entry
        and/or expansion would  take  place on  the  long-haul  routes covered by  this
       commitment, whereas most of the remaining competitors indicated that “it depends”
        (5 out of 14).2026 Three competitors replied that it would make such entry and/or
        expansion more likely.
(2085)  Overall, the Commission considered that there was not enough evidence to conclude
        with sufficient likelihood that the Connectivity Commitment would have been taken
       up by any competitors on each of the long-haul routes of concern covered by the
        Connectivity Commitment of the Second Commitments.
14.4.3.  Conclusion on the Second Commitments
(2086)  In  light  of  the  above  assessment,  the  Commission  concludes  that  while
       improvements were made compared to the Initial Commitments, the deficiencies of
         the Second Commitments as described in the sections above meant that the Second
       Commitments did not meet the standard for acceptable commitments under the
      Remedy Notice.
14.5.   Final Commitments
14.5.1.  Description of the Final Commitments
14.5.1.1. Short-Haul commitments
(2087)  Apart from the changes described below, the Final Commitments concerning the
         short-haul routes of concern substantially incorporate the short-haul remedies as set
        out in the Second Commitments.
14.5.1.1.1.   New Entrant Remedy
(2088)  In the Final Commitments, the Parties extended the scope of the New Entrant
      Remedy to include two additional routes: (i) Rome – Hamburg, and (ii) Milan (MXP
        or LIN) – Vienna, both with a minimum of 7 weekly frequencies in both the summer
       and winter  seasons.2027 The New Entrant Remedy  in  the  Final Commitments
         therefore covers ten routes (i.e., Rome – Frankfurt, Rome – Munich, Rome – Zurich,
      Rome – Brussels, Rome – Hamburg, Milan (MXP or LIN) – Düsseldorf, Milan
        Linate – Frankfurt, Milan (MXP or LIN) – Hamburg, Milan (MXP or LIN) –
         Brussels, and Milan (MXP or LIN) – Vienna).2028
(2089)  In addition, the Final Commitments remove the requirement for the Short-Haul
      Remedy Taker to first exhaust all reasonable efforts to obtain the necessary slots to
        operate the Remedy Short-Haul Routes through the normal workings of the General
         Slot Allocation Procedure. Instead, the slots will be transferred directly by the
          Parties, avoiding delays, and reducing complexity.

14.5.2.  Lufthansa and MEF’s view
(2111)  The  Parties submit  that  the  Final Commitments  are  suitable  to remove  the
        competition concerns raised by the Transaction. Specifically, the Parties argue that
         the following:
        (1)   the New Entrant Remedy will “establish a new market entrant on all Remedy
            Short-Haul Routes, enabling the Short-Haul Remedy Taker to grow into an
              effective competitive force, before the acquisition of grandfathering rights for
             the Remedy Short-Haul Routes”;2051
        (2)   the inclusion of an SPA will “enable the Short-Haul Remedy Taker to offer an
              indirect connection on all the Remedy Direct/Indirect Short-Haul Routes and,
             thereby, be  in a  position  to  replicate ITA’s  activities  pre-merger”.2052 In
              addition, the Parties submit  that, “as the SPA grants access to the entire
            domestic  network  of  ITA,  the  Short-Haul  Remedy  Taker  can  enhance
             connectivity with regard to its own operations to and from FCO and LIN”;2053
        (3)   the LIN Slots “are highly attractive to any competitor already or potentially
             active at LIN. as this is a congested airport with intense competition for any
               slots. By divesting a significant number of these highly attractive slots to the
            Short-Haul Remedy Taker, the latter is put in a position to create a reliable base
              in Linate, from where further operations at the discretion of the Short-Haul
          Remedy can be expanded. The Commitment thereby results in the creation of a
           new, solid competitive force at LIN, fuelling competition vis-à-vis the merged
              entity post-merger”;2054 and
        (4)   the “Long-Haul Remedy will bring a structural change to market conditions.
             Either a new (direct or indirect) offer is established on the Long-Haul Remedy
             Routes,  or an  already  established  player  can  expand and  improve  its
             operations.”2055

14.5.3.  The Commission’s Assessment
                     14.5.3.1. Short-Haul Commitments
(2112)  For the reasons set out below, the Commission considers that, together, the New
        Entrant Remedy  and  the SPA  Commitments  as  provided  under  the  Final
       Commitments, once implemented, will address the competition concerns raised and
         are adequate and sufficient to eliminate the significant impediment to effective
        competition that would otherwise arise on the short-haul routes of concern, as
         identified in section 9.
14.5.3.1.1.   New Entrant Remedy
(2113)  The Commission considers that the Parties have sufficiently addressed the most
         material deficiencies identified with respect to the New Entrant Remedy as discussed
        under section 14.4.2.1.1.
(2114)   First, by adding Rome – Hamburg and Milan – Vienna in the scope of the Remedy
        Short-Haul Routes, the Parties ensured that the scope of the New Entrant Remedy
        covered all the direct/direct short-haul routes of concern. In addition, the Parties
        expressly provide in Clause 23 of the Commitments that preference will be given to a
         single Short-Haul Remedy Taker.
(2115)  Second,  the  Parties  clarified  in  the  text  of  the  Final Commitments  that  the
        frequencies listed in Clause 13 constituted minimum frequencies to be flown by the
        Short-Haul Remedy Taker. This was added to ensure that the frequencies offered by
         the Short-Haul Remedy Taker could not go below the minimum required to replace
         the  loss of competition on the Remedy Short-Haul Routes  resulting from the
         Transaction.
(2116)  Third, the transfer process was streamlined and clarified, adding more certainty to
         the modalities of implementation. In the first instance, the process is less complex
       and likely to be delayed as the Short-Haul Remedy Taker is no longer required to
           first exhaust all reasonable efforts to get the relevant slots through the general slot
         allocation procedure. In the second instance, the Parties clarified in the text of the
         Final Commitments the relevant deadlines. In particular, the Final Commitments
        provide (i) in Clauses 5 and 23 that Lufthansa and MEF commit to find a Short-Haul
      Remedy Taker and enter into the Entry Commitment Agreement and the Slot
        Transfer Agreement2056 with the Short-Haul Remedy Taker as early as possible, but
         in any event within a specific time frame from the date of this Decision at the latest;
       and (ii) in Clauses 5 and 26, that “the Slots and assets required and requested by the
        Short-Haul Remedy Taker (as the case may be) to be transferred in the context of the
      New Entrant Remedy (including the LIN Remedy Slots) as well as the LIN Remedy
        Taker Slots will be divested ideally before the IATA Historics Baseline Date, namely
        [before a certain date], but in any case timely before [the start of a specific season]
        with the objective of permitting entry of the Short-Haul Remedy Taker [within a
         specific season]”.
(2117)  Fourth, the Parties have also included an upfront remedy taker clause. Clause 13
        provides that the closing of the Transaction can take place, in addition to those
        conditions related to the Long-Haul Commitments, once the Parties “have entered
         into a final and binding Entry Commitment Agreement and Slot Transfer Agreement


2056     Defined in Section A of the Final Commitments as “the agreement between DLH, MEF and the Short-
       Haul Remedy Taker organizing the transfer of the Slots to the Short-Haul Remedy Taker”.


                                    515

[PÁGINA PDF 518]
        with the Short-Haul Remedy Taker, ITA has entered into an SPA or an agreement of
         similar kind to enable connectivity with the Short-Haul Remedy Taker, and the
       Commission has approved the proposed Short-Haul Remedy Taker(s) and the terms
         of the Entry Commitment Agreement, the Slot Transfer Agreement and the SPA or
        agreement of similar kind to enable connectivity”. This shifts the risk that a remedy
         taker is not found on the Parties, rather than on the Commission, and ultimately the
         public. As per paragraph 54 of the Remedy Notice, “an up-front buyer will allow the
       Commission to conclude with the requisite degree of certainty that the commitments
         will be implemented, as such a commitment creates greater incentives for the parties
         to close the divestiture in order to be able to complete their own concentration”. In
         addition,  the Short-Haul Remedy  Taker(s)  will need  to be approved by  the
       Commission. In order to be approved, the potential remedy taker(s) will need to meet
         the criteria set out in Section C of the Final Commitments.
(2118)  Fifth, the Parties have made significant improvement to the back-up remedy clause,
       whereby the Parties commit to find a new remedy taker (“New Remedy Taker”) in
        case the Short-Haul Remedy Taker ceases to operate. In the first place, Clause 8 now
         defines the notion of “ceases to operate”, to encompass the situations where “the
        Short Haul Remedy  Taker  (i)  completely  interrupts  scheduled  air  transport
        passenger operations on the Short-Haul Remedy Routes, (ii) uses any of the Short-
       Haul Remedy Routes Slots for other routes without having obtained alternative or
        retimed Slots, (iii) operates any of the Short-Haul Remedy Routes with less than 80%
         of the initially envisaged Frequencies in a specific season during the Minimum
        Period, or (iv) operates less than 80% of the LIN Remedy Taker Slots in a specific
        season during the Minimum Period [i.e.] (each a “Slot Utilization Shortfall Event”),
       and  unless  the Short-Haul Remedy Taker  is  forced  to cancel  flights due  to
        Operational Risks”. In the second place, Clause 8 also provides for an appropriate
         process. For example,  the back-up remedy  clause now  provides  that  (i)  the
       Commission and the Monitoring Trustee will be responsible for confirming that a
         Slot Utilization Shortfall Event of sufficient magnitude has occurred to  justify
         replacing the Short-Haul remedy taker and approve the new Entry Commitment
        Agreement, (ii) there should not be more than one IATA season between the shortfall
        event and the entry of the New Remedy Taker, (iii) the New Remedy Taker should
       meet the same criteria as set out in the Final Commitments for the Short-Haul
      Remedy Taker.

         (as the connections the Short-Haul Remedy Taker may provide through Linate

14.5.3.1.3.   LIN Slot Remedy
(2126)  The Commission considers that the LIN Slot Remedy under the Final Commitments,
        once implemented, will address the competition concerns raised and are adequate
       and sufficient to eliminate the significant impediment to effective competition that
       would otherwise arise with respect to LIN airport dominance, as identified in
         section 11.
(2127)  First, under the Final Commitments, all LIN slots to be divested will go to the Short-
       Haul Remedy Taker, with no possibility for the surplus to go to the slot pool, thus
         eliminating the risk of excessive fragmentation of the slot portfolio. In connection to
          that, it needs to be noted that the Final Commitments provide for the total divestment
         of 204 weekly slots in the Summer and 192 weekly Slots in the Winter, which goes
       beyond  the  increment added  to  the  Parties’  portfolio  through  the  Proposed
         Transaction. This was done with the aim to put the Short-Haul Remedy Taker in a
         position to  establish a  sustainable, credible base  at LIN, which addresses the
         potential foreclosure concerns identified by the Commission, and to allow  it to
         potentially offer its own connections on the direct/indirect routes of concern in the
         future.
(2128)  Second, the Final Commitments eliminate the risk that a suitable Remedy Taker
       would not be found, as they introduce an upfront buyer clause, preventing the Parties
       from closing the Proposed Transaction before the Commission approves the Remedy
        Taker and the Slot Transfer Agreement.
(2129)  Finally, as explained in further detail in paragraph (2114), the Final Commitments
        introduce an improved mechanism for replacing the Remedy Taker in the event they
        cease to operate or significantly reduce operations of the Linate slots during the
      Minimum Period.

        capable of rendering the Transaction compatible with the internal market and the

          result are generally obligations on the parties. Where a condition is not fulfilled, the

        market is no longer applicable. Where the undertakings concerned commit a breach
         of an obligation, the Commission may revoke the clearance decision in accordance
        with Article 8(6) of the Merger Regulation. The undertakings concerned may also be
         subject to fines and periodic penalty payments under Articles 14(2) and 15(1) of the
       Merger Regulation.

         conditions and obligations, this Decision should be made conditional on the full

1.     EXECUTIVE SUMMARY
(1)     This Annex outlines the regression analysis carried out by the Commission to assess
         the relationship between the competitive landscape and Lufthansa’s average prices
       on both long-haul and short-haul routes. This analysis can help in the assessment of
        whether the presence of competitors, and in particular ITA, has an impact on the
         prices charged by Lufthansa, as well as in quantifying the magnitude of this impact.
      As such, the regression analysis contributes to assessing whether the Transaction is
         likely to significantly impede effective competition.
(2)     Regression  analysis  is  a  statistical  tool commonly  used  in  economics  for
        understanding the relationship between two or more variables. In this case, the main
         variables are on the one hand Lufthansa’s prices, and on the other hand the number
        of competitors. To shed light on the relationship between these two variables, the
         analysis has to control for the role played by other variables, for example demand
       and supply factors that can also influence Lufthansa’s prices on a route.
(3)     The Commission  applied a methodology commonly known  as  ‘fixed  effects’
         regressions to a panel of data that allows to isolate the factors that influence
        Lufthansa’s prices. The fixed effects methodology takes account of important but
        unobserved (or unmeasured) effects on price that do not vary over time on any given
         route or that vary over time but are the same across all routes. In addition, further
         control variables take account of important observed effects that may vary over time
       on a given route. As a result, the estimated effects will capture changes in prices on a
         route when changes in competition occur on that route (as opposed to simply
       comparing prices across routes where competition may differ).
(1)     The data and analysis could then show whether Lufthansa offers lower prices on
        average on a route when there is more competition compared to when there are less
         operators. That  is, the regression models and the data give rise to the testable
        hypothesis that the competitors’ presence  is associated with a  statistically1 and
        economically significant reduction in Lufthansa’s prices in the various routes where
        they overlap.
(2)     The results of the regression analysis for short-haul routes suggest that (i) increased
        competition on a route is associated with lower average Lufthansa’s prices; and
            (ii) ITA’s presence is associated with lower average Lufthansa’s prices. These results
         indicate that a reduction in the number of competitors active on a route is likely to
         increase prices.
(3)    More specifically, the results of the regression analysis on short-haul routes indicate
          that:
          (a)   Routes with a higher number of competitors have prices on average [10-20]%
             lower than routes where Lufthansa is a monopolist.2
         (b)  The first competitor is associated with Lufthansa’s prices being reduced by
              [5-10]-[5-10]%,3 while each subsequent additional competitor beyond the first

         ITA/Alitalia, excl. Lufthansa)”.

               additional percentage points.4
          (c)  The robustness analysis carried out suggests that the effect on Lufthansa’s
               prices associated to the first competitor can range between 5% to 22%,5 while
              the effect from each subsequent additional competitor can be as large as
            10 percentage points.6
(4)     The Commission’s fixed effects regression methodology also allows one to assess
         the relationship between ITA’s presence and Lufthansa’s prices. The results of this
         regression analysis indicate that the presence of Alitalia/ITA is associated with on
        average approximately [10-20]-[20-30]% lower DLH prices.7
(5)      Further results imply that Lufthansa’s prices are estimated to be:
          (a)   about  [5-10]-[5-10]%  higher on monopoly compared  to duopoly  routes
              (“2-to-1”  impacts),  but  about  [10-20]%  higher  where  the  competitor
              disappearing is ITA, and
         (b)   about [0-5]-[5-10]% higher8 on duopoly compared to three-or-more-carrier
              routes (“3-to-2” impacts), but about [10-20]% higher where the competitor
              disappearing is ITA.
(6)     This Annex also provide an assessment of the Parties’ claims in their Response to the
         6.1.c Decision and in a subsequent submission9 about Ryanair exerting significant
        competitive pressure on Lufthansa, whereas ITA not exerting the same competitive
         pressure. As explained in more detail below, the Parties’ analysis is methodologically
        flawed and unreliable. The results of the Commission’s regression analysis indicate
         that both ITA and Ryanair exert a competitive pressure on Lufthansa, but Ryanair
        does not compete more closely with Lufthansa than ITA. And, the opposite is true
        with Lufthansa’s prices being on average lower in response to ITA’s entry on a city-
         pair route than in response to Ryanair’s entry.

4       See Annex I, column (4) of Table 4 and Table 10, row labelled “Average effect from 3 to 2 carriers on a
         route”. The effect of 3% is statistically significant only at 12% in the overall sample that include both
      IATA summer and IATA winter seasons, which indicates a moderate likelihood that the observed
       outcome is not due to random chance, though scientific research in economics typically consider a
          stricter threshold of 10% to minimize the risk of false positives. This effect is nonetheless economically
         relevant: in smaller samples, even economically meaningful effects may  fail to reach  statistical
         significance due to the lower number of observations, whereas in larger samples, even small effects can
        achieve statistical significance. Therefore, the absence of statistical significance does not necessarily
        imply the absence of an economically meaningful relationship. Moreover, this effect is also larger and
          statistically significant at 10% in the sensitivity based only on IATA summer seasons. When the
         analysis  is  carried out on only IATA summer seasons, the  first competitor  is associated with
        Lufthansa’s prices being reduced by [10-20]%, while each subsequent additional competitor with a
         further [5-10] percentage points reduction. The estimated effect appears instead milder in IATA winter
         seasons.

(7)      Finally, the results of the regression analysis for long-haul routes also suggest that
        increased competition on non-stop routes to North America is associated with lower
        average prices. Thus, the results clearly indicate that a reduction in the number of
        competitors active on a route is likely to increase prices. In particular:
          (a)   Routes with a higher number of competitors have lower prices by up to
             [20-30]-[20-30]% compared to routes where Lufthansa is a monopolist.
         (b)  The  first  competitor  of  Lufthansa  entering  a  route  is  associated  with
              Lufthansa’s prices being reduced by [5-10]%, while each additional competitor
            beyond the first one with a further [10-20] percentage points reduction.
(8)     These results are consistent when including in our analysis indirect competitors as
         well:
          (a)  The  first  additional  indirect  competitor  decreases  prices by  only  about
              [0-5]%.10
         (b)  Two or more additional indirect competitors decrease prices by about [5-10]%
            compared to monopoly, which means an additional indirect competitor beyond
              the first one is associated with Lufthansa’s prices being about approximately
              [5-10] percentage points lower.
(9)     The  structure of  this Annex  is as  follows. Section 2 describes  the data and
       methodology used in the regression analysis, Section 3 presents the results from the
         short-haul regressions, as well as an assessment of the Parties’ price analysis, Section
       4 presents the long-haul regressions. Section 5 summarises the Parties’ arguments as
        per their Response to the 6.1.c Decision, their Response to Statement of Objections,
          their Response to Second Letter of Facts, as well as the other ancillary submissions

        well as the methodology followed.

        or the airport), and which Lufthansa’s entity operated the flights.12,13 The data covers

2.2.    Methodology
2.2.1.   Overview of the Commission’s approach to the regression analysis
(10)    The Commission followed an empirical strategy similar to the ones employed in
        previous cases16 in the aviation industry. In particular, the methodology is a reduced-
       form analysis, which is a common technique in econometrics to investigate the
         relationship between a dependent variable and a set of independent variables. The
        independent variables include the variables of interest to proxy for competition, as
        well as ‘control variables’. These control variables are added to ‘control’ for demand
        or supply factors that can influence prices besides competition. Not including the
         control variables might lead to falsely attributing some price effects to competition
          (this is also known as omitted variable bias).

2.2.2.   Proxies for competition
(12)   As indicated above, the term                     represents the proxies used in the
         regression analysis to assess competition on the routes. Because regression analysis           is a relatively flexible statistical𝑓𝑓(𝐶𝐶𝐶𝐶𝐶𝐶𝐶𝐶𝐶𝐶𝐶𝐶𝐶𝐶𝐶𝐶𝐶𝐶𝐶𝐶𝐶𝐶𝑖𝑖𝑖𝑖)tool, it can be used to test alternative hypotheses
        regarding how to represent competition. The objective of the Commission’s analysis
           is therefore twofold:
          (a)  To estimate how much Lufthansa’s average prices change as the number of
              competitors active on a route changes. This type of analysis allows to assess to
            what extent there is a relationship between DHL prices and the number of
              competitors.
         (b)  To estimate how much Lufthansa’s average prices change when ITA is present
            on a route. This type of analysis allows to assess how closely Lufthansa and
           ITA compete.
(13)    The  first  set  of  analyses  focuses on  defining competition  as  the number  of
        competitors other than Lufthansa active on a route.19 To this end, the regression
         analysis includes two types of models. The  first type of models (“number of
        competitors model”) proxy competition with the number of competitors (other than
        Lufthansa) as a single variable. The second types of models (“indicator variables
        model”) use the following indicator variables: (i) Only one competitor other than
        Lufthansa; and (ii) Two or more competitors other than Lufthansa.
(14)    The first, number of competition model is more parsimonious, as  it captures the
        competition impact by only one coefficient. The second, indicator variables model
         offers more flexibility. The  first model’s single coefficient captures the average
        impact on Lufthansa’s prices of having one more competitor on a route. The
        estimated coefficients from the second model measure the expected average effect
         relative to having no competitor on a route in a given month. This specification
        allows the average effect of the first competitor to be different from the average
         effect of the arrival of a second or third competitor. The estimated coefficient for the
         indicator variable for one competitor measures the expected effect of the entry of a
        competitor  into a monopoly  city-pair  route. The  coefficient  for two or more
        competitors measures the expected average difference with respect to a monopoly
         route. It follows that the difference between two coefficients measures the impact of

19      For the long-haul regressions, the number of competitors active on the route is calculated considering

         route becoming a duopoly. Also, the estimated effects are symmetric in the case of
          exit: The difference between the coefficients estimates for having one or two

         signs are opposite in the case of entry and exit).
(15)    The second set of analyses focuses on assessing whether any specific effects on
        Lufthansa’s prices can be associated with ITA’s presence. To this end, the regression
         analysis includes an ITA specific indicator variable. This indicator variable is equal
         to 0 if ITA is not operating on a specific route in a given month, and 1 otherwise.20
(16)    The effects of competition can only be reliably estimated  if there  is sufficient
         variation in the data of market structures due to entry or exit events over time, and
        within several routes. In particular, only  if there are several instances when the
       number of competitors change (first set of analyses of overall competition), or there
           is a change in ITA’s presence (second set of analyses of ITA-specific competition),
        can the regression analysis identify the average impact of competition on Lufthansa’s
         prices. The regression analysis essentially uses this entry/exit variation to compare
        Lufthansa’s prices between periods with different market structures. Hence, the
         regression in practice calculates the increase or decrease in price when a change in
         the market structure occurs, and then reports the average effect across routes.

2.2.3.   The role of control variables
(21)    Control variables play an important role in the validity of the regression model and
           its results. These variables control for factors that can either positively or negatively
         affect ticket prices. In general, the more relevant information is included in the
        model, the more precisely can the effect on prices of the various factors – including
        those capturing competition – be estimated. If important factors are either excluded
         or imprecisely estimated due to lack of information, this may either distort the
         coefficient estimates or reduce their precision. The choice of the variables to be

         estimation sample. Nonetheless, the remaining routes are relatively sizable as they correspond to 4% of
       P2P passengers. Once routes operated by EW are excluded, the number of entry/exit events for
         Alitalia/ITA drops from 22 to four, and to two on FRA-ROM if only ITA is considered.

[PÁGINA PDF 533]
        included in the analysis is ultimately driven by economic theory that is informed by
         the specificity of the case being investigated.
2.2.3.1. Fixed effects
(22)     Prices across routes and over time can vary for many reasons. Some of these factors
         are difficult to observe or measure, and hence cannot be controlled for directly in a
         regression analysis. When an analysis does not control for such specificities, the
         results of the analysis may be biased due to the so-called omitted variable bias. In the
         present  setting, omitted variable bias could lead to the variable describing the
        competitive pressure unduly capturing variation in prices that are the result of other,
        omitted  factors. Given the panel data  structure,  this omission problem can be
        remedied by introducing indicator variables of specific groups of observations into
         the regression.24,25 These indicator variables are then also called as fixed effects, as a
        type of control variables. The most important among these are the fixed effects for
         the route city pairs.26 The inclusion of these route city pair indicator variables hence
        gives rise to the ‘fixed effects’ methodology.
(23)   By controlling for route specificities through route fixed effects, the omitted variable
         bias risk is reduced substantially. The fixed effects control for all differences across
         routes in unobservable cost or demand factors that are constant over the period
        spanned by the data. For example, this would include the type of destination, the
         popularity  of  the  route  according  to purpose  of  travel, customer  awareness,
         destination airport characteristics, number of alternative airports at destination, the
        general level of income among potential customers total duration of travel or air
          traffic regulations at country of destination.
(24)    The ‘fixed effects’ methodology can account for many structural differences across
        groups or routes. For example, it is conceivable that prices on monopoly routes are
        high not because there is no competition but because on a particular route costs are
         relatively high (for example, when high entry barriers are correlated with high
        operation costs). The opposite may also be true, prices on monopoly routes may be
         relatively low because demand on such routes is weak (or very elastic). The fixed
         effect regressions hence separate these supply/demand effects from the effects of
         variation in market structure.
(25)    Because Lufthansa combines several distinct operators, and each operator may have
        a different pricing policy, booking curve and/or marketing strategy, […]. Different
         operators active on the same route are thus assigned different fixed effects.





24     As mentioned above, the panel data structure means that several routes are observed over time. Panel
         data allows the implementation of the fixed effects methodology. To the contrary, with a cross-sectional
         data, where there is no time dimension, and the routes are observed only for one period, the fixed
         effects methodology is not feasible. Hence, in a cross-sectional data analysis  it is more difficult to
       remedy or avoid the omitted variable bias.
25     An indicator variable, also referred to as a dummy or a binary variable, is a variable that takes the value
       1 when true and 0 otherwise.
26       In this case, for example, the indicator variable for the route city pair BRU-MIL takes the value 1 only
         for those observations that refer to this route and the value 0 for all other observations. Routes are
        defined as origin and destination city pairs, for example, BRU-MIL and MIL-BRU constitute a unique
         fixed effect.


                                     10

[PÁGINA PDF 534]
(26)    The analysis also takes account of changes over time which are common to all routes
       by including time indicator variables, or time fixed effects,27 for each month-year of
         the sample period. The time indicator variables capture persistent differences over
         time, for example seasonality in demand and potentially prices.28 These variables can
         also capture general trends over time that can influence prices such as general cost
         trends for the industry or general evolution of income of customers or demand for
         leisure vacation.
(27)     Overall, the fixed effects methodology is generally regarded as the most suitable to
         assess the competitive constraint exerted by any operator and/or ITA on Lufthansa.29
2.2.3.2. Other control variables
(28)    Route and time fixed effects capture a large part of the effects that demand factors
      may have on prices.30 However, as airlines are generally interested in ensuring their
        planes are full, they may seek to adapt prices to fluctuations in demand. To control
         for this feature, the load factor31 is included as a proxy for demand.
(29)    The number of connecting passengers on a route may affect the ticket prices for the
         point-to-point passengers because tickets for connecting passengers could potentially
         influence the booking curve position of point-to-point tickets. Hence, the empirical
         specification also includes the share of connecting passengers to control for these
         potential booking curve effects.
(30)     Similarly to the demand factors, time and route fixed effects control for a large part
        of the effects that supply factors may have on prices (for example, labour or
        equipment costs, and airport fees). Supply factors in the airline industry are mainly
        labour costs, maintenance and investment costs for equipment, operational costs,
         especially fuel costs and route specific costs such as airport taxes and fees. Because
         carriers could also incur costs that may vary over time and affect routes differently,
         the average cost per available seat kilometres (CASK) is included as an additional
         control for supply factors.
(31)    The estimation  results have also been  tested by including or excluding these
         additional control variables in some specifications.

           is estimated on.

         short-haul routes. The regression analysis includes data on all Lufthansa carriers

         also reported, the sample excluding the COVID period is the baseline data set for the
         regression analysis.34

        information on the number of competitors active on a route. For long-haul, some
         inconsistencies arose from this merging of datasets that suggests the IATA DSS data
           is  incomplete. A comparison  of  the  month/city-pair  level  data on Lufthansa
        passengers and seats available from IATA DSS against the equivalent information
       from Lufthansa  fare data suggests these inconsistencies are not problematic.35
        Nevertheless, a sensitivity for the long-haul regressions is considered where the
       sample for the analysis is restricted to include only city pairs where the merge
       between the Lufthansa fare data and IATA DSS data was perfect. That is, almost half
        of the city pairs have at least one month where data on Lufthansa’s prices is available
        but no information on competitors is available from IATA DSS. If this happens, the
         entire city pair is excluded, even if the merge was perfect in all other months.

3.1.     Relationship between Lufthansa’s prices and the number of competitors
(40)    The regression analysis investigates the relationship between the general competitive
        landscape in terms of number of competitors on a route in a given month and
        Lufthansa’s  prices. This analysis  tells us whether on average the presence of
         additional competitors is associated with lower ticket prices charged by Lufthansa,
        while controlling for other influencing factors.
3.1.1.   Description of the regressions analysis
(41)    Table 4 shows the regression analysis based on the number of competitors. Each
       column is an alternative specification to investigate the effect of competitive pressure
       on Lufthansa’s average prices. Specifications (1) and (2) measure the average effect
        of an additional competitor regardless of the number of competitors already on the
         route (other than Lufthansa and  its subsidiaries), while specifications (3) to (6)
       measure competitive pressure via indicator variables corresponding to the number of
         operators active on the routes. These latter specifications allow the effect of an
         additional competitor to vary depending on whether the competitor  is the  first,
        second or third on the route.
(42)    All specifications include route and operator fixed effects and time effects and
         controlling for additional factors affecting prices. Specifications (1) and (3) do not
        include any control variables, and thus allow to understand how the choice of control
         variables for demand and supply factors may affect the results. Specifications (1) to
         (4) are estimated on the full sample of data, excluding the COVID period, while
         specifications (5) and (6) are estimated respectively on the sample of only IATA
       summer and winter seasons. Specification (4) is the baseline specification of our

(43)    In  all these specifications, the estimated coefficients capturing competition are
          statistically  highly  significant,  and  sizeable  in  magnitude. The  fact  that  in
         specifications (1) to (6) the estimated coefficients consistently increase with the
       number of competitors implies that more competition results in lower prices.
(44)   More in detail, the results of specifications (1) and (2) in Table 4 imply that, on
        average,  a  competitor’s  entry  on  a  route  decreases  Lufthansa’s  prices  by
        approximately [0-5]%. These specifications assume a linear relationship between
         price effect and the number of competitors, and thus suggest that Lufthansa’s prices
         relative to a monopoly are about [0-5]% lower on a duopoly route, about [10-20]%
        lower on a route with two competitors, and about [10-20]% with 3 competitors.
(45)    The results of specifications (3) and (4) can instead be interpreted as follows:
       Compared to a situation where Lufthansa is a monopolist on the route, Lufthansa’s
         prices are on average:
          (a)   [5-10]% lower if there is one additional competitor.


                                     14

[PÁGINA PDF 538]
         (b)   approximately [10-20]% lower if there are two or more additional competitors.
             This also implies that the entry of an additional competitor on route where
              already two carriers are active would reduce prices by about [0-5]-[0-5]%.
(46)     Specifications (5) and (6) imply how these effects vary should we look at the IATA
       summer and winter seasons separately. These specifications suggest that the findings
        of the model are stronger for summer than for winter:
          (a)   In summer, Lufthansa’s average prices are approximately [10-20]% lower if
               there is one additional competitor and approximately [10-20]% lower if there
              are two or more additional competitors. Entry of an additional competitor on
              route where already two carriers are active would reduce prices by about
             [5-10]%, and this effect is statistically different from zero.
         (b)   In summer, Lufthansa’s average prices are approximately [5-10]% lower  if
               there is one additional competitor and approximately [5-10]% lower if there are
            two or more additional competitors, but this latter effect is not statistically
               different from zero.
(47)      It is worth to keep in mind, however, that as these two subsamples include fewer
        observations than the overall sample. For instance, the number of observations of the
      IATA summer seasons sample is about 62% of the number of observations of the
         overall sample, while that of the IATA winter seasons is about 38% that of the
         overall sample when is reduced only, or to only the IATA winter seasons or to only
         the period after November 2021.
(48)    Table 5 shows two types of robustness checks: (i) including the COVID period into
         the estimation sample; and  (ii) weighting the regressions by the number of P2P
        passengers, that is, assigning larger importance to larger routes. Table 5 confirms that
         the findings of the regression analysis are robust not only to alternative model
         specifications, but also to alternative estimation samples and alternative modelling
         techniques.

3.1.2.   Conclusion on the impact on prices

         effects of competition are particularly important in already concentrated markets.
        Table 6 provides a summary of how the regression results can be interpreted for
        understanding the expected impact of the Transaction.
          (a)  A reduction in the number of competitors active on a route from two to one,
             such as that of a merger to monopoly, on average increases prices by [5-10]%.
           The robustness analysis carried out suggests this effect can range between
            [5-10]% to [10-20]%.
         (b)  A reduction in the number of competitors active on a route from three to two,
             such as  that of a merger  to a duopoly, on average increases  prices by

               large as [5-10]%.

3.2.    Closeness of competition between Lufthansa and ITA
(50)    The regression analysis further allows to investigate whether ITA’s presence on a
         route in a given month affects Lufthansa’s average prices, controlling for the other
         influencing  factors. This  section discusses two  different  alternative models  to
         investigate this relationship:
          (a)    First, whether ITA’s presence on a route affects Lufthansa’s average prices.
             This model also allows to assess whether Lufthansa’s average prices differs
             according to how many other competitors are active on the route (that  is,
             excluding Lufthansa and ITA). If ITA were a close competitor to Lufthansa,
              the results would show that Lufthansa’s average prices would react in response
               to the entry/exit of ITA on the route.
         (b)   Second, whether the impact of ITA’s presence on a route on Lufthansa’s
             average prices varies according to how many competitors are active on the
               route. This model is a refinement of the above as  it allows to investigate
             whether the impact of ITA’s presence on Lufthansa’s average prices is the
           same when only Lufthansa and ITA are active on a route or whether one or
           more other competitors are also active. Whereas the previous model relies on
              the overall variation in competitive interactions across routes,  this model
              focuses specifically on the variation in prices that are directly correlated with
              the variation of ITA’s presence on a particular route.
(51)    In line with the analysis presented above, competitive pressure due to competitors is
       measured through indicator variables for the presence of one, or two or more


36       This needs to be taken with caution. a statistical test of the difference of two coefficients, as performed
         in this regression model, and its test value is a function of the coefficients and the standard error of the
          coefficient. Especially the standard error depends on the number of observations used for the estimation
         of the coefficient. If only a limited number of observations identify the specific effect of e.g. increasing
         the number of competitors from 2 to 3, which  still reveals the correct coefficient  if the model is
         correctly specified, the standard errors increases. A high standard  error, which may  result in a
         potentially erroneous rejection of the statistical test, only indicates that the estimation is not very precise
        but not necessarily wrong. The Commission acknowledges  the  rejection of  the  significance  in
         differences between some of the coefficients but the consistent general pattern, greater negative effects
        with higher number of competitors,  still suggests that any additional competitor  is likely to be
         associated with lower ticket prices charged by Lufthansa.


                                     17

[PÁGINA PDF 541]
        competitors other than the Parties. ITA’s presence is represented by an indicator
         variable equal to one if either ITA or Alitalia is present on the route in a given
        month, and zero otherwise. As ITA’s presence is excluded from the number of other
         competitors,  the  indicator  variable  describing ITA’s presence can be  directly
         interpreted as to whether ITA’s presence can be associated with a change in
        Lufthansa’s prices.

         (b)  The presence of additional competitors other than Lufthansa and ITA on a
              route  is associated with lower Lufthansa’s average prices in the order of
             approximately [10-20]% compared to monopoly routes.
(54)    The findings of the regression analysis appear robust to alternative estimation
        samples and to applying weights where larger routes (in terms of P2P passengers) are
        assigned greater weight than smaller routes. It is worth to keep in mind that the

         the estimation sample becomes smaller. Nevertheless, the impact of ITA’s presence
       on Lufthansa’s price is consistently negative and highly statistically significant. That
            is, ITA’s presence is statistically associated with lower prices charged by Lufthansa,
        independently from the sample considered or the modelling approach chosen.

3.2.3.   Conclusion on closeness of competition
(59)    This set of models investigating the relationship between Lufthansa’s prices and
       ITA’s presence on a route can also be used for understanding the expected impact of
         the Transaction.
          (a)  The presence of ITA/Alitalia on a route is associated with on average [10-20]%
             lower Lufthansa’s prices, if no distinction is made on how many competitors
              are active on the route. The robustness analysis carried out suggests that this
                effect can range between [10-20]% and [10-20]%. Whereas accounting for the
            number of competitors active on the route indicates that the presence of
              ITA/Alitalia on a route is associated with on average approximately [10-20]%
             lower Lufthansa’s prices if no other competitor is present, approximately [20-
           30]%  lower  Lufthansa’s  prices   if  another  competitor  is  present,  and
             approximately [10-20]% lower  Lufthansa’s  prices  if two  or more  other
              competitors are present.
         (b)  A reduction in the number of competitors active on a route from two to one,
             such as that of a merger to monopoly where the competitor disappearing is
            ITA, on average increases prices by [10-20]%. The robustness analysis carried
              out suggests this effect can be as large as [10-20]%.
          (c)  A reduction in the number of competitors active on a route from three to two,
             such as that of a merger to a duopoly where the competitor disappearing is
            ITA, on average increases prices by [10-20]%. The robustness analysis carried
              out suggests this effect can be as large as [10-20]%. Compared to a scenario
             with the presence of additional competitors other than the Parties, the presence
              of ITA on a route is systematically associated with lower Lufthansa’s average
                prices.
         (d)   This  effect  is  statistically significant and stable over  different  alternative
               specifications. As discussed above, however,  that, should the analysis be
               carried out exclusively on winter seasons, the effect appears weaker as the
               variation in the data may not allow to estimate both the effect associated to the
             change in the number of competitors and that associated to ITA’s entry.
