3.4.    Conclusion on the short-haul regressions
(66)    The Commission relied on a fixed effects regression to assess the relationship
       between the competitive landscape and Lufthansa’s prices, and the results clearly
         indicate that increased competition on a route  is associated with lower average
         prices.

37       This needs to be taken with caution. a statistical test of the difference of two coefficients, as performed
         in this regression model, and its test value is a function of the coefficients and the standard error of the
          coefficient. Especially the standard error depends on the number of observations used for the estimation
         of the coefficient. If only a limited number of observations identify the specific effect of e.g. increasing
         the number of competitors from 2 to 3, which  still reveals the correct coefficient  if the model is
         correctly specified, the standard errors increases. A high standard  error, which may  result in a
         potentially erroneous rejection of the statistical test, only indicates that the estimation is not very precise
        but not necessarily wrong. The Commission acknowledges  the  rejection of  the  significance  in
         differences between some of the coefficients but the consistent general pattern, greater negative effects
        with higher number of competitors,  still suggests that any additional competitor  is likely to be
         associated with lower ticket prices charged by Lufthansa.


                                     27

[PÁGINA PDF 551]
(67)   More specifically, the results of the regression analysis indicate that:
          (a)   Routes with a higher number  of competitors have  prices approximately
            [10-20]% lower than routes where Lufthansa is a monopolist.
         (b)   Specifically, the first competitor reduces prices by [5-10]-[5-10]%, while each
             subsequent additional competitor reduces prices by an additional [0-5]-[5-10]
              percentage points.
(68)    The Commission’s fixed effects regression also allows to assess the relationship
       between ITA’s presence and Lufthansa’s prices, and the results of the regression
         analysis indicate that the presence of Alitalia/ITA is associated with on average
       [10-20]% lower Lufthansa’s prices.
(69)     Lastly, the regression analysis also allows to estimate the predicted impact of the
        Transaction:
          (a)   Average prices are estimated to be about [5-10]-[5-10]% higher on 2-to-1
               routes, and specifically [10-20]% higher where the competitor disappearing is
            ITA, and
         (b)  Average prices are estimated to be about [5-10]-[5-10]% higher on 3-to-2
               routes, and specifically [10-20]% higher where the competitor disappearing is
            ITA.
3.5.    Assessment of the Parties’ price analysis on closeness of competition
(70)     In their Response to the 6(1)c Decision, the Parties submitted a descriptive analysis
        based on three sets of two charts showing the relationship between price and number
        of  competitors  (Figures  3-4),  the  relationship  between  price  and  distance
        (Figures 5-6), and the relationship between price and ITA/Ryanair’s share of seats
        (Figures 7-8). In each set the Parties highlight first routes where Ryanair is active and
        then routes where ITA is active.
(71)    The Parties claim38 that this analysis shows that:
          (a)   Ryanair exerts significant competitive pressure on Lufthansa and Lufthansa’s
             average revenues per P2P passengers on routes where Ryanair is present; and
                that
          (b)  ITA does not exert the same competitive pressure on routes where ITA
             competes with Lufthansa.
(72)    Later in the proceedings, the Parties also presented a supplementary cross-sectional39
         regression analysis where they used statistical techniques to assess whether these
         price differences reported in their Response to the 6(1)c Decision were statistically
         different from zero.40
          (a)    First, studying  the  relationship between  price and competition  in  airline
             markets through  descriptive analyses  like  scatterplots41 or  cross-sectional
              regression analyses alone fundamentally ignore business and market dynamics.

38      The Parties’ Response to the 6.1.c Decision, paragraph 46 to 57.
39       Cross-sectional analysis refers to a data analysis based on observations from a set of routes in only one
        (and the same) time period.
40      Supplementary regression analysis named “ppt - Closeness of competition - 060324 - Final” submitted
       on 7 March 2024. The underlying files necessary to run the analysis were submitted on 8 March 2024.
41       Scatterplots refer to the type of charts used by the parties, where each city-pair route’s price  is
         represented by a dot in a two-dimensional plane.


                                     28

[PÁGINA PDF 552]
              In particular, the analyses submitted by the Parties ignore differences across
                city-pairs, and implicitly assume that all city-pairs are the same. Against this
             background, significant heterogeneity across different city-pair routes exists in
                 reality,  including  variations  in demand,  airport  infrastructure,  regulatory
             environments, and competitive conditions.
         (b)   Second, drawing a link between prices across routes and competitors’ presence
            on that route ignoring differences across city-pair routes  is equivalent to
            assuming that carriers decide to enter a certain city-pair for reasons unrelated to
           demand and supply factors specific to the city pair itself. In essence, comparing
               prices across city-pair routes without accounting for the variations in demand
            and supply factors among the different city pairs is equivalent to suggesting
                that Ryanair, ITA, and other competitors make decisions to enter specific
              routes  entirely  at  random,  disregarding  any  economic  considerations
             underpinning their strategic choices.
          (c)   Third, such descriptive analyses are inconsistent with established best practices
               in economics and econometrics. Scatterplots and cross-sectional analyses that
                 treat  all markets homogeneously oversimplify the pricing and competition
             dynamics. As described  in Section  2, panel  data,  that  is, several routes
             observed over time, as opposed to a single cross-section of routes in one time
               period, is more suitable to identify competition effects. This is because in a
              panel data context the entry and exit events of various carriers provide valuable
              information on the impact of competition. This information is ignored by the
               cross-sectional analysis. Moreover, as explained above, fixed-effect methods in
             a panel data context provide a tool to account for heterogeneity across routes
                that is not possible with cross-sectional data. In particular, standard fixed-effect
             econometric models, by  controlling  for  city-pair  fixed  effects and  other
             unobserved factors, explicitly account for heterogeneity across markets, and
              help isolate the impact of changes in the number of competitors on prices while
              holding constant other influences specific to each route.
         (d)   Fourth, descriptive analyses or cross-sectional regression analyses that examine
              snapshots of data at a single point in time may overlook temporal trends and
                  fail to capture the dynamic nature of competition and pricing behaviour. This is
               true even if a month like April 2023 or October 2022 is chosen:42 Prices and
              the number of competitors on city pairs fluctuate over time due to various
            exogenous shocks, seasonal  patterns, and market dynamics. Ignoring  this
              source of variation may lead to statistically biased and inconsistent results. On
              the other hand, as explained above, standard panel data analysis combined with
               fixed-effect methods provide a reliable framework to account for temporal
            dynamics and trends.
          (e)   Fifth, in any event, and notwithstanding the severe limitations of the analysis,
              the results of the Parties’ cross-sectional regression analysis indicate that in
              addition  to  Ryanair  other  competitors  also  exercise  a  significant  price
               constraint on  Lufthansa. The  Parties’  cross-sectional  regression  analysis
               predicts that Lufthansa’s prices on its routes on average are [10-20]% lower if
                     it faces competition from an airline career other than Ryanair, including ITA,
            and [30-40]% lower if it faces competition from Ryanair. Even taken at face
               value,  it  is questionable how these  results of the  Parties’ cross-sectional

42      Response to the 6(1)(c) decision, footnote 53.


                                     29

[PÁGINA PDF 553]
              regression  analysis  would  help  alleviating  the  preliminary  competition
             concerns stemming from the Transaction that the Commission identified (and
               detailed  in the Statement of Objections);  if anything, the  Parties’ cross-
               sectional regression analysis supports the Commission’s preliminary finding
                that the Transaction would  significantly impede  effective competition on
               several routes, even when the presence of Ryanair is taken into account.
(73)    Table 16 below shows how the Commission would assess the relationship between
        Lufthansa’s average prices and the presence of Ryanair on a route. This table
          illustrates the limitations of non-standard analysis.
          (a)   Specification (1) presents a regression analysis that mirrors closely the Parties’
                scatterplots and  cross-sectional  regression  analysis:43 Lufthansa’s average
               prices are regressed against only two variables, namely, indicator variables
               signalling whether Ryanair and/or ITA are active in a city pair. Only data for
              April 2023 is included. That is, the data is a single cross-section of routes. This
            model ignores all differences in supply and demand factors across city pairs
            and over time. That  is, apart from the indicator variables no other control
               variables are used in the regression.
         (b)   Specification  (2)  includes  all  the  other months where  data  is  available
              (excluding the COVID period) and, more importantly, includes city-pair and
            month indicator variables (fixed-effects). This specification is a fixed effect
              regression as discussed in Section 2.2 above.
          (c)   Specification (3) and (4) are further refinements of (2) where respectively are
               also included: (i) indicator variables for all other competitors active on the city
               pair as well as both these indicator variables and covariates to account for
           demand and supply factors that vary over time within a city pair.
(74)   Two main findings can be evinced from Table 16:
          (a)  The Parties’ statement that Lufthansa’s average prices are lower on routes
            where Ryanair is active almost entirely stems from a biased and erroneous
             modelling  where  differences among  city  pairs  are  not  accounted  for.
               Specification (1) in Table 16 shows that Lufthansa’s prices are on average
             approximately [30-40]% lower on  routes where Ryanair  is  active while
              Lufthansa’s prices are on average not statistically different in city pairs where
           ITA is active. However, as illustrated by the subsequent specifications in the
                table,  these  findings  are  due  to  comparing  different  city  pairs  while
              disregarding any difference in demand and supply factors.
         (b)  Once differences across city pairs are accounted for via the fixed effects
             methodology, in Specifications  (2), (3) and  (4), the picture drawn above
             changes dramatically: Ryanair’s presence on a route is associated with lower
              Lufthansa’s average prices in the order of approximately [10-20]-[10-20]%,
             whereas ITA’s presence is associated with even lower Lufthansa’s average
                prices, in the order of approximately [10-20]-[10-20]%.

         in order to provide a  full comparison between the Parties’ methodology and the Commission’s
        methodology.

(75)    The impact of ITA’s presence  is consistently negative and highly  statistically

         prices charged by Lufthansa.44 The impact of Ryanair’s presence is also consistently

        Ryanair competes more closely with Lufthansa than ITA as argued by the Parties in
          their Response to the 6(1)c Decision. If anything, possibly the opposite is true.
(76)    In their response to the SO, the Notifying Parties further followed up on this
       argument by relying on the Commission’s methodology as per Section 3.2.2 to
         investigate the impact of Ryanair’s entry on Lufthansa’s prices.45 The Commission
        acknowledges  that  this approach  is  a  significantly  better way  to  assess  the
         relationship between Lufthansa’s prices and Ryanair’s entry than what the Notifying
         Parties  has  previously  considered. However,  the Commission  also  notes  the
         following.
          (a)   Such analysis is ultimately of little relevance for the Transaction for the very
             simple fact that the Transaction can entail a loss of competition between
             Lufthansa and ITA, which would be operated jointly post-merger, and not
            between Lufthansa and Ryanair, which will continue to compete. Should
             Lufthansa consider a merger with Ryanair, then indeed the Notifying Parties’
               analysis represented an appropriate way to investigate its impact.
         (b)  The Parties’ conclusions that “Ryanair has a stronger impact on Lufthansa’s
              prices than a generic first competitor” and that “If Ryanair is present, the next
              competitor has almost no further effect on Lufthansa’s prices” disregards that
              these results are not particularly relevant to the affected routes. In fact, as
              flagged during the Oral Hearing, ITA is rarely present on the routes underlying
              the Parties’ analysis, and even a competitor like TUI is more frequently present
              than ITA. In contrast, the Commission’s approach focuses directly on ITA’s
             impact on the routes of concern, and finds that ITA competitively constrains
           LH, and irrespectively from the presence of Ryanair.

4.     REGRESSION ANALYSIS – LONG HAUL
(77)    This Section describes the results of the regression analysis for non-stop long-haul
         routes, as well as long-haul routes taking into account indirect competitors.
4.1.     Description of the regressions analysis for non-stop routes
(78)    The regression analysis described in this section mirrors the one carried out for short-
        haul routes in Section 3.1. That is, the analysis investigates the relationship between
         the general competitive landscape in terms of number of competitors on a route in a
        given month and Lufthansa’s prices. This analysis indicates whether on average
         additional competitors are associated with lower ticket prices charged by Lufthansa,
        while controlling for other influencing factors.
(79)    The question of closeness of competition between Lufthansa and ITA on long-haul
         routes cannot be answered via the same approach as adopted in Section 3.2 for short-
        haul routes. This is because data on Lufthansa’s JV partners has not been made
         available to the Commission, and non-stop overlaps between the Parties arise only
       between ITA and Lufthansa’s JV partner, United. Therefore, regression analysis for
        non-stop long-haul routes can only investigate whether Lufthansa’s prices react to
        changes in the number of competitors active on these routes.
(80)   As above, each column is an alternative specification to investigate the effect of
        competitive pressure on Lufthansa’s average  prices. Specifications  (1) and  (2)
       measure the average effect of an additional competitor regardless of the number of

45 See Response to the SO, Annex I, section 5.2.


                                     32

[PÁGINA PDF 556]
        competitors already on the route (other than Lufthansa,  its subsidiaries, or JV
         partners), while specifications (3) to (6) measure competitive pressure via indicator
         variables corresponding to the number of operators active on the routes. These latter
         specifications allow the effect of an additional competitor to vary depending on
        whether the competitor is the first or the second on the route.
(81)    All  specifications  include  route and  operator  fixed  effects and  time  effects.
         Specifications (1) and (3) do not include any additional control variables, and thus
        allow to understand how the choice of control variables for demand and supply
         factors may affect the results. Specifications (1) to (4) are estimated on the full
       sample of data, excluding the COVID period, while specifications (5) and (6) are
        estimated respectively on the sample of only IATA summer seasons and IATA
        winter seasons.
(82)    The regression analysis is exclusively estimated on non-stop routes between North
       America and Europe, where Europe includes Lufthansa’s hubs and a few other
         airports from which Lufthansa has flown non-stop connections between 2019 and
       2023 like Geneva and Düsseldorf. All other routes to Asia, South America, Africa,
       and Israel are excluded. This is for the following reasons:
          (a)   Focusing just on routes between North America and Europe allows to consider
             a relatively large sample of data, corresponding to about 80% of all passengers,
             while at the same time to rely on a relatively homogenous set of routes.
             Pooling all routes worldwide may risk not to account adequately for opposing
               seasonality patterns. For example, the effects of seasonality on flights from
             North America to Europe can differ from flights from Europe to Asia.
         (b)  The non-stop long-haul routes where overlaps exist between ITA and United
              are also routes between North America and Europe, and therefore these results
              are also economically relevant for the assessment of the Transaction. This
            economic relevance is valid even if ITA is not directly present on any of the
             sample routes nor are the overlapping city pairs part of the estimation sample.
(83)    Table 17 shows the baseline regression analysis while Table 18 shows a series of
        robustness  checks. As  above, each column  is an  alternative  specification  to
         investigate  the  effect  of  competitive  pressure on  Lufthansa’s  average  prices.
         Specifications (1) and (2) measure the average effect of an additional competitor
         regardless of the number of competitors already on the route (other than Lufthansa,
           its subsidiaries, or JV partners), while specifications (3) to (6) measure competitive
        pressure via indicator variables corresponding to the number of operators active on
         the routes. These latter specifications allow the effect of an additional competitor to
        vary depending on whether the competitor is the first or the second on the route.
(84)    All  specifications  include  route and  operator  fixed  effects and  time  effects.
         Specifications (1) and (3) do not include any additional control variables, and thus
        allow to understand how the choice of control variables for demand and supply
         factors may affect the results. Specifications (1) to (4) are estimated on the full
       sample of data, excluding the COVID period, while specifications (5) and (6) are
        estimated respectively on the sample of only IATA summer seasons and IATA
        winter seasons.
(85)    The regression analysis is exclusively estimated on non-stop routes between North
       America and Europe, where Europe includes Lufthansa’s hubs and a few other
         airports from which Lufthansa has flown non-stop connections between 2019 and

(86)     Specification (4) is the baseline specification of the analysis, all other specifications
         are sensitivities and robustness checks. In  all these specifications, however, the
        estimated coefficients capturing competition are statistically significant, and sizeable
         in magnitude. The results imply that more competition results in lower prices.
(87)    In detail, the results of specifications (1) and (2) in Table 17 imply that, on average, a
        competitor’s  entry on a  route  decreases  Lufthansa’s  prices by approximately
        [5-10]%. These specifications assume a linear relationship between price effect and
         the number of competitors, and thus suggest that Lufthansa’s prices relative to a
       monopoly are about [5-10]% lower on a duopoly route and about [10-20]% lower on
        a route with two competitors.
(88)    The results of specifications (3) and (4) can instead be interpreted as follows:
       Compared to a situation where Lufthansa is a monopolist on the route,
          (a)   Lufthansa’s prices are on average [5-10]% lower  if there is one additional
              competitor, and
         (b)   Lufthansa’s prices are on average [20-30]% lower if there are two or more
               additional  competitors, and  in  particular  this means  that one  additional
              competitor beyond the  first competitor drive average prices down by an
               additional [10-20] percentage points.
(89)     Specifications (5) and (6) show how these effects vary should across the IATA
       summer and winter seasons separately. These specifications suggest that the findings
        of the model are stronger for summer than for winter:
          (a)   In summer, Lufthansa’s average prices are approximately 8% lower if there is
            one additional competitor and approximately 16% lower if there are two or
           more additional competitors. This effect is statistically different from zero.
         (b)   In winter, the effect of an additional competitor is not statistically different
            from zero and  it  is not possible to estimate the  effect of two or more
              competitors on prices as there are not enough entry or exit events to analyse.
(90)      It is worth to keep in mind, however, that as these two subsamples include fewer
        observations than the overall sample, the precision of these estimates is lower. For
         instance, the number of observations of the IATA summer seasons sample is about
      64% of the number of observations of the overall sample, and consequently that of
         the IATA winter seasons is about 37% of the overall sample.
(91)    Table 18 shows three types of robustness checks: (i) an estimation sample including
         also the COVID period (specification 1); (ii) an estimation sample including only
        data where the matching between Lufthansa fare data and IATA data was perfect
         overall the whole period (specification 2);46 and (iii) weighted regressions giving
         larger  routes  (in  terms  of  passengers)  a  greater  weight  than  smaller  routes
         (specifications 3 to 5). Table 18 confirms that the findings of the regression analysis
         are robust not only to alternative model  specifications, but also to alternative
        estimation samples and alternative modelling techniques.

4.2.    Additional  evidence  to  account  for  the  constraint  exerted  by  indirect
        competitors.
(92)    According to Paragraphs 79 to 82 of the Notifying Parties’ response to the SO, the
       Commission’s regression analysis on long haul routes is inconsistent with its market
         definition as ‘the Commission implicitly assumes [in its regression analysis] that
        competition in the market is only driven by direct flights and that indirect flights do
        not exert any competitive pressure on Lufthansa.’
(93)   As already indicated in paragraph 75 of the Annex I to the SO, the Commission notes
         that the regression analysis on long haul routes focuses exclusively on direct flights
        because the Notifying Parties themselves did not make available any data on
        Lufthansa’s JV partners. The Commission underlines, however, that the analysis is
        indeed relevant to assess the impact from increased competition derived from
         indirect  flights  on  Lufthansa’s  prices  on  non-stop  flights. As  discussed  in


                                     36

[PÁGINA PDF 560]
        Sections 6.6 and 10.1.5 of the SO, indirect flights are perceived as better alternatives
         to direct connections the more limited the direct connections are, therefore the effect
       on Lufthansa’s prices on non-stop flights associated to a greater number of indirect
        competitors also depends on the number of non-stop competitors already present on
         the route. If indirect competitors were already constraining Lufthansa’s prices on
        non-stop flights, then the regression analysis would have not identified any effect on
        Lufthansa’s prices from non-stop carriers. With respect to the second element of the
        Notifying Parties’ critique, the Commission updated its own regressions analysis on
        long haul routes to account for the constraint exerted by indirect competitors. This
        update is discussed in the following paragraphs, and the results of the Commission’s
         regression analysis are included in Annex II to this letter.
(94)    The Commission followed the same methodology adopted in the SO and included in
         the following regression analysis both a measure of how many non-stop carriers are
         active on the city-pair routes and a measure of how many indirect carriers are active
       on those routes. Table 19 shows the baseline regression analysis while Table 20
       shows a series of robustness checks. The specifications are identical to the ones
         detailed above regarding non-stop routes.
(95)    With respect to the effect on Lufthansa’s prices associated to the number of non-stop
         competitors, the results of this updated regression analysis confirm those included in
         the SO. In particular:
          (a)   Lufthansa’s prices are on average [5-10]% lower  if there is one additional
              competitor, and
         (b)   Lufthansa’s prices are on average [20-30]% lower if there are two or more
               additional competitors. This means that one additional competitor beyond the
                  first competitor drive average prices down by an additional [10-20] percentage
               points.
(96)    With respect to the effect on Lufthansa’s prices associated to the number of indirect
        competitors:
          (a)  One additional indirect competitor decreases prices by about [0-5]%. (47)
         (b)  Two or more additional indirect competitors decreases prices by about [5-10]%
            compared to monopoly, which means an additional indirect competitor beyond
              the first one is associated with Lufthansa’s prices being about approximately
              [5-10] percentage points lower.





(47)     This effect is not statistically significant at 10% once the COVID period is included in the analysis.

5.     ASSESSMENT OF THE PARTIES’ STATEMENTS
(99)    This section describes the Notifying  Parties’ remarks about the Commission’s
         analysis and details the Commission’s rebuttals.
5.1.    Non-randomness of the residuals
5.1.1.   The Notifying Parties’ view
(100)   The Notifying Parties argue in Section 3.2 of their response to the SO, as well as in
          their response to the Letter of Facts, that the common trends assumption is not met,
            i.e. that there are “specific factors that drive changes in prices on the specific routes”
         that are not accounted for by the control variables used by the Commission or the
        applied fixed effects.
(101)   Moreover, the Notifying Parties, in paragraph 44 of their response to the SO state
         that ‘one would expect to see no particular pattern in the residuals (48) estimated for
         individual routes’ and  that ‘we should observe residuals trending “randomly”
       around zero’, while ‘we do observe systematic route-specific patterns of residuals. In
       some cases the residuals increase over time, in others they decrease. Moreover, they
         often exhibit different trends pre- and post-COVID. This means that some route
         specific factors that drive changes in prices on the specific routes have not been
        explained by the econometric models used by the Commission  - neither by the
        applied fixed effects, nor by the remaining control variables.’ In their response to the
         Letter of Facts, the Parties argue that the significance test showcases the presence of
         linear patterns in the residuals for more than 66% of all routes, underlining the



(48)     Residuals are differences between the observed values of prices and the values predicted by the model.


                                     40

[PÁGINA PDF 564]
         existence of statistically significant linear trends. For the Parties, the results are thus
        mostly driven by route-specific trends uncontrolled for in the Commission’s analysis.
5.1.2.   The Commission’s view
(102)   Regarding the Parties’ claim that the Commission’s model suffers from omitted
         variable bias, the Commission underlines that its chosen model, the fixed effects
        model, is generally widely regarded as a more suitable approach to address omitted
         variable bias concerns than the cross-section analysis supported by the Parties.
        Indeed, the cross-section analysis would completely ignore any difference in price
         trends across routes. As discussed in great detail in Section 2.2 of this Annex,
        including city pair 'fixed effects’ and month indicators allow to control for a wide
        range of demand and supply factors so to minimize the impact of potential omitted
         variable bias concerns.
(103)   Regarding  the  residual  analysis,  the Commission notes  that  the  route-specific
         patterns visually observed on Figure 3 and Figure 4 of their response to the SO are
        not actually statistically different from zero, and that even some residuals appear to
         increase over time and  others  decrease, most  of  these  route-specific  patterns
        observed by the Notifying Parties’ are not statistically different from zero. The
        majority of all residual trends, if counted as a whole or based on city pairs as per the
         Parties’ methodology in their response to the LoF, is not statistically significant.
5.2.    Relevant control variables
5.2.1.   The Notifying Parties’ view
(104)   The Notifying Parties raised a concern over the adequacy of the control variables
        chosen in the Commission’s regression analysis, notably due to (i) their lack of
         significance and (ii) their inability to effectively proxy demand. This, in the Parties’
        view, biases the economic analysis conducted by the Commission.
(105)   In paragraph 44 of their Response to the SO as well as in Section 3.2.2, the Notifying
         Parties argue that ‘the relevant control variables, such as route-specific cost or
       demand measures, chosen by the Commission are not statistically significant in the
       Commission’s short-haul analysis’. This, in their view, goes against economic theory
        as demand has no systematic impact on prices.
(106)   The Notifying Parties agreed in their response to the Letter of Facts that not all
         control variables must be significant in order for an econometric model to be valid.
       However, they argue that, considering that the common trend assumption is not met,
             it is worrying that the additional control variables are not significant, as for them it
       means they are unable to explain differences in the evolution of prices across routes.
(107)   The Notifying Parties also argue in section 3.2.2 of their response to the SO that the
         control variables do not add any explanatory power, as the    of the Commission’s
       model does not change when including them. They state this in paragraph 47 of the        response to the SO: ‘the chosen control variables do not help𝑅𝑅2to improve the validity
         of the regression models estimated by the Commission’.
(108)   The Notifying Parties, in paragraph 6 as well as in paragraph 50 of their Response to
         the SO, question  the economic  validity of  the  control  variables used by  the
       Commission, notably the load factor. They argue that using the load factor to proxy
       demand brings issues of endogeneity, as this measure is driven not only by demand
        but also by the prices that Lufthansa charges, thus creating biased results.



                                     41

[PÁGINA PDF 565]
5.2.2.   The Commission’s view
(109)   The Commission disagrees with the Parties’ statements and makes the following
         observations.
(110)    First, control variables can capture significant information regarding the price trends
        across routes even if they are statistically insignificant. It is not necessary for all the
         additional control variables to be statistically significant for the model to be valid.
       These control variables are economically relevant, thus whether they are statistically
         significant or not in this type of modelling is not relevant to understand whether the
       model itself is valid. Furthermore, the Notifying Parties appear to ignore that some
       demand variables are in fact statistically significant, as for example the share of
        connecting passenger in the short haul regressions and the CASK variables in the
        long haul regressions.
(111)   Second, as explained in detail in this Annex as well as in Annex I to the SO, the
       Commission’s regression analysis also includes city-pair fixed effects and month
         indicators, which are also controls for demand and supply factors, and are also
          statistically significant. City-pair fixed effects allow to control for demand and
        supply factors that are specific to a city-pair and that do not vary over time (for
        example, certain city-pairs are more attractive than others), while month indicators
        allow to control for demand and supply factors that are specific to a month and
      common to all city-pairs (for example, a sudden increase in fuel costs). Including
         these additional control variables allows to control for the effect of demand and
        supply factors that are specific to a city-pair and that vary over time. This holds even
            if they do not turn out to be statistically significant.
(112)   Third, the Notifying Parties assert that using the load factor as a proxy for demand
        introduces endogeneity issues because the load factor is influenced not only by
       demand but also by the prices that Lufthansa charges, and this interplay between
       demand and prices can result in biased estimates. The Commission acknowledges
         that the load factor is an imperfect proxy for demand. However, the Commission
        notes that even if endogeneity were present due to a demand-side shock, it tends to
         attenuate the coefficients towards zero. As a result, the true effect of competition on
         prices is possibly even higher than what estimated by the Commission.
5.3.    Robustness of long haul results regarding the COVID Period
5.3.1.   The Notifying Parties’ view
(113)   The Notifying Parties highlight  that the COVID pandemic led to fundamental
        changes  in the  airline industry, making  it impossible  to use a pooled dataset
       combining both pre- and post-COVID periods.
(114)   Moreover, the Parties underline that the definition of the COVID period used by the
       Commission, namely from January 2019 to June 2020, is not the correct one to use in
          their opinion. In Section 4.2.2 of their response to the SO, the Notifying Parties argue
         that a more appropriate definition of the COVID period would start in March 2020
       and end either in August 2021 or March 2022.
(115)   The Notifying Parties also point out that changing the definition of the COVID
        period affects the statistical significance of the economic analysis.
5.3.2.   The Commission’s view
(116)   The Commission disagrees with the Notifying Parties' statements for the following
         reasons.


                                     42

[PÁGINA PDF 566]
(117)    First, the Commission’s definition for the COVID period is based on Lufthansa’s
      own internal document and aligns with Lufthansa’s own internal analysis. The
        Notifying  Parties’ arguments  are  therefore  inconsistent with  Lufthansa’s own
        methodological choices.
(118)   Second, the Notifying Parties’ alternative definitions for the COVID period exclude
      many months where Lufthansa itself was actually active. If Lufthansa was active in
         these months, then excluding these months from the analysis overlooks interactions
         that are relevant to understand the competitive interactions between carriers.
(119)   Third, the Commission would also like to point out that a number of competitors did
          start to enter North American routes in July 2021. Such post-Covid entry events are
         certainly meaningful to inform about competitive dynamics. It is thus incorrect to
       expand the COVID period beyond June 2021.
5.4.     Insufficient variation in the sample
5.4.1.   The Notifying Parties’ view
(120)   In Section 3.1.2 of their response to the SO, the Notifying Parties argue that the
       number of entry/exit events of competitors, and especially of ITA, is insufficient to
        conduct a robust fixed effects analysis, which is the econometric approach chosen by
         the Commission.
(121)   This view is restated in the Notifying Parties’ response to the Letter of Facts, in
         relation to the long haul analysis, where the Parties underline the very low number of
        observations where there is no or only one indirect competitor.
5.4.2.   The Commission’s view
(122)   The Commission disagrees with the Parties’ claim that the number of entry/exit
        events is insufficient.
(123)    First, as stated by the Parties themselves in Paragraph 30 of their response, “there is
       no clear-cut threshold for the necessary number of entry-exit events to conduct a
         reliable analysis”, and actually, from a mathematical and statistical point of view, a
         single entry-exit event is sufficient to conduct this type of analyses.
(124)   Second, the number of entry/exit events of ITA is significantly higher than what
        claimed by the Notifying Parties. When routes operated by EuroWings are also
         included, as indicated in Table 3 and footnote 23: 22 and not two. Furthermore, as
        can be seen in specification 5 of Table 7, Table 8, Table 12 and Table 13, the results
        appear fairly robust to the inclusion and exclusion of entry-exit events on routes
        operated by EuroWings.
(125)   Third, regarding the number of observations with no or one indirect competitor in
        long haul that the Parties consider as insufficient, the Commission notes that the
         results are statistically significant. Such statistical significance also implies that the
       number of entry-exit events is inherently sufficient.
5.5.     Implausibility of the Commission’s results
5.5.1.   The Notifying Parties view
(126)   Regarding the short haul analysis, the Notifying Parties state that the Commission’s
         results are inconsistent and implausible. Most notably, they argue that, in the SO
       Annex Section 3.1, the Transaction is stated to have a statistically not significant
         effect on prices on ‘3 to 2’ routes whereas it is stated in the SO Annex Section 3.2.
         that the Transaction would have a sizeable and statistically highly significant price


                                     43

[PÁGINA PDF 567]
         effect on ‘3 to 2’ routes. In the Parties’ views, this is implausible as “There is no
        reason to assume ITA should be so different from other network carriers (such as Air
        France, KLM or LOT) or carriers operating routes point-to-point (“P2P”)”.
(127)   Regarding the long-haul analysis, the Notifying Parties underline that the main result
        of  the Commission  is  implausible, as  the  first competitor has a smaller and
          statistically weak significant effect on prices, whereas the second competitor has a
        twice as strong ([10-20]%) and highly significant effect. Such results are, for the
          Parties, at odds with economic theory suggesting differences in prices should be
         larger between a monopoly and a duopoly.
5.5.2.   The Commission’s view
(128)   The Commission disagrees with the Notifying Parties’ statements.
(129)    First, regarding the short haul analysis, the Commission disagrees that there is any
         implausibility in  its results. Indeed, such results simply stem from closeness of
        competition between ITA and Lufthansa, and from the fact that rivalry between the
         parties has been an important source of competition on the market.49 The impact is
        bigger and statistically significant when looking specifically at ITA because it is such
        a close competitor of Lufthansa.
(130)   Second, regarding the long-haul analysis, the Commission notes that only the FRA-
     NYC route offers sufficient data variation helpful to assess the impact on Lufthansa’s
         prices when a single competitor enters the market. As a result, this limited data
         variation explains the smaller price effect observed with the entry of the  first
        competitor. Conversely, numerous other  routes  exhibit  significantly more data
         variation helpful to identify the effect on Lufthansa’s prices associated to entry of
       more than one competitor. This greater variation in the data results in more robust
       and reliable statistical effects for the 3-to-2 competitor scenario.





49       Horizontal Merger Guidelines, paragraph 2

Minima: has the meaning described in Section B.

Monitoring Trustee: one or more natural or legal person(s) who is/are approved

the Decision.

Operational Risks:  risks  outside  the Short-Haul Remedy Taker’s  area  of
influence, such as global pandemics, labor actions, volcanic eruptions, acts of war
and/or  riots, cyber-attacks  at  airline or service partners, withdrawal of any
relevant regulatory approval, whereas this list is not exhaustive.

Parties: the Notifying Parties and ITA.

Proposed Transaction: The concentration notified in Case COMP/M.11071,
namely the proposed acquisition by DLH of a 41% stake with  additional
governance rights over ITA from MEF within the meaning of Article 3(1)(b) of
Council Regulation (EC) No. 139/2004.

Commitments.

I.   Short-Haul, LIN and Long-Haul Commitments

    1.  In order to maintain effective competition, DLH and MEF commit to procure
       the entry and the launch of operations by the Short-Haul Remedy Taker on all
       ten  (10) Remedy Short-Haul Routes by  transferring  to  the Short-Haul
     Remedy Taker all the necessary Slots and providing other necessary elements
         (if any), to be defined based on the Short-Haul Remedy Taker’s needs (“New
      Entrant Remedy”).

    2. The corresponding commitments of the Short-Haul Remedy Taker under the
      Commitments are set out in the Entry Commitment Agreement.2 The Entry
      Commitment Agreement in particular provides for the commitment by the
       Short-Haul Remedy Taker to enter on the Remedy Short-Haul Routes and
       operate at least the minimum Frequencies provided under clause 14 on these
       routes during  the Minimum  Period, including  the provision of  suitable
       enforcement  steps  against  the  Short-Haul  Remedy  Taker  to  ensure
      compliance with the Entry Commitment Agreement.

   3. DLH and MEF commit to ensure the enforcement of the commitments of the
       Short-Haul Remedy Taker under  the Entry Commitment Agreement  to
       continue  to  operate  at  least  the minimum Frequencies provided under
       clause 14 on all Remedy Short-Haul Routes during the Minimum Period.

    4.  Furthermore, DLH and MEF commit to divest the LIN Total Slots. These
       Slots will be divested by

               i.   a transfer of the Slots to the Short-Haul Remedy Taker to take up the

       Short-Haul Remedy Taker in […].

SPA

    27. DLH and MEF commit to enter into an agreement, which will take at the
       option of the Short-Haul Remedy Taker the form of either a Special Prorate
      Agreement  (“SPA”)  or  of  an  agreement  of  similar  kind,  to  enable



                                 16

[PÁGINA PDF 584]
       connectivity in relation to ITA’s domestic network, including all Remedy
       Short-Haul  Direct/Indirect  Routes,6  in  order  to connect  the Short-Haul

       during a period of five (5) years from the entry of the Short-Haul Remedy
      Taker in […], subject to the approval of the SPA by the Commission,
        respectively. For the avoidance of doubt, all provisions applicable to the SPA
        in the Commitments are  also, to the extent possible, applicable to any
       agreement(s) of similar kind which are entered into based on the requirements
       of the Short-Haul Remedy Taker.

    28. The commercial terms of the SPA shall reflect the conditions of similar
       agreements for the domestic network of ITA, i.e., the better of
         a.  a SPA agreement ITA and DLH would agree on in a post-closing scenario
          with the guarantee that the agreement with the Short-Haul Remedy Taker
            shall be equal to or better than any SPA between ITA and DLH during a
          period of five (5) years from the entry of the Short-Haul Remedy Taker in
         […], subject to the approval of the SPA with the Short-Haul Remedy
          Taker by the Commission, enabling the Short-Haul Remedy Taker to
           benefit (during  this five-year period) from any changes of any SPA
         between ITA and DLH to its advantage, or
        b.  a comparable SPA agreement ITA has in place or enters into with its
           alliance partners during the period of five (5) years from the entry of the
          Short-Haul Remedy Taker in […], subject to the approval of the SPA with
           the Short-Haul Remedy Taker by the Commission.

      The Parties will provide the Monitoring Trustee with the agreements referred
        to in a. and b. to assess the Parties’ compliance with this commitment. In case
       the Short-Haul Remedy Taker is technically not in a position to implement
       such an SPA, the Parties and the Short-Haul Remedy Taker shall procure an
       equivalent solution with commercial terms that replicate the above as closely
       as possible.

    29. As a reference, such SPA offered to potential remedy takers shall be based for
       published through fares on a so called Straight-Rate-Proration (“SRP”) with
     minimum prorates to be paid by the marketing carrier to the operating carrier
      („Minima“). This implies that the prorate to be paid for the feeder route is
       determined by the price for the complete itinerary, set by the remedy taker. It
        shall offer access to all of ITA’s operating Reservation Booking Designators
      (“RBD”) as to be agreed on between ITA and the Short-Haul Remedy Taker.
      The settlement shall be based on SRP with four (4) different Minima based on

III. Long-Haul Commitments

    31. DLH and MEF commit to enter into Long-Haul Remedy Agreement(s) with
       the Long-Haul Remedy Taker(s), within […] from the Effective Date and for
       a duration of three (3) years (starting with the beginning of the season
       following the approval of the agreement by the Commission) which will take
       the form of either:

         i.   agreements with Long-Haul Remedy Taker(s) in order to establish a

        Remedy Taker(s) to operate their own (existing or new) operations on the
         Long-Haul Remedy Routes, in order to establish a frequency increase of
            at least ten (10) weekly Competitive Indirect Connections (as an average
          value per season), offered across two (2) Long-Haul Remedy Takers, out
           of which one Long-Haul Remedy Taker shall rely on its own operations

          be at least three (3) weekly additional Competitive Indirect Connections,

            Indirect Connections (ii.) on the Long-Haul Remedy Routes, as set out in
          Schedule 1.

Section C.    The Remedy Taker Criteria

I.     Short Haul Remedy Taker Criteria

    34. In order to be approved by the Commission, the Short-Haul Remedy Taker
      must fulfil the following criteria:

            a.  The  Short-Haul  Remedy  Taker  shall  be  independent  of  and
            unconnected to the Notifying Parties and their Affiliated Undertakings
                (this being assessed having regard  to the  situation following the
               divestiture).

           b. The Short-Haul Remedy Taker shall have the financial resources,
            proven expertise and incentive to act as a viable and active competitive
              force in competition with the Parties and other competitors on the
          Remedy Short-Haul Routes and the Remedy Short-Haul Direct/Indirect
            Routes as described in clause 6, it being understood that in the latter
             case the domestic leg of the Remedy Short-Haul Direct/Indirect Routes
               will be enabled through own connecting flights of the Short-Haul
          Remedy Taker or an SPA or an agreement of similar kind with ITA.

            c.  The operations on the Remedy Short-Haul Routes and the offer on the
          Remedy Short-Haul Direct/Indirect Routes by the Short-Haul Remedy
            Taker must neither be likely to create, in light of the information
              available to the Commission, prima facie competition concerns nor
             give rise to a risk that the implementation of the Commitments will be
              delayed. In particular, the Short-Haul Remedy Taker must reasonably
            be expected  to  obtain  all necessary approvals from  the  relevant
              regulatory authorities for the operations on the Remedy Short-Haul
            Routes and the Remedy Short-Haul Direct/Indirect Routes. It shall be
             understood  that  the  domestic  leg  of  the  Remedy  Short-Haul
              Direct/Indirect Routes will be enabled through own connecting flights
              of the Short-Haul Remedy Taker or an SPA or an agreement of similar
             kind with ITA.

    35. The final binding agreement (as well as ancillary agreements) relating to the
      Agreements shall be conditional on the Commission’s approval. When the
        Parties have reached an agreement with a Short-Haul Remedy Taker, they
        shall submit a fully documented and reasoned proposal, including a copy of
       the  final  agreement(s),  within one week  to  the Commission and  the
       Monitoring  Trustee. The  Parties must be  able  to  demonstrate  to  the
      Commission  that  the  Short-Haul Remedy Taker  fulfils  the  Short-Haul
     Remedy Taker  Criteria and  that  the Entry Commitment Agreement  is
       consistent with the Commission's Decision and the Commitments. For the
       approval, the Commission shall verify that the Short-Haul Remedy Taker

                                 20

[PÁGINA PDF 588]
         fulfils the Short-Haul Remedy Taker Criteria and that the Agreements are
       consistent with the Commitments including their objective to bring about a
        lasting structural change in the market.

II.    Long-Haul Remedy Taker Criteria
    36. In order to be approved by the Commission, the Long-Haul Remedy Taker
      must fulfil the following criteria:

            a.  The  Long-Haul  Remedy  Taker  shall  be  independent  of  and
            unconnected to the Notifying Parties, their Affiliated Undertakings and
              the A++ JV Partners.

           b. The Long-Haul Remedy Taker  shall have the financial resources,
            proven expertise and incentive to act as a viable and active competitive
              force in competition with the Parties, the A++ JV Partners and other
             competitors on the Long-Haul Remedy Routes.

            c.  The operations on the Long-Haul Remedy Routes by the Long-Haul
          Remedy Taker must not be likely to create, in light of the information
              available to the Commission, prima facie competition concerns. In
               addition, the Long-Haul Remedy Taker must reasonably be expected to
              obtain all necessary approvals from the relevant regulatory authorities
               for the operations on the Long-Haul Remedy Routes.

    37. The final binding agreement (as well as ancillary agreements) relating to the
      Long-Haul Remedy Agreement(s) shall be conditional on the Commission’s
       approval. When the Parties have reached an agreement with a Long-Haul
     Remedy Taker, they shall submit a fully documented and reasoned proposal,
       including  a copy  of  the  final  agreement(s),  within one week  to  the
      Commission and  the Monitoring  Trustee. The  Parties must be  able  to
       demonstrate to the Commission that the Long-Haul Remedy Taker fulfils the
      Long-Haul Remedy  Taker  Criteria  and  that  the  Long-Haul Remedy
      Agreement   is  consistent  with  the  Commission's  Decision  and  the
      Commitments. For the approval, the Commission shall verify that the Long-
      Haul Remedy Taker fulfils the Long-Haul Remedy Taker Criteria and that the
      Long-Haul Remedy Agreement(s) are  consistent with  the Commitments
       including their objective to bring about a lasting structural change in the
       market.

[PÁGINA PDF 589]
Section D. Trustee

         I.      Appointment procedure

    38. The Parties shall appoint a Monitoring Trustee to carry out the functions
       specified in these Commitments for a Monitoring Trustee. The Parties commit
       not to close the Concentration before the appointment of a Monitoring
       Trustee.

    39. The Monitoring Trustee shall:

           a.  at the time of appointment, be independent of the Notifying Parties and
                 its Affiliated Undertakings;
          b.  possess  the necessary  qualifications  to carry out  its mandate,  for
           example have sufficient relevant experience as an investment banker or
             consultant or auditor; and
           c.  neither have nor become exposed to a Conflict of Interest.

    40. The Monitoring Trustee shall be remunerated by the Notifying Parties in a
     way that does not impede the independent and effective fulfilment of  its
       mandate.

             Proposal by the Parties

    41. No later than two weeks after the Effective Date, the Parties shall submit the
     name or names of one or more natural or legal persons whom the Parties
       propose to appoint as the Monitoring Trustee to the Commission for approval.
      The proposal shall contain sufficient information for the Commission to
       verify that the person or persons proposed as Monitoring Trustee fulfil the
       requirements set out in clause 39 and shall include:

           a.  the  full terms  of  the proposed mandate, which  shall  include  all
             provisions necessary to enable the Monitoring Trustee to fulfil its duties
            under these Commitments;
          b.  the outline of a work plan which describes how the Monitoring Trustee
             intends to carry out its assigned tasks.

             Approval or rejection by the Commission

    42. The Commission shall have the discretion to approve or reject the proposed
       Monitoring Trustee(s) and to approve the proposed mandate subject to any
       modifications  it deems necessary for the Monitoring Trustee to  fulfil  its
        obligations. If only one name is approved, the Parties shall appoint or cause to
      be appointed the person or persons concerned as Monitoring Trustee, in
       accordance with the mandate approved by the Commission. If more than one

                                 22

[PÁGINA PDF 590]
   name is approved, the Parties shall be free to choose the Monitoring Trustee
    to be appointed from among the names approved. The Monitoring Trustee
    shall be appointed within one week of  the Commission’s approval,  in
   accordance with the mandate approved by the Commission.

        New proposal by the Parties

43. If all the proposed Monitoring Trustees are rejected, the Parties shall submit
    the names of at least two more natural or legal persons within one week of
   being informed of the rejection, in accordance with clauses 38 and 42 of these
   Commitments.


           Monitoring Trustee nominated by the Commission

44. If all further proposed Monitoring Trustees are rejected by the Commission,
    the Commission shall nominate a Monitoring Trustee, whom the Parties shall
    appoint, or cause to be appointed, in accordance with a trustee mandate
   approved by the Commission.


   II.       Functions of the Monitoring Trustee

45. The Monitoring Trustee shall assume its specified duties and obligations in
    order to ensure compliance with the Commitments. The Commission may, on
     its own initiative or at the request of the Monitoring Trustee or the Parties,
   give any orders or instructions to the Monitoring Trustee in order to ensure
   compliance with the conditions and obligations attached to the Decision.

           Duties and obligations of the Monitoring Trustee

46. The Monitoring Trustee shall:

         a.  propose in its first report to the Commission a detailed work plan
       describing how  it intends to monitor compliance with the obligations
      and conditions attached to the Decision.

         b.  monitor the performance of the Commitments by the Parties.

         c.  inform the Parties promptly about any request or notification by the
       Short-Haul Remedy Taker.

         d.  propose  to the  Parties such measures as the Monitoring Trustee
       considers necessary to ensure the Parties’ compliance with the conditions
      and obligations attached to the Decision.


                              23

[PÁGINA PDF 591]
                e.  review and assess the agreements and the requests for extension of
           agreements submitted by the Parties for approval by the Monitoring
             Trustee, in consultation with the Commission.

                   f.  advise and make a written recommendation to the Commission as to
            the fulfilment of the Completion condition under clause 13.

               g.  review and assess the progress of the procurement of the entry by the
           Short-Haul Remedy Taker and verify that, dependent on the stage of the
             process, the Short-Haul Remedy Taker receives sufficient and correct
            information relating to the Remedy Short-Haul Routes.

               h.  review and assess the progress of the transfer/release of the LIN Slots.

                     i.  review and assess the progress of entering into the SPA;

                     j.  review and assess the progress of the Long-Haul Remedy;

               k.  provide to the Commission, sending the Parties a non-confidential
          copy at the same time, a written report within 15 days after the end of
           every month that shall cover (i) the operation and management of the
         Remedy Short-Haul Routes as well as the facilitation of entry so that the
          Commission can assess the progress of the process until the moment of
            entry on all Remedy Short-Haul Routes by the Short-Haul Remedy Taker,
          whereby after the moment of entry on all Remedy Short-Haul Routes, the
           Monitoring Trustee shall provide its reports on a IATA seasonal instead
            of a monthly basis, and (ii) the development of the Parties’ activities on
            the Long-Haul  Remedy Routes based on  certain Key Performance
             Indicators (e.g., number of seats offered, market shares incl. indirect), in a
          manner consistent with the Commitments.

                     l.  promptly report in writing to the Commission, sending the Parties a
            non-confidential copy at the same time,  if  it concludes on reasonable
           grounds that the Parties are failing to comply with these Commitments.

           m. assume the other functions assigned to the Monitoring Trustee under
            the conditions and obligations attached to the Decision.

III.         Duties and obligations of the Parties

        47. The Parties shall provide and shall cause their advisors to provide the
           Monitoring  Trustee  with   all  such  co-operation,  assistance  and
            information  as  the  Monitoring  Trustee may  reasonably  require  to
           perform its tasks. The Monitoring Trustee shall have full and complete
            access to any of their books, records, documents, management or other


                                   24

[PÁGINA PDF 592]
    personnel,  facilities,  sites and  technical  information  necessary  for
    fulfilling its duties under the Commitments and the Parties shall provide
    the Monitoring Trustee upon request with copies of any document. The
    Parties shall make available to the Monitoring Trustee one or more
    offices on their premises and shall be available for meetings in order to
   provide the Monitoring Trustee with all information necessary for the
   performance of its tasks.

48. The Parties shall indemnify the Monitoring Trustee and its employees and
    agents (each an “Indemnified Party”) and hold each Indemnified Party
   harmless against, and hereby agrees that an Indemnified Party shall have
   no liability to the Parties for, any liabilities arising out of the performance
    of the Monitoring Trustee’s duties under the Commitments, except to the
    extent that such liabilities result from the willful default, recklessness,
    gross negligence or bad faith of the Monitoring Trustee, its employees,
    agents or advisors.

49. At the expense of the  Parties, the Monitoring Trustee may appoint
    advisors (in particular for corporate finance or legal advice), subject to
    the Parties’ approval (this approval not to be unreasonably withheld or
   delayed)  if the Monitoring Trustee considers the appointment of such
    advisors necessary or appropriate for the performance of its duties and
    obligations under the Mandate, provided that any fees and other expenses
    incurred by the Monitoring Trustee are reasonable. Should the Parties
    refuse to approve the advisors proposed by the Monitoring Trustee the
   Commission may approve the appointment of such advisors instead, after
   having heard the Parties. Only the Monitoring Trustee shall be entitled to
    issue instructions to the advisors. clause 48 of these Commitments shall
   apply mutatis mutandis.

50. The  Parties  agree  that  the  Commission may  share  Confidential
   Information proprietary to the Parties with the Monitoring Trustee. The
   Monitoring Trustee shall not disclose such information and the principles
   contained in Article 17 (1) and (2) of the Merger Regulation apply mutatis
   mutandis.

51. The Notifying Parties agree that the contact details of the Monitoring
   Trustee are published on the website of the Commission's Directorate-
   General for Competition and they shall inform interested third parties of
    the identity and the tasks of the Monitoring Trustee.

52. For a period of 10 years from the Effective Date the Commission may
    request all information from the Parties that is reasonably necessary to
   monitor the effective implementation of these Commitments.



                           25

[PÁGINA PDF 593]
IV.        Replacement, discharge and reappointment of the Monitoring Trustee

         53. If the Monitoring Trustee ceases to perform  its functions under the
          Commitments or for any other good cause, including the exposure of the
           Monitoring Trustee to a Conflict of Interest:

                       a.  the Commission may, after hearing the Monitoring Trustee and
                 DLH, require the Parties to replace the Monitoring Trustee; or
                     b.  the Parties may, with the prior approval of the Commission,
                       replace the Monitoring Trustee.

         54. If the Monitoring Trustee is removed according to clause 53 of these
          Commitments, the Monitoring Trustee may be required to continue in its
            function  until a new Monitoring Trustee  is  in  place  to whom  the
           Monitoring  Trustee  has  effected  a  full hand  over  of  all  relevant
            information.  The new  Monitoring  Trustee  shall  be  appointed  in
           accordance with the procedure referred to in clause 38 et seq of these
          Commitments.

         55. Unless removed according  to clause 53 of these Commitments, the
           Monitoring Trustee shall cease to act as Monitoring Trustee only after the
          Commission has discharged it from its duties after all the Commitments
           with which  the  Monitoring  Trustee  has been  entrusted have been
           implemented. However, the Commission may at any time require the
           reappointment of the Monitoring Trustee if it subsequently appears that
            the  relevant  remedies  might  not  have  been  fully  and  properly
           implemented.

 Section F.    The review clause

     56. The Commission may at its discretion extend the time periods foreseen in the
       Commitments in response to a request from the Parties or, in appropriate
         cases, on its own initiative. Where the Parties request an extension of a time
         period, they shall submit a reasoned request to the Commission no later than
       one month before the expiry of that period, showing good cause. This request
         shall be accompanied by a report from the Monitoring Trustee, who shall, at
         the same time send a non-confidential copy of the report to the Parties. Only
         in exceptional circumstances  shall the  Parties be  entitled  to request an
        extension within the last month of any period.

     57. The Commission may further, in response to a reasoned request from the
         Parties showing good cause waive, modify or  substitute, in exceptional
        circumstances, one or more of the undertakings in these Commitments. This
         request shall be accompanied by a report from the Monitoring Trustee, who
          shall, at the same time send a non-confidential copy of the report to the
          Parties. The request shall not have the effect of suspending the application of


                                   26

[PÁGINA PDF 594]
       the undertaking and, in particular, of suspending the expiry of any time period
        in which the undertaking has to be complied with.

Section G.    Sunset clause

       58. In the event that the Proposed Transaction lapses, these Commitments
            shall lapse.

Section H.    Entry into force

       59. The Commitments shall take effect upon the date of adoption of the
          Decision.
